title: Japan records its first ‘cruelly hot day’ as cities swelter in 40-degree heat
summary:
In April Japan coined new term kokushobi for days above 40C as country advises workers to wear shorts to the office to cope with stifling heat

Japan logged its first official kokushobi or “cruelly hot day” on Tuesday since the new term for when temperatures top 40 degrees Celsius was introduced in April. The Japan Meteorological Agency coined the new designation to warn the public of the heat dangers of days that were once freak weather events but have now become more common.

The central Japan cities of Gujo and Tajimi in Gifu prefecture, along with Toyota in Aichi prefecture, all hit 40C. Gujo’s 40C and Toyota’s 40.1C were all-time highs recorded at their respective weather stations.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Japan logged its first official kokushobi or “cruelly hot day” on Tuesday since the new term for when temperatures top 40 degrees Celsius was introduced in April. The Japan Meteorological Agency coined the new designation to warn the public of the heat dangers of days that were once freak weather events but have now become more common.
The central Japan cities of Gujo and Tajimi in Gifu prefecture, along with Toyota in Aichi prefecture, all hit 40C. Gujo’s 40C and Toyota’s 40.1C were all-time highs recorded at their respective weather stations.
Across 914 weather stations nationwide, 278 registered temperatures exceeding 35C or moshobi – “extremely hot days,” the highest level of warning until the recent introduction of the new terminology. Days over 25C are called natsubi or “summer days”, while those exceeding 30C are known as manatsubi – “true summer days.”
On Monday, a man in his 40s was found dead on a street in Sanjo, Niigata prefecture, while another in his 70s died in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo. Both are believed to have succumbed to the heat.
Heatstroke deaths topped 2,000 for the first time in 2024, while more than 100,000 people were taken to hospital last year between the beginning of May and late September, according to the fire and disaster management agency.
The rising heat is affecting many aspects of Japanese life – including yields and the quality of rice, a staple. In response, farmers are planting more heat-tolerant varieties, while some are switching to crops such as avocado that have not traditionally been grown at scale in Japan.
Impacts are also being seen in sport, with the most high-profile being the restructuring of the hugely popular koshien national high school baseball tournament. Played in the sweltering heat of August, the games have been split into morning and evening sessions since 2024 to reduce the chances of heatstroke for both players and spectators.
Meanwhile, office workers are being encouraged to wear shorts on hot summer days, the latest relaxing of Japan’s buttoned-down corporate culture as part of “Cool Biz” measures to reduce electricity consumption through lower use of airconditioning. Previous initiatives have encouraged “salarymen” to shed jackets and ties, and wear short-sleeved shirts but this year’s expected scorching summer has prompted calls for another level of casualness.
Tokyo governor Yuriko Koike announced the new clothing recommendations for office wear which also include polo shirts, T-shirts and trainers where appropriate, against the backdrop of expected high temperatures and a “challenging outlook for electricity supply”.
A study by the National Institute for Environmental Studies (NIES) and Tokyo’s Waseda University in 2025 found that without drastic cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, school sports will become unplayable outdoors by the 2060s.
Average summer temperatures in Japan have risen about 1.3C over the past 100 years, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). Both 2023 and 2024 were the hottest years since records began in 1898, but last year saw those levels surpassed again. The summer of 2025 was 2.4C above the average of the previous three decades, with 132 weather stations logging their highest ever average heat and a new all-time Japanese high of 41.8C at Isesaki, Gunma, north of Tokyo, on 5 August.

title: People with secret ‘safe phones’ advised to turn off devices during national test of AusAlert emergency warning
summary:
Ten-second ‘siren’ to blare on most phones on Monday as part of national test despite reservations from some states

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An unsilenceable siren will blare out of most phones in Australia on Monday afternoon for 10 seconds, with the federal government confirming a national test of the new AusAlert emergency alert system will go ahead, despite reservations from some state governments.

Domestic violence campaigners and the National Emergency Management Agency have also repeated advice that people who may have secret “safe phones”, kept hidden for personal safety reasons, may want to turn off their devices for up to 24 hours after the test scheduled for 2pm (AEST) on Monday.

iPhones 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later;

Apple Watch SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later;

Android devices running Android 12 or later.

Continue reading...
full_text:
An unsilenceable siren will blare out of most phones in Australia on Monday afternoon for 10 seconds, with the federal government confirming a national test of the new AusAlert emergency alert system will go ahead, despite reservations from some state governments.
Domestic violence campaigners and the National Emergency Management Agency have also repeated advice that people who may have secret “safe phones”, kept hidden for personal safety reasons, may want to turn off their devices for up to 24 hours after the test scheduled for 2pm (AEST) on Monday.
AusAlert, built after recommendations from the royal commission into the black summer bushfires for a better national warning system, is slated to come into effect from October.
Most phones and some smartwatches and tablets will emit a loud siren for 10 seconds, and receive a test alert notification pop-up. The federal government says AusAlert is an improvement on current SMS-based alerts, which can be less reliable in disasters.
But ahead of an emergency services ministers’ meeting on Wednesday, concerns emerged from several states, including Queensland and Western Australia, that AusAlert warnings would not reach landline phones, older devices or those connected to satellite signals.
The federal emergency management minister, Kristy McBain, said AusAlert was working to add voice alerts to reach landlines, and that the existing Emergency Alert system would continue running for this year while that capability was added. Federal government sources said they were confident that would be confirmed soon.
Sources also said they were listening to concerns from state governments, and were comfortable with progress on AusAlert, but that states would not be forced to use the new system and could still use current Emergency Alerts.
“It’s one of the reasons those two systems will run alongside each other for this high-risk weather season,” McBain said.
McBain called AusAlert “more capable” and “far superior” technology.
“The 2020 bushfire royal commission into national natural disaster arrangements highlighted the fact that we don’t have a system that is capable of resilience currently, that it has its failings and that we do need to move towards a nationally consistent alert system so that people know what to expect,” she said.
Some older phones may not receive the alert on Monday. Nema said the alert will go to:
- 
  iPhones 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later; 
- 
  Apple Watch SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later; 
- 
  Android devices running Android 12 or later. 
Older Androids, or those not using iOS or Android, “might still receive AusAlerts”, Nema said, but Apple iPads will not.
The blaring alarm has raised concerns about the risk of exposing “safe phones”, or devices kept hidden for safety reasons by those experiencing violence. The alert will sound even if phones are on silent or do not disturb mode.
Nema said the agency had engaged with family violence experts about the test, including assisting advocates to disseminate safety information, and posting a safety guide on its website.
Nema’s interim coordinator general, Pat Hetherington said phones switched off or on aeroplane mode would not receive the alert.
“The message for safe phones and hidden phones is very much [to switch off for] a 24 hour period.”
Groups such as the Women’s Safety Commissioner, DV Connect and the Council of Single Mothers and their Children have issued safety advisories to this effect.
“We know that many people who are living with domestic and family violence and sexual violence have a hidden phone as part of their safety plan,” the CEO of women’s services network Wesnet, Karen Bentley, said.
“Wesnet’s recommendation is that on Monday, if you do have a concealed or hidden phone to support your safety, that you consider turning that device off or switching it into aeroplane mode one hour before the national test on Monday and to keep it off or in aeroplane mode for 24 hours.”
Queensland’s minister for emergency services, Daniel Purdie, said on Wednesday AusAlert was “potentially life-saving technology” and his state supported it, but voiced some reservations. 
 “We need to make sure Queenslanders aren’t put at risk and there are concerns around the gaps as we look to transition from the Emergency Alert system … Queensland is the most disaster-prone state and we’ve got a lot of people in regional communities that rely on those landlines,” he said.
NSW’s emergency services minister, Jihad Dib, said the system may need “further improvements” after the test and indicated states had “concerns”.
“We’re really happy to make sure that we continue working alongside the commonwealth to develop a system that’s going to be better than the current one that we have,” he said.

title: Brittany Higgins accuses Pauline Hanson of victim-blaming for calling domestic violence a ‘two-way street’
summary:
One Nation leader criticised by advocates after telling women being abused: ‘don’t put up with it’

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Pauline Hanson has described domestic violence as “wrong” but a “two-way street”, and that women being abused should not put up with it, drawing condemnation from advocates who have accused the One Nation leader of victim-blaming.

On Wednesday, Hanson told radio station 4BC domestic violence in Australia was a scourge but that society was under “so much pressure”, when asked to call out the issue.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Pauline Hanson has described domestic violence as “wrong” but a “two-way street”, and that women being abused should not put up with it, drawing condemnation from advocates who have accused the One Nation leader of victim-blaming.
On Wednesday, Hanson told radio station 4BC domestic violence in Australia was a scourge but that society was under “so much pressure”, when asked to call out the issue.
“It is wrong but it’s also a two-way street. I’m not saying that it’s just men, women can lose their cool as well. Society is under so much pressure … Everyone is under so much pressure and it’s really hard,” Hanson said.
“Domestic violence is a scourge but look … I’ve been through it myself in my life. And I just feel if you’re not in a house where you feel safe … then you shouldn’t put up with it. If these women are getting abused by men out there, then don’t put up with it.”
Tarang Chawla, an activist whose sister Nikita was murdered by her partner in a jealous rage in 2015, aged 23, said the responsibility should not be on the woman facing abuse.
“My sister Niki tried to do what Ms Hanson suggests. Terrible advice. He murdered her,” he said.
“It is not as simple as ‘don’t put up with it’. The responsibility isn’t on the victim. It’s on the person who is abusive or violent. Overwhelmingly, that person is a man.”
The minister for women and finance, Katy Gallagher, said the comments “are ill-informed and risk sending a dangerous message that lets perpetrators off the hook”.
“We should be backing victim-survivors and making it clear that the responsibility for violence lies with the person who chooses to use it,” Gallagher said.
The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said Hanson should focus on supporting survivors “rather than belittling them”.
“Senator Hanson has a voice and she is using it to send a message to victims that violence is their fault and to those that use violence that it’s excusable … saying women should leave completely misses the point. It’s the most dangerous time, it’s when they are more likely to face escalated or lethal violence.”
Hanson also faced criticism from Brittany Higgins, now executive director of the Vida Fund, who accused the One Nation leader of victim-blaming.
“‘Mutual abuse’, ‘two way street’, ‘just leave’ – normalising this victim blaming rhetoric in relation to domestic violence when 38 Australian women have already been lost to femicide is atrocious,” Higgins said in a social media post.
The Women’s and Girls’ Emergency Centre called the comments from Hanson “vile and shameful”.
The centre’s chief executive, Nicole Yade, said it did not reflect the fact that violence was gendered, with the majority of family violence perpetrated by men against women and children.
“Senator Pauline Hanson’s comments today are vile and shameful,” Yade said. “She is speaking from a position of privilege and complete misunderstanding that characterises practically every word that leaves her mouth.
“Having experience of domestic and family violence herself, Senator Hanson’s comments are deeply disappointing. Rather than offering empathy and understanding, they reflect a victim-blaming narrative that has no place in conversations about domestic and family violence.”
In 2019, Hanson secured a controversial inquiry into the family court system, which women’s groups warned could become a platform for men’s rights activists who believed the court system was biased against fathers.
At the time, she claimed women were fabricating family violence complaints to keep their children. The claim is a prominent grievance among men’s rights groups but has been widely discredited in multiple studies.
“There are people out there who are nothing but liars and who will use that in the court system,” she had told the ABC. “I am hearing too many cases where parents are using domestic violence to stop the other parent from seeing their children.”
In 2017, Hanson had told the Senate her sons had domestic violence claims made against them “that were not warranted” and said broadly “I feel for the men out there that are going through this, because it’s unjustified”.

title: Alleged rape victim ‘could have done a lot better’ if she had made up claims against well-connected Melbourne man, court told
summary:
Prosecutor tells court that ‘gaps or inconsistencies’ in the woman’s account ‘enhances her credibility’, but the defence maintains she is lying

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A woman who accused a well-connected Melbourne man of rape “could have done a much better job” if she was inventing the story for money, a Melbourne court has heard.

The man, who cannot be named, faces two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault, and has pleaded not guilty in Victoria’s county court.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A woman who accused a well-connected Melbourne man of rape “could have done a much better job” if she was inventing the story for money, a Melbourne court has heard.
The man, who cannot be named, faces two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault, and has pleaded not guilty in Victoria’s county court.
The alleged offences occurred in March 2023 after the woman – a former personal assistant for the accused – said she spent an evening drinking and taking cocaine with him, while listening to music and watching the football.
It’s alleged by the prosecution that the woman was at the man’s house when he tried to kiss her and sexually assaulted her. He then allegedly raped her twice, the trial previously heard.
The accused did not give evidence during the trial, and the alleged victim gave evidence before a closed court.
The man’s lawyer, Dermot Dann KC, has told the court the alleged offending never occurred.
In his final address to the jury, prosecutor Matthew Fisher said the case came down to six key aspects.
These included the evidence of the complainant; what happened immediately after the alleged incident, including that she was at the accused’s house when police arrived and was captured speaking to them on a body-worn camera; and her alleged motive to lie.
Fisher said trauma did “strange things” to memory, and accounts of sexual assault often differed. He said, however, that the complainant had not wavered in her description of what happened to her in accounts to her mother, police and a doctor in the 24 hours after the alleged incident.
He said the jury may also consider there is some “complexity” to her personality, given her demeanour while she gave evidence, though that did not mean she was lying about the allegations.
“I concede there were some gaps, some differences, some inconsistencies in her evidence, she was cross-examined for a number of hours about all of those things,” Fisher said.
“Mr Dann is a very experienced barrister, he is a very good barrister.
“Despite all of that cross-examination she remained adamant about the alleged offending: ‘This happened. This is what he did to me’.”
Fisher said these inconsistencies actually underlined the truthfulness of the alleged victim.
“If she really wanted to make all this up … she could have done a better job. Could have done a lot better,” he said.
“She would have been clear and consistent, from start to finish, if this was … part of this masterplan to get the accused in trouble, or get some money from him.
“The existence of some gaps or inconsistencies … enhances her credibility.”
Fisher said that the complainant’s interactions with other witnesses, including a former friend, and two friends of the accused who spent part of the evening before the alleged incident with them, were also a key aspect of the case.
Another aspect was the complainant’s relationship with police. The court heard on Tuesday from two police who were involved in pulling the complainant over for drink-driving in 2019.
The complainant accused one of the officers of saying to her “I love getting little sluts like you off the road” in a complaint she made to police in 2022.
On Tuesday, the officers both denied making the comment. This previous experience with police was referred to by the complainant on the night of the alleged rape as a reason she did not want to report the matter to the authorities, despite the urgings of her mother.
Fisher criticised the evidence of the senior officer, Det Sen Cons David Barlow, saying that he was “loose” and “untrue”, and that the jury could find he had made the comment to the complainant.
He said that while Dann had repeatedly accused the complainant of lying under oath, it was Barlow who the jury should find was untruthful.
“One of them is lying under oath,” Fisher said.
Dann described the allegation made by the complainant against police as false in his opening statement to the court.
The trial continues.

title: Rebel Wilson wins defamation case brought by co-star after bitter dispute
summary:
Judge finds Wilson did not defame Charlotte MacInnes, lead actor in Pitch Perfect star’s directorial debut The Deb

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

After a blistering dispute that spanned continents and years, Hollywood A-lister Rebel Wilson has been found not to have defamed her co-star in a series of social media posts.

The Pitch Perfect star was sued by Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film The Deb.

Continue reading...
full_text:
After a blistering dispute that spanned continents and years, Hollywood A-lister Rebel Wilson has been found not to have defamed her co-star in a series of social media posts.
The Pitch Perfect star was sued by Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film The Deb.
After the verdict on Wednesday, Wilson thanked the judge and the Australian legal system, saying the process had tested her and reinforced her belief in “standing up for what I believe is right, while continuing to create work that brings people joy”.
MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in a series of social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.
The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.
MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.
Two months after the conclusion of the hotly contested court battle in the federal court, justice Elizabeth Raper found in favour of Wilson.
“MacInnes has failed to establish that the publications have caused or were likely to cause serious harm,” she said on Wednesday.
MacInnes’ barrister, Sue Chrysanthou SC, accused Wilson of a “complete revision of history” littered with dishonesty during her emphatic closing address in May.
“She is a fantastical liar who has made up terrible, terrible allegations about multiple people and her own witnesses have discredited her,” she said.
“We say Ms Wilson cannot be believed on anything she has said.”
But Wilson repeatedly denied accusations she fabricated the complaint or raised it for leverage during disputes with her co-producers over the film’s budget and writing credit.
“I am known as a truth-teller,” she declared during the hearing.
That was what she had been doing when she posted the stories to her 11 million social media followers, the Bridesmaids star said. “I don’t classify it as an attack, I classify it as telling the truth,” she told the court.
Her barrister, Dauid Sibtain SC, said his client had “no motive to lie” about something that would endanger her film by driving a wedge between her lead actor and a producer.
Instead, he accused MacInnes of dishonestly withdrawing the complaint about Ghost to ensure her relationship with the producer continued to be fruitful.
MacInnes had received a lead role in a stage production and a six-figure record deal that were linked to Ghost, he argued, and she wanted to ensure she continued to rise.
“MacInnes is someone who gave false evidence under oath,” he said.
“[She] has suffered no harm, let alone serious harm.”
The young actor sought aggravated damages for the harm allegedly caused by the posts, including anxiety and a period without work.
In a social media post published after the verdict, Wilson said directing Australian music comedy The Deb was her “dream job”.
“[The Deb] was my dream job … my directorial debut, a celebration of Australian stories, and something I poured years of passion into alongside an incredible cast and crew. Seeing that journey disrupted has been incredibly difficult, but I have always believed it was a story worth telling.
“This process has taught me a lot. It has tested me, but it has also reinforced something I’ve always believed. I want to live my life standing up for what I believe is right, while continuing to create work that brings people joy.
“Thank you to everyone who has supported me. I’m grateful this chapter has reached its conclusion and I’m looking forward to getting back to what I love most, my family and my work. Thank you to the Judge and the Australian legal system who I have the utmost respect for”.

title: Meat multinational faces legal challenge over green credentials of $6bn global expansion plan
summary:
Greenpeace petitions Dutch courts to order JBS to disclose how its aims are compatible with responsibilities to climate and human rights

The world’s biggest meat company, JBS, faces a landmark legal challenge to disclose how its $6bn (£4.5bn) global expansion plan is compatible with responsibilities to the climate, nature and human rights.

Courts in the Netherlands, where JBS is headquartered, will assess the petition filed by Greenpeace for information on whether the company is compliant with Dutch laws on “duty of care” as well as its own publicly stated commitments.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The world’s biggest meat company, JBS, faces a landmark legal challenge to disclose how its $6bn (£4.5bn) global expansion plan is compatible with responsibilities to the climate, nature and human rights.
Courts in the Netherlands, where JBS is headquartered, will assess the petition filed by Greenpeace for information on whether the company is compliant with Dutch laws on “duty of care” as well as its own publicly stated commitments.
Lawyers said the case opened a new frontier in the fight against climate change, potentially creating a precedent for legal challenges against the agriculture sector, which is the biggest cause of deforestation and a major source of methane emissions.
“The primary objective is to challenge JBS’s business model and expansion model,” said Richard Brown, legal counsel at Greenpeace International. “We have a suspicion that they’re flying blind and not pulling together the information they need to understand the impacts.”
He said the request for information is a preliminary stage towards filing formal litigation against the multinational meat company.
Until now similar lawsuits have only been filed against fossil fuel companies. Last month, a Paris court ruled that the French oil company TotalEnergies must disclose the climate risks linked to emissions from its oil and gas products, and set out plans to address them in a case brought by NGOs and the city of Paris, but did not order specific measures such as limiting overseas exploration and production.
In the Netherlands, Shell is being challenged in The Hague by environmental groups Milieudefensie (Friends of the Earth Netherlands) and Friends of the Earth to reduce the company’s carbon dioxide output by 45% by 2030 in line with the Paris climate agreement. A final ruling is expected in early 2027.
At the centre of the petition against JBS is a perceived lack of transparency over its massive expansion plans in Nigeria. In the coming years, the meat company plans to invest $2.5bn in six giant meat-processing plants that are seen as a bridgehead to the fast-growing African market.
Civil society groups say there is scant information about whether JBS has assessed the social and environmental consequences of this plan, which would threaten smallholder farmers, domestic food security, land-use priorities, as well as locking in huge quantities of methane emissions. Methane is one of the most climate-destabilising greenhouse gases.
“This is the biggest agriculture investment that I have heard of in Nigeria’s history but there have been few details and no consultation for civil society,” said Elujulo Opeyemi, the spokesperson for Youth in Agroecology and Restoration Network.
“The information is not there. We want the Nigerian government to take a pause until we can make a concrete cost-benefit analysis. This investment will only be worthwhile if it is good for the people and planet. Otherwise it will just create more problems.”
To illustrate the risks, he said the Niger state government has already promised 1.2m hectares to JBS.
JBS, which was founded in Brazil in 1953, moved its headquarters to the Netherlands last year as part of its strategy to list on the New York Stock Exchange. The shift allowed the company to tap international financial markets for expansion funds, and to enable the founding family’s Batista brothers – Joesley and Wesley Batista – to significantly raise their ownership stake.
But the move to Europe also exposed the company to more rigorous transparency rules. “We say that if you come to the Netherlands, you have to play by Dutch rules and be held to account to Dutch standards,” said Brown. “Ultimately this is about a global conglomerate and how its activities should be limited within safe planetary boundaries.”
Behind the lawsuit is dismay at JBS’s environmental track record, particularly in its home country, Brazil, where it has repeatedly made sustainability commitments that it later abandoned or postponed.
Beef production is the primary driver of deforestation, as trees are cleared to raise cattle, and scientists warn this has pushed the Amazon close to a tipping point that would accelerate its shift from a carbon sink into a carbon emitter. JBS, which dominates the Brazilian cattle market, promised to address this with a commitment to clean up its beef supply chain in the region by the end of 2025. But the Guardian and its investigative partners revealed last year that JBS would break its promise. JBS then failed to meet its year-end deadline and has since scrapped its “net zero by 2040” pledge. Its latest sustainability report also excluded the calculations of indirect emissions, primarily methane, from cows – which are a primary component of JBS’s climate impact.
Marieke Vellekoop, the executive director at Greenpeace Netherlands, said that the NGO had been left with “no choice but to seek our right to information through the Dutch courts.”
Opeyemi said Nigeria needed transparency from JBS to ensure the full consequences of its planned investment can be calculated for the people, the environment and the wider region. “Once JBS has a foothold in Nigeria, they can encroach across Africa. That’s why the Nigerian government has to get this right,” he said. “This court case is helpful so we can get clarity.”
In an email to the Guardian, JBS said it “does not comment on potential legal proceedings of which it has not been notified”.

title: Wednesday briefing: How Trump’s Iran gamble has produced a crisis reshaping the global order
summary:
In today’s newsletter: ​A White House operating without expertise, strategy or restraint ​is stuck in a conflict with no easy way out, which is sending economic shockwaves far beyond its own borders

Good morning. Within two hours of entering No 10 on Monday afternoon, Andy Burnham had his first call with Donald Trump. After chit-chatting about the football (both agreed England had an “excellent tournament”) and Manchester (our new prime minister invited the president to visit the city Trump once described as a “town”), they got on to far trickier territory: the strait of Hormuz.

The US has attacked Iran for the eleventh consecutive night, hitting aircraft hangars and drone storage sites across the country. It came after Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US air bases and neighbouring Gulf states, which have accused it of deliberately targeting desalination plants that are essential to life in the region. Each side now claims it is preventing the other from gaining control over the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil was shipped before the war began. Vessels carrying crucial shipments of oil, gas and fertiliser remain at a standstill.

full_text:
Good morning. Within two hours of entering No 10 on Monday afternoon, Andy Burnham had his first call with Donald Trump. After chit-chatting about the football (both agreed England had an “excellent tournament”) and Manchester (our new prime minister invited the president to visit the city Trump once described as a “town”), they got on to far trickier territory: the strait of Hormuz.
The US has attacked Iran for the eleventh consecutive night, hitting aircraft hangars and drone storage sites across the country. It came after Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US air bases and neighbouring Gulf states, which have accused it of deliberately targeting desalination plants that are essential to life in the region. Each side now claims it is preventing the other from gaining control over the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil was shipped before the war began. Vessels carrying crucial shipments of oil, gas and fertiliser remain at a standstill.
“Operation Epic Fury” started with the aim of regime change. Since then, its objective has morphed into reopening the strait and undoing the damage caused by the US and Israel’s decision to start the war. The president drastically underestimated Iran’s capacity for enduring pain, and is now trying to bomb his way out of a conflict that he created. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to Vali Nasr, professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies and author of Iran’s Grand Strategy, about the war over the world’s most critical bottleneck. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK politics | Andy Burnham is under mounting pressure to explain how he will pay for his policy pledges as he implored his new cabinet to examine “all possible ways” to tackle the cost of living crisis. 
- 
  UK news | A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe. Joshua Kerry, 28, is accused of killing the former Conservative minister at her home in Haytor, Devon, by hitting her on the head with a hammer 21 times. 
- 
  Middle East | The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, told the Senate the US-Israel war on Iran had cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. 
- 
  Climate crisis | About 23 million people will be banned from using hosepipes by this weekend, as England and Wales moves closer to drought status. 
- 
  Ukraine | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has fired Ukraine’s commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and offered a “prominent position” to the defence minister he sacked last week in a move that sparked nationwide protests. 
In depth: ‘In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation’
“I’m not going to start wars,” Donald Trump told voters on election night in 2024. His decision to bomb Iran on 28 February in partnership with Benjamin Netanyahu was astonishing both in its aggression and its audacious break with this promise. Trump did nothing to prepare the US for war, gave seemingly no thought to the fact that Iran would inevitably hold the strait hostage if it came under attack, and resorted to contradictory explanations for his decision. In the war’s early days, he described “what we did in Venezuela” as a model for what he hoped to achieve. “He thought he would go down in history as the American president who had resolved the Iran problem,” Nasr told me. “In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation that would be quick and cost-free.”
That has proven a fatal miscalculation. Pete Hegseth, the US self-styled “secretary of war”, said the early US strikes that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, had “cut off the head of the snake.” But regime change is now a distant prospect. Trump underestimated the resilience of the Iranian regime and overestimated the power of protests against it. After just five months, his misadventure is as unpopular with American voters as the Vietnam war was six years in. It could yet escalate into a wider regional conflict, with the Houthis threatening a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia. Even Trump – whose private firm, The Trump Organization, is at work on a skyscraper in Dubai – won’t be insulated from the consequences of this violence.
What happened to the ceasefire?
The memorandum of understanding, a vague, short document that the US and Iran signed on 17 June, gave a brief respite from the strikes and (supposedly) initiated a 60-day negotiation period in which time both sides could reach permanent agreement on – among other things – the future of the strait. But it broke down when Iran fired on three commercial tankers that had used a shipping lane close to the shores of Oman, rather than a route off the Iranian coast approved by Tehran. “When ceasefires are violated, you have two options; either react to preserve the ceasefire, or use the violation as an excuse to end it,” Nasr says.
Trump went with the latter option, calling Iran’s leaders “scum” and declaring the ceasefire “over” earlier this month. This week, the US energy secretary Chris Wright said the US mission had shifted towards ensuring oil shipments could move through the strait. It’s worth remembering that the strait had never been closed for an extended period. Before 28 February, ships had been sailing through it without obstruction. The US is now framing the potential of a return to this old status quo as a victory.
Iran and the US are still negotiating, and Tehran has signalled its desire to permanently control the strait, including by charging tolls on passing vessels. “The US is now in a situation where it either has a long, protracted war, which would keep the strait closed, or keeps escalating to the next level with the hope of knocking Iran out,” Nasr says.
A serious misjudgment
There are signs that Trump and Netanyahu seriously misjudged the likelihood that Iran would seize control of the strait. In an interview earlier this year, Netanyahu admitted “the problem of the Hormuz strait became understood as the war went on.” As our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour wrote at the time, in a piece suggesting the consequences of Trump’s excursion could prove greater than the Vietnam war, this was an “astonishing admission.” The closure of the strait is the type of doomsday scenario that previous administrations, and most Iran experts, would have considered.
But the US government now has very few Iran experts, because Trump has instead chosen to surround himself with a royal court of loyalists. Nate Swanson, a former state department representative on Trump’s Iran negotiating team, was forced out earlier this year after far-right activist Laura Loomer accused him of disloyalty.
“Folks who’ve watched this Iranian system … would have told [Trump]: ‘They’re not businessmen from New York. They’re made of a different type of DNA’,” Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington DC, recently told Guardian US political correspondent, Robert Tait.
Consequences, consequences
Inflation caused by rising oil prices is making everyday life more expensive and hiking the costs of borrowing for governments (including Burnham’s here in the UK). If there is no agreement until 2027, some are predicting global growth could fall by 1.3%, if not more. Europe may be uniquely exposed: since the Russia-Ukraine war, the continent has turned towards the Middle East for its gas, particularly to Qatar, which has had to slow production during the conflict. We could be facing a winter of shortages, bringing to mind the 1970s oil crisis, when the British government enforced power cuts to conserve energy supplies.
Who’s in charge of the sea?
Many of Trump’s proposed solutions to the conflict seem to have been thought up on the spot. He briefly suggested that the US could charge tolls on ships entering the strait in exchange for safe passage, despite European leaders and even Marco Rubio, his own secretary of state, having pr

title: Iran’s foreign minister describes moment of attack that killed Khamenei
summary:
Abbas Araghchi says he has kept on the move since being pulled from rubble after strike on first day of war

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has described how he was pulled from the rubble of a leadership compound after the US-Israeli airstrike that killed the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the war, and has survived since by constantly moving around the capital, Tehran, by car.

In an interview with the Iranian journalist Javad Mogouyi, Araghchi confirmed Israel and the US had accurate intelligence on the location of Khamenei and other officials, enabling them to target Iran’s senior leadership.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has described how he was pulled from the rubble of a leadership compound after the US-Israeli airstrike that killed the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the war, and has survived since by constantly moving around the capital, Tehran, by car.
In an interview with the Iranian journalist Javad Mogouyi, Araghchi confirmed Israel and the US had accurate intelligence on the location of Khamenei and other officials, enabling them to target Iran’s senior leadership.
He said he had yet to meet the country’s new leader, Khamenei’s son Mojtaba, but said his appointment sent “a very important message to the world that there would be no change in the regime’s policies and ideals”.
Speaking to Mogouyi before the resumption of all-out hostilities 10 days ago, Araghchi said he had always doubted that negotiations with the US earlier this year would work, but said they had been necessary, even if there was only a 10% chance of success – not least to ensure there was no room for doubt that Iran had pursued diplomacy. “No one would be able to tell us that it was our fault,” he said.
In the interview published online on Sunday, Araghchi confirmed that Iran had offered the US a deal on its nuclear programme in the final round of talks in Geneva, but said Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, told him the following day that the mood in Washington had suddenly become more bellicose.
The joint US-Israeli strikes began shortly after 9am the next day, when senior officials had gathered for meetings at the ministry of intelligence, the strategic council on foreign policy, and the defence council.
“What matters, in my view, is the fact that Israel had intelligence about these meetings,” Araghchi said, adding: “This may point to a security gap that probably still exists. This needs to be fixed.”
Araghchi was reporting back to Khamenei’s deputy chief of staff, Ali Asghar Hijazi, when the building was shaken by three blasts within seconds – each closer than the last, he said. “The third explosion was almost next to our building. The section where Mr Hijazi’s office was located was directly hit, and the left side of the building was completely destroyed.”
Hijazi’s secretary was killed instantly, but Araghchi and Hijazi escaped the full force of the detonation.
“We were on the other side of the building, and after the explosion, the ceiling, walls, and everything collapsed on us. I grabbed Mr Hijazi’s hand, and we made our way through the beams and boards and pieces of wood, hearing the cries for help. Water was pouring from the ceiling. Everything was wrecked. We eventually got out, and I saw that various parts of the compound had been targeted.”
Araghchi was rushed to the foreign ministry by a passerby since his official car had been hit.
“For three days we were cut off from everything trying to find out who was alive and who had been martyred,” he said. “The enemy thought they could paralyse us by targeting leadership, but they failed.”
Araghchi said Iran had been prepared for such an attack, and had already drawn up plans to close the strategic strait of Hormuz if the supreme leader was targeted. The codename for such a scenario was “Code 110”, a reference to the clause of Iran’s constitution that lays out the supreme leader’s powers.
Araghchi said the US had decided to attack because it believed Iran’s government had been weakened abroad by blows to its proxies in Syria and Lebanon, and at home by economic protests – the speed and scale of which he admitted had surprised him.
Araghchi said regional governments had counselled Donald Trump against war, saying that attacking Iran would not be as easy as the US raid on Venezuela to abduct the then president, Nicolás Maduro. “Iran is different. Its support is a several-thousand-year civilisation, combined with Shia thought and beliefs about martyrdom. When these combine, they create something that cannot be easily defeated,” he said.
He told Mogouyi that Iran had warned neighbouring governments that any attack would be met with retaliation against targets in the region. “If Israel hits our nuclear facilities, we will hit theirs. Our missiles do not reach America, so we will hit their bases, which are unfortunately in your countries. If they hit our oil facilities, we will ensure that nobody in the region can sell oil,” he said.
He also said warnings to the Turkish government had prompted Ankara to shut down Trump’s plan to encourage a Kurdish revolt from Iraq into Iran. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, “talked to the Americans and adopted a very firm position in this regard. A series of efforts foiled this plot,” Araghchi said.
He added that Iran was working to exacerbate divisions between the US and Israel. “There are sometimes conflicts of objectives and positions which can be played with,” he said, without giving details.
Araghchi said that after Israel’s 12-day bombing campaign against his country in 2025, Iran had improved its missile capabilities, reducing the time needed to reactivate a base after an attack from 10–15 hours to 35–40 minutes.
Discussing the choice of diplomacy or war, Araghchi said: “We do not fight unless the cost of not fighting is higher than the cost of fighting.”

title: Balance stablecoin collapses 99% after $1 million exploit drains its bitcoin vaults
full_text:
Balance stablecoin collapses 99% after $1 million exploit drains its bitcoin vaults
An attacker fed the lending system a fake, abnormally low bitcoin price, liquidated vaults that should have been safe, and pocketed the difference in a single transaction.
- Balance Coin, an algorithmic stablecoin designed to hold a $1 peg, crashed more than 99% to about $0.0014 after an attacker exploited a pricing flaw in its protocol.
- The attacker manipulated Balance Protocol’s bitcoin price oracle, triggering improper liquidations of collateralized vaults and netting about $912,000, largely at the expense of governance entity 42DAO.
- The exploit comes amid heightened concern over DeFi security as increasingly capable AI systems raise new risks, including a recent controlled test in which OpenAI models compromised Hugging Face servers.
Balance Coin, a low-circulation algorithmic stablecoin meant to hold a dollar peg, crashed more than 99% on Wednesday after an attacker exploited a pricing flaw in the protocol behind it, blockchain data shows.
The token, which traded near its $1 peg a day earlier, fell to about $0.0014, erasing nearly all of its roughly $3.5 million in nominal value.
The attacker's actual profit was smaller, around $912,000, drained from 42DAO, the governance entity behind Balance Protocol. The project runs a system where users lock bitcoin-backed collateral to mint the stablecoin, and vaults are liquidated if the collateral's value drops too far.
Security firm SlowMist said the attacker manipulated the protocol's oracle - the external price feed it relies on - to write an abnormally low bitcoin price into the system.
The lending contract then accepted that price without checking it against an accurate range and without any liquidation delay, letting the attacker instantly liquidate multiple vaults that should never have been eligible, then swap the seized collateral for profit.
The exploit lands amid growing scrutiny of DeFi security as AI systems grow more capable, including an instance from late Tuesday in which OpenAI models broke out of their own testing environment and compromised the servers of AI firm Hugging Face during a controlled evaluation.

Bitcoin holds below $66,000 as the market waits on Alphabet to judge the AI trade
Bitcoin traded near $65,900 on Wednesday, holding just below the two-week high it touched earlier, up 1.5% on the week, per CoinDesk data.
The pause matches the broader market, where a two-day rebound in chip stocks stalled as traders waited on Alphabet's results after the U.S. close.
Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.8% and South Korea's Kospi trimmed strong early gains, with tech lagging in Europe too.
The trigger is Alphabet, which said last quarter it would more than double capital spending to as much as $190 billion this year. Investors want evidence that spending is generating returns, and the report lands just as chipmakers have been whipsawed by fears the pace of AI investment cannot hold.
Bitcoin has moved with the AI trade all month, up when the chip complex is strong and down when it wobbles, because the same risk appetite drives both and because bitcoin miners have rebuilt into AI data-center operators.
The majors were quiet otherwise. Ether held near $1,917, up 2% on the week, while Hyperliquid lagged at down 2% over seven days. The Fed meets July 28 and 29, six days after Alphabet gives the market its first hard look at whether the AI build-out is still worth paying for.

title: Bitcoin ETFs extend inflow streak to 6 days with $203M added
summary: US spot Bitcoin ETFs extended their inflow streak to six sessions, bringing in about $930 million while remaining down $4.84 billion on a net basis year to date.
full_text:
Bitcoin ETFs extend inflow streak to 6 days with $203M added
US spot Bitcoin ETFs extended their inflow streak to six sessions, bringing in about $930 million while remaining down $4.84 billion on a net basis year to date.
US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded their sixth consecutive day of net inflows on Tuesday, adding $203.1 million.
The Bitcoin ETFs attracted about $930 million over the six-session streak, their longest run of consecutive inflows since April, according to SoSoValue data.
The inflows came as Bitcoin traded above $65,000 and briefly climbed to $66,700 on Tuesday. At publication, Bitcoin traded at $65,802, up about 2% over the previous 24 hours, according to CoinGecko.
Broader crypto market sentiment also improved on Wednesday, with the Crypto Fear & Greed Index rising to “fear” from “extreme fear.”
The recovery comes as analysts said Bitcoin needs to break above and hold the $65,000 to $65,500 range to strengthen the case for a sustained uptrend.
The funds have accumulated $51.8 billion in cumulative net inflows since launch, while total net assets reached $80.9 billion. US spot Bitcoin ETFs remain about $4.84 billion in net outflows year-to-date.

title: BIS warns USD stablecoins can evade capital controls, challenging traditional market regulations
summary: BIS says that FX restrictions and capital controls are less effective against stablecoins than against foreign currency bank deposits.
full_text:
BIS warns USD stablecoins can evade capital controls, challenging traditional market regulations
Quick Take
- The Bank for International Settlements said that dollar-backed stablecoins are “largely unaffected” by capital controls.
- BIS researchers suggested that foreign exchange restrictions and capital controls are less effective against stablecoins than against foreign currency bank deposits.
We'd love your feedback.
The Bank for International Settlements said that dollar-backed stablecoins could bypass capital controls, raising concerns regarding foreign exchange restrictions in emerging markets.
In a study published Tuesday, the BIS analyzed stablecoin flows across more than 130 economies and found that stablecoins appear "largely unaffected by either broad or specific capital flow restrictions," as they partly circulate outside the regulatory perimeter.
Notably, the researchers suggested that foreign exchange restrictions and capital controls — traditional tools governments use to limit money flowing in or out of their countries — are "less effective" against stablecoins than against conventional foreign currency bank deposits.
According to the report, the growing adoption of stablecoins has created a new channel for accessing U.S. dollar liquidity, particularly in emerging markets and developing economies. The BIS warned that policymakers in emerging markets may need to rethink their strategies as "dollarization is hard to reverse once established."
Still skeptical
The latest findings build on the global institution's broader skepticism toward stablecoins. In June 2026, the BIS reiterated in its annual report that stablecoins still fall short of money in singleness, elasticity, interoperability, and integrity, which it says are the foundational properties that any monetary system must keep.
Meanwhile, stablecoins are finding growing usage in both emerging and established economies, as regulators in the U.S., EU, Japan, and other regions are establishing dedicated frameworks to bring stablecoins into the regulated financial system. The total USD stablecoin supply reached $292.6 billion as of Tuesday, up from $253 billion a year ago, according to The Block's data dashboard.

title: US seeks forfeiture of $25 million in crypto tied to global fraud investigations
summary: US prosecutors seek forfeiture of $25 million in crypto recovered from five investigations into international fraud and laundering networks.
full_text:
US seeks forfeiture of $25 million in crypto tied to global fraud investigations
Quick Take
- The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia filed five civil forfeiture complaints seeking over $25 million in cryptocurrency recovered from international fraud schemes targeting U.S. and Canadian residents.
- Prosecutors said the funds are the latest in the more than $800 million recovered as part of the Scam Center Strike Force.
We'd love your feedback.
The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to forfeit more than $25 million in cryptocurrency recovered through five separate investigations into international fraud networks that allegedly targeted residents in the U.S. and Canada.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia said in a statement on Tuesday that Secret Service Washington Field Office agents, working through the Cyber Fraud Task Force, identified multiple laundering networks and thousands of victims worldwide who were misled into believing they were making legitimate crypto investments.
According to the statement, the first investigation, flagged by Canadian authorities in late 2024, traced more than 270 suspected victim transactions and seeks roughly $10.4 million. The second, involving online romance schemes with more than 200 victims, seeks approximately $12.1 million.
The third and fourth investigations — reported in May 2026 and March 2026 respectively by victims in the National Capital Region — seek about $1.2 million and $2.4 million. The fifth investigation, involving a fee-based recovery fraud, seeks approximately $285,000.
In each of the five cases, launderers were predominantly located in Southeast Asia, with IP addresses in China, Malaysia, and Cambodia, per the statement.
Prosecutors said the funds are the latest in the more than $800 million recovered as part of the Scam Center Strike Force, an initiative launched in November 2025 by U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.
"This $25 million seizure is a direct result of the Scam Center Strike Force I launched in November 2025, and it demonstrates the power of aggressively targeting these international fraud networks," Pirro said. "Our investigators cut through complex laundering schemes, protected victims, and shut down criminal pipelines."

title: Synthesia’s AI training platform is moving beyond videos into live coaching
summary: Synthesia launched AI Roleplay Sessions, an interactive enterprise training platform where employees practice workplace conversations with AI avatars that provide feedback, scoring, and analytics to help companies measure training effectiveness.
full_text:
For years, Synthesia’s pitch was to use AI to help enterprises create interactive training videos, in minutes, for a fraction of the cost normally associated with developing corporate educational materials. The startup’s newest product is making a different bet — that the real moat in enterprise AI isn’t just generating content, but in proving that it worked.
On Wednesday, the British startup launched Roleplay Sessions, an interactive training product where employees can practice high-stakes conversations like sales pitches, performance reviews, and customer complaints with an AI avatar that talks back, pushes back, and then scores them against a rubric.
Roleplay is the first release under a broader “Sessions” platform Synthesia plans to expand into other formats, including job interviews and candidate screening, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The launch comes as enterprises take a harder look at whether their AI spend is paying off. Citing a meta-analysis of learning research, Synthesia argues that most corporate training — including, implicitly, its own core video product — stops short of actually changing behavior. The trainings tend to inform and demonstrate, but what really pushes someone into actually learning something is doing that thing, along with feedback.
“Video performs way better than text or sending out a document,” Synthesia CEO and co-founder Victor Riparbelli told TechCrunch. “But for most things, we learn the best by actually practicing something rather than just reading it.”
Roleplay also moves Synthesia into a more defensible position. The company’s avatar and voice technology are proprietary, but the underlying reasoning intelligence is OpenAI’s. By tacking on a layer that includes rubrics, performance data, and analytics, Synthesia is positioning itself less as an AI avatar company and more as a performance-management platform with a video front end.
“From a managerial executive layer, we’re seeing huge interest in mapping out the talent in their company in a way that’s been really difficult to do before,” Riparbelli said. “If you have your entire sales team practice with an AI role player, you can get very granular data on how your sales force is doing overall.”
Synthesia already has a few early Roleplay customers with scaled commercial rollouts, including “one of the top three companies by market cap in Europe, one of the top five Fortune 100, and one of the biggest recruitment companies in the world,” per a company spokesperson.
The two most popular use cases involve training sales teams and leadership — programs like practicing how to sell a product or have a difficult conversation. Much of it is soft skills training, Riparbelli said.
As with Synthesia’s main product, customers can either create their own training programs on the platform or enlist the help of Synthesia’s consultants to build a bespoke solution that relies in part on whatever training documents and context the company already has.
Roleplay is an enterprise offering for now, but the goal is to offer it more widely to small businesses, prosumers, and potentially educational institutions in the next few months as inference costs continue to fall. Riparbelli believes products like Roleplay represent the next phase of enterprise AI adoption, where companies care less about whether AI looks good in a social media demo and more about proving it generates measurable business outcomes.

title: 英國的教訓》將 AI 列為國家核心發展項目，同時砍掉科技部
summary:
英國新首相 Andy Burnham 上任隔天，就裁掉了前首相 Rishi Sunak 才成立兩年五個月的「科 […]

〈英國的教訓》將 AI 列為國家核心發展項目，同時砍掉科技部〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
英國新首相 Andy Burnham 上任隔天，就裁掉了前首相 Rishi Sunak 才成立兩年五個月的「科學、創新暨技術部」（DSIT），同一週卻任命 36 歲的 Kanishka Narayan 出任史上第一位列席內閣的 AI 部長。也在同一週，國家審計署發布報告，直指政府掛在嘴上的「數位轉型與 AI 每年可省 450 億英鎊」缺乏一致的估算方法。
（前情提要：英國 FCA 警告金融 AI「軍備競賽」：催監管 ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini等大模型）
（背景補充：臺灣政府正積極布局「主權AI」，國科會主委吳誠文：籌組國家人工智慧戰略特別委員會）
英國 1980 年代的 BBC 政治諷刺劇《Yes, Prime Minister》裡，常務次長 Humphrey Appleby 有一套被引用了四十年的「政治家三段論」。第一步，我們必須做點什麼。第二步，這就是一件什麼。第三步，所以我們必須做它。這句臺詞之所以到今天還在流通，不是因為它好笑，是因為它太少出錯。
2026 年 7 月 20 日到 21 日，英國政府用不到 48 小時，把這個三段論完整地演了一遍。
7 月 20 日，Andy Burnham 在白金漢宮見完 King Charles III，回到唐寧街 10 號門口宣誓要結束政治動盪。他是英國第 59 任首相，也是 2016 年脫歐公投以來十年內的第七位。隔天，他解散了英國唯一一個以科技為名的中央部會。也在隔天，他讓 AI 第一次坐上了內閣會議桌。
這兩件事被大部分媒體分開報導，一方面是官僚重組，一件是人事任命。
英國那個禮拜
這邊要先把英國政治情況解釋一下，因為台灣讀者通常對英國這一輪換任的來龍去脈不熟。
Keir Starmer 在 2024 年 7 月帶工黨拿下壓倒性勝利，但兩年下來個人聲望崩盤，民調顯示選民認為他沒有帶來任何看得見的改變。2026 年 6 月 22 日，Starmer 在黨內議員普遍失去信心的情況下宣布辭去黨魁與首相。
麻煩在於，工黨黨章規定只有國會議員才能參選黨魁，而當時呼聲最高的 Andy Burnham 是大曼徹斯特市長，不是議員。解法是一場補選。Makerfield 選區的議員辭職讓位，Burnham 在 6 月 18 日補選當選，接著在 7 月 17 日以 379 位議員提名（超過工黨全體議員的九成四）在無競爭對手的情況下被推舉為黨魁，7 月 20 日正式接任首相。
上任第二天，他動了 Whitehall 的組織圖。
被關掉的是「科學、創新暨技術部」，2023 年 2 月 7 日由當時的首相 Rishi Sunak 在一次改組中成立，做法是把商業、能源暨產業戰略部拆成三塊，再從數位、文化、媒體暨體育部手上抽走數位政策，拼成一個新部。首任大臣是 Michelle Donelan，這個部活了兩年五個月。
它的職能被拆成三個部分，科技與科學政策併進新成立的「商業、創新、科學暨貿易部」（DBIST），由 Jonathan Reynolds 掌管。AI 政策與公部門的 AI 匯入移進內閣辦公室。數位政府職能，連同政府數位服務（GDS）與中央數位暨資料辦公室（CDDO），回到改名後的數位、文化、媒體暨體育部。原科學大臣 Liz Kendall 去職，科技大臣這個職位就此從英國內閣消失。
同一天，Kanishka Narayan 被任命為 AI 部長，橫跨內閣辦公室與 DBIST，並列席內閣。這是 AI 第一次在英國政府裡拿到內閣層級的席位。
Narayan 的履歷本身就是一個故事，他 1989 年 11 月生於印度比哈爾邦的穆札法普，12 歲隨家人移居威爾斯的卡地夫，一家人住在一房公寓，他走路去上公立中學。後來他念了伊頓公學、牛津大學 Balliol 學院的政治哲學經濟學系，再拿了史丹佛的 MBA。進國會前，他在 David Cameron 任內的內閣辦公室與 Liz Truss 任內的環境部當過公務員。2024 年 7 月，他當選 Vale of Glamorgan 選區議員，成為威爾斯史上第一位少數族裔背景的國會議員。2025 年 9 月接下 AI 與線上安全政務次長，不到一年就升到內閣。
他上任時說，AI 大概是人類史上最重要的技術，而它能帶來的是一個再工業化的英國、更強的國安、被真正改善的公共服務。他也承認有風險，也承認民眾對就業與速度的焦慮。這段話沒有什麼可挑剔的地方，甚至很誠懇的。問題不在他說了什麼，在於這句話是在科技部被解散的第二天說出來的。
英國內閣的特殊羅奇
一個政府對某件事的真實態度，看它開了什麼機關，不如看關掉什麼機關。
設一個部會是一種政治聲明，你需要一次改組、一份公告、幾張新的組織圖。關一個部會是組織定價。你必須在既有的預算、既有的人事、既有的法定職位上動刀，而且要願意承擔重來的成本。
前者告訴你這個政府想被看成什麼樣子，後者告訴你這個內閣願意為這件事付多少錢。
英國科技業對此的反應相當一致。techUK 與 Startup Coalition 聯名寫信給 Burnham，把這個計畫形容為「錯的時間做錯的改變」。他們的理由不是留戀機關，而是拆解本身有成本。他們在信裡點名，把 AI 安全研究院、主權 AI 基金、GDS 與英國研究創新署（UKRI）這些工作打散，會在最需要速度的時候讓一切慢下來。
Startup Coalition 的 Dom Hallas 說得更白。把科技塞進超大型的商業部，等於讓英國的科技公司跟鋼鐵這類產業去搶同一位大臣的注意力。曾任 Keir Starmer AI 機會顧問的 Matt Clifford 把這件事稱為「一個大錯」。創投機構 Plural 合夥人、同時擔任英國 AI 安全研究院主席的 Ian Hogarth 的說法最不帶感情，也最刺人。他說，這種規模的重組基本上會讓相關部會分心一年。
Burnham 政府的說法是，把商業、科學與貿易放在一起，才做得出協調一致的產業戰略。這個理由不算牽強。DSIT 本來就是從商業部拆出來的，拆完之後科技政策與產業政策確實各走各的。
但兩邊講的有點錯亂，政府講的是政策協調，產業講的是注意力分配。協調可以靠流程解決，注意力不行。一個部長一天只有那麼多小時，而在把鋼鐵、貿易談判、產業補貼與 AI 放在同個屋簷下的部會裡，AI 從被服務的領域，變成需要排隊的議題。
Narayan 那張新的內閣椅子，正是為了補上這個缺口而設的。他人在內閣裡，理論上可以跨部會拉動資源。這是升級。只是升級的是一個人，降級的是一整套編制。人會換，編制才會累積。
沒有分母
真正讓這一週值得被寫下來的，不是機關圖，是同一週出現的兩個數字。
第一個數字是 18 億英鎊。這是英國預算責任辦公室（OBR）在 2025 年 11 月，替那張叫「Brit Card」的全國數位身分證估的三年成本，涵蓋 2026-27 到 2028-29 年度。這張卡原本要載明姓名、國籍、出生日期、居留身分與照片，用途是查驗工作權，藉此打擊非法就業。它在 2025 年 9 月被宣布，隨即引爆英國國會請願史上第二大的連署，將近 300 萬人簽名反對。2025 年 10 月，政府被迫拿掉強制條款，改成自願，讓護照等既有證件也能用。整個 2025 年，Keir Starmer 都在為它辯護，還開過閉門會議討論怎麼落地。2026 年 7 月，Burnham 上任後直接把它廢了。
省下來的錢去哪了？值得說清楚，因為外界一度以為會轉進 AI。實際上，Burnham 政府說這筆資源要拿去補家庭電費，作為生活成本紓困的一部分。這是一個政治判斷，不是科技判斷。
第二個數字是 450 億英鎊。這是英國政府拿來描述「數位轉型與 AI 每年可以省下多少錢」的招牌數字，出自 DSIT 在 2025 年 1 月發布的《State of digital government review》。那份報告說，公部門若全面數位化，每年有超過 450 億英鎊「尚未實現的節省與生產力效益」，相當於公部門支出的 4% 到 7%。這個數字後來被首相與部長們反覆引用，成為財政論述的地基之一。
它是怎麼算出來的？DSIT 的假設是，100% 的例行任務與 10% 的非例行任務可以被自動化。
「這是一個合理的猜測，但它當然是一個猜測。它非常難衡量。」前 i.AI（政府 AI 孵化器）主任 Laura Gilbert 在國會作證時，這樣描述 450 億英鎊。
Gilbert 不是這個數字的敵人。她在唐寧街待了四年多，是政府資料科學團隊 10DS 與 i.AI 的創辦主任，是英國政府裡最懂這件事的人之一。她說得很誠實，而誠實在這裡反而更讓人不安。
英國智庫 Institute for Government 的 Nick Davies 講得更直接。他說，除非你有認真的計畫做出相當程度的人力縮減或減少資本支出，否則要達到那 450 億會非常困難。他還補了一句，什麼叫「例行任務」到現在都沒有定義清楚，他甚至懷疑政府自己知不知道。
下議院的科學、創新暨技術委員會在《Rewiring the state》報告裡，把這個數字直接點名為「令人擔憂的樂觀」，並且列為部長帶頭「炒作」的範例，認為這種炒作不是在推動數位轉型，是在拖累它。
然後是國家審計署。7 月 15 日，NAO 發布《政府人力規劃：經驗教訓》，用審計的語言把同一件事再說一次。報告指出，英國公部門僱用 620 萬人，人事成本 2600 億英鎊，76% 的公務員預期 AI 會在五年內改變自己的工作方式。但各部會公布的效率計畫「沒有提供部會如何推匯出預期人力效率的細節」，跨政府之間也沒有一致的方法論。內閣秘書長 Antonia Romeo 自己說過，公務體系的人力計畫「沒有充分反映 AI 與科技將如何改變公務體系的樣貌」。NAO 還補了一刀，公部門本身就缺乏達成這些效率所需要的技術與數位人才。
把這兩個數字並排放，這一週的形狀就出來了。
18 億英鎊是支出。它有明確的年度區間，有一個獨立機構背書，會進預算書，會被審計，也因此可以被砍掉。450 億英鎊是節省。它沒有一致的方法論，沒有可查核的分母，來自一個關於「例行任務」的假設，而它至今沒有被砍掉，因為沒有人被要求把它算給誰看。
政府砍掉了那個可以被驗算的數字，留下了那個不能被驗算的數字。
這就是我覺得這一週真正值得記下來的地方。在會計上，支出與節省是對稱的，一邊減一邊加。在政治上，兩者完全不對稱。支出必須被辯護，節省只需要被相信。當財政缺口壓在頭上，一個沒有分母的節省數字，就是最好用的填補劑。它不用招標，不用進度報告，不用扛延宕，也不用面對將近 300 萬人的連署。
而 AI 現在是這種數字最方便的載體。它夠新，新到沒有歷史基準可以打臉；它夠廣，廣到任何一項效率都可以掛在它名下；它又夠專業，專業到質疑它的人會被說成不懂技術。
DSIT 活了兩年五個月。Brit Card 從宣布到作廢，走了十個月。工黨從壓倒性勝選到換首相，用了兩年。英國從脫歐公投到現在，換了七位首相。
台灣呢
台灣的數位發展部在 2022 年 8 月掛牌，到今天快滿四年，關於它的爭論從來沒停過。專責部會還是分散職能，資源該集中在同個部會，還是嵌進各部會，這些問題跟英國吵的完全是同樣的議題。
英國提供了現成的案例，而且是負面方向的案例。它證明為了「表達重視」而成立的部會，在下一位首相（總統）眼中可能只是能被合併的拼圖。它同時也證明把科技併進大部會，產業界首先擔心的不是政策方向，是自己還排不排得到部長的行事曆。
我不覺得台灣應該從中得出「所以要保住數位發展部」或者「所以應該廢掉」的結論。這兩個結論都太廉價了。真正該問的是，成立到現在，這個部累積出什麼是別人拿不走的？如果答案是一批真的留得住的技術人才、一套跨部會通用的資料與身分基礎建設、幾件做完並且被驗證有效的專案，那它就是拆不動的。
如果答案主要是一套新的組織圖與好幾份年度施政計畫，那它跟英國面臨的治理問題沒有差別。
對政治人物來說，「有爭議」意思是這會掉票，「有勇氣」意思是這會讓你輸掉選舉。

〈為什麼華語用戶需要自己的預測市場？yoyo market 做到了 Polymarket、Kalshi 做不到的事〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
華語用戶缺乏專屬的預測市場平台，歐美主導的Polymarket與Kalshi聚焦美國議題且門檻高。yoyo market專為亞太用戶設計，提供在地化事件（如棒球、K-pop、天氣），簡化操作介面，並通過合規策略避開敏感政治題材，填補亞洲40億人口的市場空白，打造真正的群眾智慧感測器。
（前情提要：亞洲終於有了自己的預測市場 — 由亞太團隊打造 yoyo market 全新版本上線）
（背景補充：Kalshi 世界盃吃下 543 億鎂交易量，是 Polymarket 的 2.6 倍）
二〇二四年美國大選夜，全世界盯著的不是 CNN 的計票板，而是一個叫 Polymarket 的網站——川普的勝選機率怎麼一路爬到 60%，最後與結果幾乎吻合。那一夜，預測市場第一次證明：當人們用真金白銀為判斷背書，得到的訊號，比任何民調都準。
但如果你是華語用戶，打開 Polymarket 網站的瞬間，多半只有一種感覺：這一切，好像都是別人的事。 滿屏的美國聯準會、美國大選、美式足球、好萊塢頒獎典禮——沒有一個預測事件，是為你而設。
預測市場在歐美已成氣候，但擁有四十億人口的亞洲，這塊版圖幾乎還是空白。這篇文章談的就是這個缺口，以及正在試著補上它的人。
預測市場的本質：一台聚集人類判斷的「機率感測器」
預測市場，本質上是一個用價格來聚集資訊的市場。 你針對「某件未來的事會不會發生」買賣合約，價格直接等於市場認定的機率：a16z 經濟學家 Scott Duke Kominers 把它形容成一台「機率感測器」，一張合約報價 0.50 美元，就代表市場認為這件事有 50% 的機率發生；你若認為真實機率更高，就買進、把價格推上去。
a16z 更直接點出它勝過傳統民調的四個優勢：能給出即時的機率數字、會隨新資訊動態更新、用真金白銀激勵參與者認真研究、而且任何冷門題目都能開盤。也因此它的用途遠不只下注：企業拿它預測產品上市時程、科學界拿它估實驗成功率、媒體拿它萃取「群眾智慧」。
延伸閱讀：a16z 解析預測市場潛力：不僅是賭盤，更是精準的「機率感測器」
規模也跟著證明了這不是泡沫。2024 大選後產業一度急凍，2025 下半年靠運動、地緣與總經議題二次爆發，到 2026 年 4 月，全產業單月交易量已達約 240 億美元。機構喊出的數字更兇：Bernstein 預估 2030 年交易量上看 1 兆美元；博彩研究機構 Eilers & Krejcik 同樣看到 1 兆美元的量能。這股熱度資本同樣不缺席，Kalshi 估值一年內衝上約 220 億美元，Polymarket 在獲紐交所母公司 ICE 投資後估值來到約 150 億美元。
換句話說：預測市場正在從「加密玩具」變成「導航不確定性的基礎設施」。
Polymarket vs Kalshi：全球兩大預測市場，卻打不到亞洲用戶的核心
這個賽道的兩個主角，代表了兩條路線：加密原生 vs 受監管。
- Polymarket 是全球最大的去中心化預測市場，建在 Polygon 上、以 USDC 結算、用 UMA 預言機裁決。2024 大選的川普對哈里斯單一市場交易量超過 33 億美元；2024 全年約 90 億美元、活躍交易者約 31.4 萬人；2025 年 10 月單月量突破 30 億美元，正式超越選舉峰值。它在 2025 年收購持有 CFTC 牌照的交易所 QCEX、合規重返美國，並獲 ICE 最高 20 億美元投資。
- Kalshi 走的是合規路線，是受美國 CFTC 監管的合約交易所（DCM），用法幣入金、以中央限價訂單簿（CLOB）撮合，像股票交易所一樣運作。它的交易量約八成來自體育賽事，並與 Robinhood 合作打開散戶流量、估值一路衝到約 220 億美元。
兩者規模驚人，但有一個共同點：它們的預測事件與用戶，都繞著美國轉。
40 億人的亞洲，為什麼需要自己的預測市場
因為全球最值得預測的事，有一大半正在亞洲發生，卻沒有一個讓亞洲人下注的地方。
第一，是人口與議題的錯位。亞太地區超過 40 億人、占全球人口六成以上，但 Polymarket 上是美國大選、Kalshi 上是聯準會利率與 NFL。對華語用戶而言，要在這些題目上贏錢，等於跟全世界資訊最靈通的歐美人比誰更懂歐美，即使在資訊秒傳的今天，這仍是一場先天的資訊落差。
第二，是使用門檻。Polymarket 對許多地區設區域限制、Kalshi 僅限美國境內註冊，許多亞洲用戶不是被排除就是被封鎖。卡點往往來自政治、選舉這類敏感題材牽動的法規風險，而一個從一開始就為亞洲設計、主動避開敏感議題的平台，反而能從根本繞過這道牆。
第三，亞洲的題材一點都不弱。大谷翔平每個新球季的表現是橫跨東亞的全民話題；中華職棒季後賽、世界棒球經典賽牽動數千萬人；K-pop 偶像退伍與回歸的聲量勝過任何財報；金馬、金曲、金鐘，台積電法說會、蘋果發表會，甚至「今年夏天台北會不會破 39°C、今年有沒有颱風」，這些議題的密度與黏性，遠比四年一次的選舉更能撐起一個日常平台。
難怪幣安創辦人 CZ 、Polymarket 亞洲市場負責人都喊話「亞洲是重要市場」。亞洲，已是兵家必爭之地。但看好是一回事，真正為亞洲把產品做出來、做到位，是另一回事。
yoyo market 打造亞洲預測市場的 3 大關鍵
yoyo market 創立於 2025 年，是一家美國新創、近期於香港成立分公司，專為亞太用戶打造預測市場。 天使輪由隆領投資（Longling Capital）領投，其創辦人蔡文勝正是美圖（Meitu）共同創辦人，有打造億級用戶產品的實績；投資人還包括 Impa Ventures、Hermitage Capital 等 Web3 投資人與業界專家。
而 yoyo 真正和 Polymarket、Kalshi 拉開差距的，是三根支柱：
1｜在地共鳴（Local by Design）
預測事件是規劃過的，不是翻譯來的。 yoyo 的每一個事件，都由本地團隊從選題開始策劃，圍繞亞太用戶真正在乎的事：東亞體育、K-pop 與華語歌壇、電影、蘋果發表會、天氣氣溫、颱風，乃至牽動區域的社會時事，如台灣在地的媽祖繞境參與人次等。用戶打開平台看到的，是和自己切身相關的議題，而不是別人世界裡的事。
2｜直覺易用（Built for Everyone）
交易輕鬆，沒興趣「滑掉」、感興趣「點」一下。 yoyo 在打造產品，以行動體驗為核心：瀏覽市場時不感興趣的就「滑掉」、感興趣的「點」一下就可以交易。yoyo 沒有複雜的下單介面、不必打開電腦、不需要懂任何鏈上術語，打開手機，五秒完成一筆預測交易。
操作介面越簡單，用戶越能專注在自己的專業判斷上，下單就交給平台處理。
3｜合規優先（Compliance in Mind）
主動劃出邊界，因為想走得更遠。 yoyo 正在申請美國 CFTC 牌照（Kalshi 走過、也是預測市場走向主流的必經之路），並明確不上架選舉、政治、軍事衝突等過度敏感議題。這既是對用戶的保護，也是它想走得長遠所做的選擇。
綜合這三點，結論不難得出：
當你想對美國大選下注，你會去 Polymarket；當你想交易聯準會利率，你會去 Kalshi。但當你想下的是台北或高雄今天氣溫最高幾度、樂天vs味全龍、大谷翔平本季幾轟、哪個 K-pop 團體先回歸、金馬獎誰奪后；這些盤 Polymarket 和 Kalshi 不會開，而願意為亞洲用戶開的，目前就是 yoyo market。
對於亞洲題材有興趣的讀者，可以上 yoyo market 市場小試身手：app.yoyomarket.com

title: 韓國政府拿 512 張 B200 換全民免費 AI，目標國產模型吃下 8 成用量
summary:
韓國科學技術情報通訊部（과학기술정보통신부）7 月 13 日開出「모두의 AI」（全民 AI）標案，要選 2 […]

〈韓國政府拿 512 張 B200 換全民免費 AI，目標國產模型吃下 8 成用量〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
韓國科學技術情報通訊部（과학기술정보통신부）7 月 13 日開出「모두의 AI」（全民 AI）標案，要選 2 到 3 家民間業者，用國產 AI 模型做出全民免費、不限用量的聊天機器人加公共服務代理人，9 月推 beta、12 月正式上線，投標 8 月 11 日截止。政府端出 512 張 NVIDIA B200 當補貼，單一業者最多拿 256 張，外國模型只准用在國產做不到的功能。
（前情提要：韓國端出 8800 億鎂 AI 國家戰略：半導體、實體 AI、資料中心，三個核心要領先）
（背景補充：臺灣政府正積極布局「主權AI」，國科會主委吳誠文：籌組國家人工智慧戰略特別委員會）
韓國科學技術情報通訊部（과학기술정보통신부，以下簡稱科技部）7 月 13 日正式開出「모두의 AI」標案，中文可以直譯成「全民 AI」。政府要從民間挑 2 到 3 家業者，用國產 AI 模型做一套全民都能免費使用、而且不設用量上限的通用聊天機器人，外加一個能幫民眾查詢和申辦政府服務的公共 AI 代理人。
時程壓得很緊，投標受理到今年 8 月 11 日下午 5 點，8 月底選出業者，9 月推出 beta 版，12 月正式對全國開放。
韓國政府這次不是發錢，是發顯卡，標案寫明今年提供 512 張 NVIDIA B200 GPU 給得標者，如果只選 2 家，兩邊各拿 256 張；如果選 3 家，第一順位拿 256 張，第二、第三順位各拿 128 張，最終數量再依業者需求與評選結果調整。
政府當算力包租公，業者只出一成
補助怎麼算？韓媒引述的政府基準是每張 GPU 每月 660 萬韓元，以 256 張計一年約 202.75 億韓元，換算大約 1,350 萬美元，512 張全開則接近 2,700 萬美元。
得標者不是白拿，但也沒有到對等出資。民間對應投資的比例是大企業約政府支援額的 10%、中堅企業 6%、中小企業 5%。政府出九成、業者出一成，這個比例基本上已經寫明瞭誰是主辦方，誰是承包商。
錢也不是隻給一年，2027 年起改由政府預算直接支應營運費用，支援期一路開到 2030 年 12 月 31 日。
國產模型要吃下八成，Naver 已經被刷掉
標案要求得標者的服務必須有 50% 以上使用符合「獨自 AI 基礎模型」標準的國產 AI 模型，另外還要再串接 30% 以上的其他公司國產模型，比例以輸出 token 計算。外國模型只允許用在高難度推論或多模態這類國產真的做不到的功能上，而且不列入政府補助範圍，用太多還會被扣評選分數。
換句話說，八成的輸出必須是韓國自己的模型跑出來的，而且不能全押自家那顆，得分一杯羹給同業。這條規則同時解決了兩件事，把國產模型的實際使用量硬拉上來，又不讓單一大廠獨吞整個國民級入口。
沒有自家模型的公司也能參賽，科技部說明業者可以透過 API、開源版本或授權協議去用別人的國產基礎模型。7 月 21 日的說明會來了約 100 家公司，包括 LG U+、SK Telecom、Naver Cloud、Kakao 以及一票 AI 新創，官方預估最後大概 10 家左右實際投標。
評選也不走跑分那一套，官方說「使用者實際感受到的效能」比技術 benchmark 重要，之後每年評估一次，使用者數太難看的業者會被換掉。使用者數當 KPI，這對做慣了政府標案的韓國大廠來說是完全不同的遊戲規則。
要理解「國產模型」是誰，得回頭看韓國那個 2,136 億韓元（約 1.42 億美元）的「獨自 AI 基礎模型」計畫，也就是韓媒口中的「國家代表 AI」。2025 年選出 5 支精銳隊，分別是 Naver Cloud、LG AI 研究院（LG AI연구원）、SK Telecom、Upstage 與 NC AI，目標是做出效能追上最新全球模型九成五的自研模型。
512 張卡要扛 5,100 萬人
韓國在野質疑聲音很直接，表示 512 張 B200 只佔韓國目前已投入獨自模型、產學研究與國家計畫的約 11,600 張 B200 等值算力的 4.4%。一位 AI 業者主管對韓媒說，512 張再切給 2 到 3 家營運商，全民尖峰流量時「算力不足的可能性相當大」。
而且這套服務不是只跑聊天，還要吃下多模態請求與行政系統串接，每則查詢的算力消耗都是加乘的。韓國科技部的反駁是，這不是訓練基礎模型的專案，不需要動輒上千張卡，業者本來就得自己補基礎設施，初期也只有基本聊天與簡單公共服務，「token 消耗量不會太誇張」。

title: 50 萬筆 ChatGPT 對話，34% 對話量拿來寫同人色情小說
summary:
華盛頓大學與科羅拉多大學波德分校的研究團隊分析 57 萬筆真實 ChatGPT 對話，想搞懂人類到底怎麼用 A […]

〈50 萬筆 ChatGPT 對話，34% 對話量拿來寫同人色情小說〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
華盛頓大學與科羅拉多大學波德分校的研究團隊分析 57 萬筆真實 ChatGPT 對話，想搞懂人類到底怎麼用 AI 寫小說，結果撞見一名匿名使用者在數個月內上千次要模型一直寫同一個小說場景。更關鍵的是用 GPT 寫小說的帳號裡面， 2% 的人就寫掉超過 8 成對話量。
（前情提要：人腦比機器好？幾萬人在網站上假裝自己是 ChatGPT）
（背景補充：Deezer 警告 44% 新上傳音樂是 AI 生成，人類創作者的血汗錢正被集體洗劫）
在學校的社團教室裡，一個叫 Natsuki 的女高中生摀著肚子說，Sakura，偏偏挑這種時候，你決定要在這裡出生，不能再等兩個月嗎。
社長 Monika 問她怎麼了。她咬著牙回答，羊水破了，Sakura 要出來了，而她完全不知道該怎麼辦。
然後這段劇本在一句話的中間戛然而止。「我的身體⋯⋯它」，句子斷在這裡，沒有下文。
這不是遊戲的原始劇情，是有人手打出來貼進 ChatGPT 對話方塊的一段文字。斷句是刻意的，那是留給模型接手的位置。
然後這個人把幾乎一模一樣的東西，再貼一次。接著又一次。持續了好幾個月，上千次。
這個奇怪現象出現在論文裡
上面那段對話，完整收錄在 2026 年 6 月 22 日上傳到 arXiv 的論文《AI Fiction in the Wild》（編號 2606.22748）裡。作者是華盛頓大學資訊學院的 Neel Gupta 與 Melanie Walsh，以及科羅拉多大學波德分校資工系的 Maria Antoniak。這篇論文 2025 年 9 月在普渡大學的 MFS Cultural AI 研討會發表過，預計刊登於文學期刊《MFS: Modern Fiction Studies》。
7 月初，日媒 AUTOMATON 與電競媒體 Dexerto 幾乎同時報導了論文裡這個橋段，截圖隨即在 X 上瘋傳，成為七月最大的科技迷因之一。
先修正一件事，中英文報導普遍稱這名使用者為「極端離群值（extreme outlier）」，但論文全文並沒有出現過這個詞。研究者實際用的說法是「特別多產的離群值」，以及一個他們自創的分類，「無限故事索求者（infinite story demander）」，指的是那些在很長一段時間裡反覆索取同一個或高度相似故事橋段的人。
《Doki Doki Literature Club!》（心跳文學社）是 2017 年上架的視覺小說遊戲，表面上是清新的校園戀愛題材，玩下去才會發現它是一款玩弄後設敘事的心理恐怖作品。Natsuki、Monika、Yuri、Sayori 是文學社的四名成員。這款遊戲在台灣的知名度不算高，但在英文網路上是同人創作重鎮。
三分之一的對話都在寫小說
研究團隊用的資料集叫 WildChat，總共 573,453 筆英文對話。經過分類後，其中 195,271 筆涉及虛構內容生成，佔 34%。
在這 19 萬筆小說類對話裡，同人創作佔 95,450 筆（49%），情色小說內容佔 52,231 筆（27%）。兩者高度重疊。
而最受歡迎的作品世界觀，第一名就是《Doki Doki Literature Club!》，22,381 筆對話，佔小說子集的 11.5%。
第二名是動作遊戲《Freedom Planet》，5,204 筆，2.6%。接著是英雄聯盟 4,514 筆、火影忍者 4,342 筆。
論文特別點出，這份排行榜跟全球最大同人平台 AO3 的熱門作品完全不同。AO3 上排前面的是哈利波特、星際大戰、漫威這類西方主流 IP。WildChat 的榜單長得完全不一樣。
2% 的人寫掉 8 成的對話
論文裡有一句話很誇張。
「小說子集裡 2% 的使用者，要為超過 80% 的對話負責。」
這裡要精確一點，素材流傳的版本說「2% 的帳號貢獻超過 8 成互動量」，但論文講的單位是對話數，不是互動量、訊息數或 token 數。這個區別很重要，因為對話數才是各家 AI 公司最常拿出來公布的那種指標。
而這 2% 的人在做什麼？研究者算了一個「prompt 重複率」，看同一個使用者的提示詞有多高比例落在同一個語意群集裡。
一般使用者（至少有兩筆對話）的重複率是 42%。
前 2% 的重度使用者，69%。
最多產的前十名使用者，85%。
這 57 萬筆對話是從免費 GPT 撈的
這是最容易被誤讀的一環，而它決定了整篇論文能推論到什麼程度。
WildChat 由艾倫人工智慧研究院（AI2）收集，時間是 2023 年 4 月 9 日到 2024 年 5 月 1 日。收集方式不是從 OpenAI 拿資料，而是在 Hugging Face Spaces 上架設免費的 GPT-3.5 Turbo 與 GPT-4 聊天介面，使用者點兩次同意彈窗，就能換到不用登入、沒有速率限制的免費使用權，代價是聊天紀錄可能被公開。
論文自己在方法論裡寫得很清楚，WildChat 不是所有 ChatGPT 使用者的代表性樣本。研究者推測這群人「比一般使用者更懂技術、更活在網路上」，也可能是來自低收入地區、來自 ChatGPT 被禁的國家，或者單純想測試模型底線、生成平台明令禁止內容的人。
34% 掉到 7.1%
研究團隊接著做了一件很簡單、但結果很兇的事。
他們用雜湊過的 IP 位址推估使用者身分，12,947 個 IP 收斂成大約 10,082 名使用者。然後，每個使用者只保留一筆對話。
小說類的佔比，從 34% 掉到 7.1%。
同一批資料，同一個問題，換一種演算法，答案差了將近五倍。
不只總量。論文在註腳裡補了一刀，一人一則之後，《Doki Doki Literature Club!》的排名「急遽下滑」，取而代之爬上榜的是《權力遊戲》和《寶可夢》這種真正大眾的作品。
也就是說，「ChatGPT 使用者最愛寫《Doki Doki Literature Club!》同人」這個結論，本身就是少數幾個人重複行為堆出來的假象。
上千次寫一個生小孩的橋段
值得注意的是，論文對這名匿名使用者的態度不是嘲笑。
研究者把這種行為放進「重複消費」的心理學脈絡裡，重看同一部電影、重逛同一座城市、重訪同一間美術館，有些研究甚至認為這類體驗「沒有人們以為的那麼重複」。
他們還借用了角色扮演遊戲的術語「re-rolling（重骰）」，玩家反覆重開，直到跑出滿意的數值。研究者觀察到，這名使用者通常會在某一次之後，把模型剛剛生成的回覆接回自己的提示詞裡，再重開一局，代表他終於喜歡上了那個版本。
論文對他的敘事給了一個很準的描述，「用大型語言模型生成的故事，每一個結局都稍有不同，同一個故事被重新做成新的」。
在這篇論文的框架裡，他不是異常，他是一種新讀者的極端形態。研究者稱之為「唯我論的讀者兼作者（solipsistic reader-writer）」，一個人在封閉的對話迴圈裡同時生產與消費故事，另一端沒有其他人類。
寫作與閱讀，向來需要兩個人。但用 AI 創作這兩個角色很可能是同一人。
所有「AI 正在重塑創作」的句子，都少了一個主詞
回到最開始那個問題。
我們每天都在讀這樣的句子。AI 正在改變人類創作。AI 生成內容爆炸性成長。某平台每月生成幾億則內容。某模型週活躍使用者突破幾億。
這些句子沒有一句是假的。它們只是全部省略了同一件事，誰在用，用了幾次。
一份 57 萬筆對話的資料集，34% 跟寫小說有關，聽起來像是一個時代的轉向。攤開來看，是一萬人裡的兩百個人，各自在同一個坑裡挖了幾千次。把每個人的權重拉平，這個時代的轉向就縮水成 7.1%。
下一次你看到某個 AI 產品公布「本月生成一億則內容」，值得多問那一億則是幾個人生成的？
這不是要否認 AI 創作正在發生。研究者自己也說，他們認為類似的重度使用者「很可能也在 ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini 上強迫性地生成小說」。這件事是真的。
真正的問題在於，用「使用量」去描述「使用者」，是一種結構性的誤讀。而整個 AI 產業目前公布的每一個數字，用的都是前者。
本文源自 arXiv: AI Fiction in the Wild，由動區動趨整理報導。

title: 日本 Sakana AI 丟出資安模型 Fugu-Cyber，自評與 Mythos-Preview 同等級
summary:
日本 AI 獨角獸 Sakana AI 於 7 月 21 日推出資安特化模型 Fugu-Cyber，官方公告指 […]

〈日本 Sakana AI 丟出資安模型 Fugu-Cyber，自評與 Mythos-Preview 同等級〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
日本 AI 獨角獸 Sakana AI 於 7 月 21 日推出資安特化模型 Fugu-Cyber，官方公告指出在漏洞驗證榜單 CyberGym 拿下 86.9% 成功率、威脅情報榜單 CTI-REALM 拿下 72.1%，並自評與 OpenAI 的 GPT-5.5-Cyber、Anthropic 的 Mythos-Preview 等資安前沿模型「同級」。
（前情提要：日本 AI 獨角獸上線 Sakana Fugu：自動呼叫多種模型可媲美 Claude Mythos？跑分、價格一次看）
（背景補充：GPT-5.5-Cyber 資安能力打敗 Claude Mythos！白宮放行 vs 被封殺兩種命運）
日本 AI 獨角獸 Sakana AI（サカナ AI）7 月 21 日在官方部落格宣布，旗下編排模型 Sakana Fugu 家族新增資安特化版本 Fugu-Cyber，以獨立 API 端點提供。官方公告指出，Fugu-Cyber 在 CyberGym 取得 86.9% 成功率、在 CTI-REALM 取得 72.1%，並直接點名這個成績「與 GPT-5.5-Cyber、Mythos-Preview 這類專攻資安的前沿模型相當（comparable to）」。
這裡先幫中文圈的讀者校正一件事。官方用的字是「相當」，不是「超越」，公告裡也沒有排名表。部分簡中媒體把標題寫成「效能超越 GPT-5.5-Cyber」，那不是 Sakana AI 說的。
兩個榜單測的完全不是同一件事，值得用白話講清楚。CyberGym 是加州大學柏克萊分校（UC Berkeley）做的評測，把 188 個真實開源專案、1,507 個真實漏洞丟給 AI，要 AI 讀懂整包程式碼、追依賴、推理記憶體行為，最後做出一個能觸發漏洞的驗證程式。CTI-REALM 則是要 AI 讀一份威脅情報報告，翻成資安團隊能直接上線的偵測規則，中間還得對映 MITRE 攻擊技術、寫出 KQL 查詢。前者是「找洞」，後者是「守洞」。
2025 年 6 月 CyberGym 論文剛發表時，當時最強的 AI agent 成功率只有 11.9%。一年出頭，題目沒換，數字站上 86.9%。這條斜率本身比誰排第一名更值得盯著看。
不自建大模型
Fugu-Cyber 不是 Sakana AI 從零訓練的新大模型，這點是整件事最關鍵的地方。
Sakana Fugu 的本體是一套「多代理編排」（orchestration）系統，白話說就是它自己不解題，而是當排程員。收到任務後，它動態把一群專長不同的模型分派成 Thinker（想）、Worker（做）、Verifier（驗）三種角色，跑完再把結果收斂成一個回覆，對外只露出一個 API。這套排程邏輯出自 Sakana AI 兩篇 ICLR 2026 論文 TRINITY 與 the Conductor，底下實際叫了哪幾家的模型，官方明講「屬於專有資訊，設計上就不對外揭露」。
Fugu 家族目前有三個版本，Fugu（日常均衡）、Fugu Ultra（複雜推理）、Fugu Cyber（資安）。換句話說，7 月 21 日這一發不是新引擎，是同一副骨架換上資安專用的配置與使用條款。
這正是 Sakana AI 一貫的打法。這家公司 2023 年由前 Google 研究員 David Ha 與 Llion Jones（2017 年《Attention Is All You Need》論文共同作者之一）在東京創立，招牌是演化式模型合併、AI Scientist 這類「不靠堆算力」的路子。去年 11 月的 B 輪拿下 320 億日圓（約 2 億美元），投後估值約 4,320 億日圓（約 27 億美元），股東名單裡除了 MUFG、Google、Salesforce Ventures，還有美國情報體系的創投 In-Q-Tel。一家日本資安模型公司的股東名單上出現 In-Q-Tel，這個組合本身就滿有畫面的。
價格分兩級，門檻卡在申請表
計價方式官方公告本身沒寫，實際費率掛在 Sakana Fugu 產品頁的 Token Plan。Fugu-Cyber 每百萬 token 輸入 6 美元、輸出 36 美元、快取輸入 0.6 美元；上下文超過 272K token 之後跳一級，輸入 12 美元、輸出 54 美元、快取輸入 1.2 美元。
所以外傳的「輸入 6 到 12 美元、輸出 36 到 54 美元」不是浮動區間，是兩段式階梯，多數情況下你付的是 6 與 36。對照家族內另一款 Fugu Ultra 的 5 美元與 30 美元，資安版只貴了兩成。
真正的門檻在 Fugu-Cyber 採申請制，使用者必須填表說明用途、附上已驗證的聯絡資訊，由 Sakana AI 團隊逐件人工審查，透過才給存取權。同時公告搭配修訂後的使用條款，明文禁止攻擊性濫用。

title: Suno 帳號 5530 萬組個資外洩，駭客順手丟出「侵權鐵證」到唱片公司
summary:
AI 音樂平台 Suno 在 2025 年 11 月遭駭，5,530 萬組使用者 email 與數萬筆 Str […]

〈Suno 帳號 5530 萬組個資外洩，駭客順手丟出「侵權鐵證」到唱片公司〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
AI 音樂平台 Suno 在 2025 年 11 月遭駭，5,530 萬組使用者 email 與數萬筆 Stripe 付款紀錄外流，直到今年 7 月 20 日才被 Have I Been Pwned 收錄。更麻煩的是駭客連 2023 至 2024 年的原始碼一起丟出來，裡面清楚寫著 Suno 從 YouTube Music、Deezer、Genius 等來源抓了超過 38 萬小時音樂與歌詞，而這正是 Sony Music 與 UMG 現在告它的核心指控。
（前情提要：Sony 告 Suno 本月開庭：AI 拿版權歌曲訓練算不算「合理使用」首度上法庭）
（背景補充：AI 音樂新創 Suno 估值半年翻倍衝上 54 億美元，與華納和解簽下版權授權將推新產品）
帳號外洩本身已經夠糟，真正致命的是駭客順手附上的那份原始碼。
這場入侵發生在 2025 年 11 月，被攤在陽光下卻是八個月後的事。資安通報服務 Have I Been Pwned 於 7 月 20 日新增 Suno 條目，創辦人 Troy Hunt 在登入說明中指出，這批資料含有超過 5,530 萬組不重複的 email，若使用者當初是用手機號碼註冊，電話也一併在內。Troy Hunt 另外提到，其中 24% 的 email 早就出現在 HIBP 既有的外洩資料庫裡。
登入說明指出，外洩資料還包含數萬筆 Stripe 紀錄，欄位涵蓋姓名、實體地址、購買金額，以及卡別、到期日與卡號末四碼。Suno 澄清公司本身無法透過 Stripe 讀取完整卡號，直接盜刷的風險有限。這說法沒錯，但姓名加地址加消費紀錄的組合，本來就是釣魚信最好用的原料。
Suno 發言人 Rachel Racusen 沒有否認受影響人數，也確認公司在 2025 年 11 月發生資安事件。不過 Suno 官網至今沒有公告這件事，也沒有提出通知使用者的紀錄。真正把訊息推出來的是 404 Media 的報導，公司是跟在後面承認的那一方。
外洩原始碼把爬蟲公開
對唱片公司來說，帳號外洩只是開胃菜。駭客同時發布 2023 至 2024 年的 Suno 原始碼，裡面直接寫著訓練素材的來源與規模。404 Media 清點後列出的清單，除了外界原本就在猜的 YouTube Music、Deezer、Genius，還有音效素材庫 Pond5、Jamendo、Freesound、國際樂譜圖書館計畫（IMSLP），以及透過 RSS 抓取的 podcast。
光是 YouTube Music 就有 2,013,545 段音樂片段、113,879 小時，另一組標記為 ytm_tagged 的 152,162 小時，加上 Pond5 的 62,117 小時、IMSLP 的 19,514 小時、Genius 的 17,615 小時、Deezer 的 12,287 小時、Jamendo 的 3,726 小時。全部加總超過 38 萬小時，換算大約 43 年不間斷的音訊。程式碼裡的資料夾名稱就寫著 genius_hq、youtube_music、deezer、ytm_tagged，連包裝都懶得做。
這份清單的價值在於它不需要翻譯。過去兩年，唱片公司要證明 AI 模型吃過自家歌曲，得靠音訊指紋比對、拿輸出結果反推，還要請專家證人上庭解釋演算法。
Warner 已經上岸，Sony 跟 UMG 還在水裡
訴訟背景要拉回 2024 年。美國唱片業協會（RIAA）代表 Sony Music Entertainment、UMG Recordings 與 Warner Records 對 Suno 與 Udio 提起著作權訴訟，核心指控就是未經授權大規模抓取版權錄音訓練模型。Suno 一路的抗辯都是合理使用，甚至在法律檔案中承認自己訓練用了「網路上開放取得、品質合理的幾乎所有音樂檔案」，規模達數千萬首錄音。
三家原告後來分道揚鑣。Warner Music Group 在 2025 年 11 月 25 日和解並轉為授權合作，Suno 估值隨後翻倍衝上 54 億美元。Sony 與 UMG 選擇繼續打，本月才剛就合理使用進行首度正面攻防。
