Australia’s emergency services and military personnel are being trained to read paper maps, navigate without GPS support, and sail by the stars in case something knocks out the nation’s space capabilities.

A panel at the 19th Australian space forum in Adelaide on Wednesday was asked to consider what would happen “if we suddenly lost access to critical space infrastructure – no satellites, no GPS, no remote sensing, no secure communications?”

Continue reading...
full_text:
Australia’s emergency services and military personnel are being trained to read paper maps, navigate without GPS support, and sail by the stars in case something knocks out the nation’s space capabilities.
A panel at the 19th Australian space forum in Adelaide on Wednesday was asked to consider what would happen “if we suddenly lost access to critical space infrastructure – no satellites, no GPS, no remote sensing, no secure communications?”
The experts warned that Australians are unaware just how dependent they are on space, and how vulnerable that connection is to enemy attacks and solar flares.
It’s “not science fiction”, Optus satellite and space systems head, Nick Leake, said.
He described ATM networks going down, emergency services losing their situational awareness, aircraft navigation degrading, defence losing secure communications and remote communities being entirely cut off.
Aviation, freight and energy grid communications all rely on satellites, and financial systems could face “immediate cascading failure”, he said. People may only realise their service is being delivered by a satellite when they lose it.
“Most Australians have no idea that space is part of their everyday life,” Leake said.
“This isn’t science fiction. This is how critical satellite infrastructure is. Australia has one of the highest per capita dependencies on satellite infrastructure in the world.
“Right now, it’s largely unguarded.”
Flinders University adjunct professor Jackie Craig AM is an expert in cyber and virtual warfare and an incident management team leader with the South Australian state emergency service.
She said emergency services are “increasingly dependent on increasingly vulnerable systems”.
She said they now teach members to navigate with street directories and maps instead of phones – a once ubiquitous skill that has become lost in the age of Google Maps.
“What we discovered is the young people of the digital revolution can’t actually use a UBD [street directory]. They’re also very poor at reading and using maps,” she said.
“A lot of us can’t navigate.”
She said if the satellite systems went down emergency services would be “back to pencil and paper”, radios, and hard copies of procedure manuals.
Michael Murphy, deputy chief executive of the Royal Flying Doctor Service SA/NT, said if satellite systems went dark tomorrow, they would continue as normal – for about 24 hours, thanks to inbuilt contingencies and redundancies. Then, they would prioritise life-saving missions, relying on manual procedures and alternative communication methods.
He said they could go “old school” with high frequency radio and use the bush telegraph to share information in an analogue way.
“[And] we’ve got heaps of really good landmarks, the river systems, deserts, ranges, borders, water. If you’re familiar with the land, you’ll get around pretty well,” he said.
The Australian Defence Force’s air commodore, Chris Robson, said planning for a loss of satellite support wasn’t “doomsday prepping” or a “scare tactic” but “something we need to be honest about”.
“I don’t think the general public understands,” the space forces group and joint forces space component commander said.
The defence force is already offering sextant training, so members can navigate by the stars, along with terrestrial navigation training. But Robson did not think it would be frequently used.
“I don’t think that you will see too many people sitting on the bridge looking at a sextant,” he said.
The biggest risk was not an enemy attack, he said, but “that big orange glowing thing that on any single day can have a hiccup and take out a significant portion of our space capabilities”.
The panel discussed ways to make the network more resilient, including having satellite redundancy in multiple orbits, more Earth stations, and sovereign satellite capabilities, instead of relying on US giants Amazon and Starlink.

title: Great Barrier Reef microbiome mapped as researchers discover 500 bacterial species previously unknown to science
summary:
Research identifies 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what scientists estimate to be 362,802 different viruses

More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.

Analysing DNA from seawater samples of 48 reefs, researchers have mapped the microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef, documenting more than 360,000 distinct viruses as well as more than 500 new bacterial species not previously known to science.

full_text:
More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.
Analysing DNA from seawater samples of 48 reefs, researchers have mapped the microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef, documenting more than 360,000 distinct viruses as well as more than 500 new bacterial species not previously known to science.
The research, published in the journal Nature, was led by scientists at the University of Queensland and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).
Dr Yun Kit Yeoh, a senior research scientist at AIMS and a senior author of the paper, described microorganisms as a “very important part of the reef ecosystem” that underpinned marine food chains.
“Many of the microbes on the reef can photosynthesise … like plants, they can take light energy [and] can convert carbon dioxide into oxygen.
“They are eaten by krill and other zooplankton which are then consumed by other animals.
“We haven’t been able to really study a lot of them except for a select few that we can grow properly in the lab on petri dishes.”
But recent technological advances have allowed scientists to sequence DNA taken from the environment, giving a fuller picture of these microscopic communities.
The field – known as metagenomics – is akin to solving thousands of jigsaw puzzles simultaneously; a single drop of seawater can contain the DNA of thousands of different microbes.
“We wouldn’t have been able to do this, say, 10 years ago, but fortunately computing power keeps increasing at an exponential rate,” said Prof Philip Hugenholtz, a microbiologist at the University of Queensland and a senior author on the paper.
The research, which first began more than five years ago, identified 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what the researchers estimate to be 362,802 different viruses.
The analysis also identified 5,283 bacterial and archaeal genomes representing 876 distinct species – 584 of which have never been documented before.
Hugenholtz said those large figures were expected. “This is just how huge the microbial world is,” he said. “We know that everywhere we sequence … there’s always new viruses turning up.
“I was a little bit surprised that we found over 500 new bacterial species.
“The human gut and the marine ecosystem I would say are the two most sequenced ecosystems on the planet.”
The discovery raises the question as to whether the species were unique to the Great Barrier Reef, or were yet to be discovered in other reef ecosystems, Hugenholtz added.
The researchers believe the mapped microbiome could be used as a reef monitoring tool. “We can now use it to start exploring what makes a healthy reef system,” Yeoh said. “Then we can examine how these microbes respond to, say, changes … associated with climate change, with heat stress, bleaching, human activity, or other environmental perturbations.
“Microbial communities can tell you an awful lot. Often you’ll see changes in the microbial populations before you see more visible changes [on the reef].”
The microbes in a particular marine area can indicate whether fishing has occurred in a no-take zone, for example. They can also indicate whether heavy metal contamination has occurred.
“It’s quite expensive to get a readout of heavy metals – it’s cheaper to get a read out of the changes that they have on microbial communities,” Hugenholtz said.
The researchers used long-read sequencing technology, which enables large strands of DNA to be read at one time, without the need to break them into smaller fragments.
Hugenholtz likens it to doing jigsaw puzzles with bigger pieces, “which means you’ll be able to put those jigsaw puzzles back together more easily”.

title: France recorded more than 5,700 excess deaths during June heatwave
summary:
Figures come as large parts of southern Europe endure another record-breaking period of extreme temperatures

France recorded more than 5,700 excess deaths during its June heatwave, authorities have said, as swathes of southern Europe continue to endure another record-breaking period of extreme temperatures.

The French national health agency said on Wednesday that it had recorded 5,764 excess deaths ⁠between ​17 June and 2 July, an excess mortality rate of 36%.

Continue reading...
full_text:
France recorded more than 5,700 excess deaths during its June heatwave, authorities have said, as swathes of southern Europe continue to endure another record-breaking period of extreme temperatures.
The French national health agency said on Wednesday that it had recorded 5,764 excess deaths between 17 June and 2 July, an excess mortality rate of 36%.
More than half of the “unprecedented” total were recorded between 25 and 27 June, with deaths of people aged 75 and older accounting for about two-thirds of the excess mortality, the agency said.
Those who lost their lives between June 17 and July 2 died of “all causes”, none yet clearly linked to the heat, it said. France reported slightly fewer excess deaths – 5,722 – over the whole summer last year.
The announcement came as firefighters in Spain battled one of the country’s largest ever wildfires, which has burned about 32,000 hectares (79,000 acres) in the Guadalajara region north of Madrid, forcing the evacuation of 1,200 people from 34 villages in the sparsely populated area and confinement orders in 14 others.
Authorities said on Wednesday that the fire was beginning to stabilise, and residents of five villages were allowed to return home. The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said on a visit to the area that Spain had already suffered 22 major wildfires so far this year, four times more than in the same period last year.
More than 100,000 hectares had burned, the same as the whole-year average over the past decade, he said, adding that more must be done to prevent fires. “We must raise public awareness and we not trivialise the climate emergency,” he said.
The national weather agency, Aemet, said the danger of wildfires remained “very high or extreme” and was expected to increase further in the coming days. It urged people to exercise extreme caution amid highs of 42-44C and a dry westerly wind.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, while also creating conditions for sudden, destructive storms.
The Guadalajara fire comes less than two weeks after a deadly blaze devastated a small expatriate community in southern Spain, killing 13 people including several foreigners in one of the country’s deadliest wildfires on record.
Spain’s ecological transition minister, Sara Aagesen, described the Guadalajara blaze as “one of the largest in the recent history of our country”, with data showing it was exceeded only by the 37,000 hectares burned by a fire in north-west Spain last year.
In France, where two firefighters died in their vehicle in the south-western region of Gironde on Tuesday, authorities urged people to avoid using barbecues in areas experiencing heatwaves, saying nine out of 10 fires started as a result of human activity.
A wildfire has burned through 2,500 hectares in the south-eastern Var department, forcing 400 people to flee. “The situation has been very difficult, 1,100 firefighters fought all night,” William Vogl, a spokesperson for the Var firefighters, said.
In Greece, where temperatures were forecast to top 41C, authorities banned outdoor work at peak midday sun. In Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, 11 people were admitted to hospital, three with serious injuries, after a severe storm on Tuesday.
In Italy, several fires burned across Sicily on Wednesday, prompting scattered evacuations. The country’s civil protection agency has declared all of the island at the highest risk for wildfires, with high winds and 40C-plus temperatures fuelling several blazes.
Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: ​Andy Burnham’s ​domestic ​revolution ​could ​unobtrusively pull Britain ​closer to Europe
summary:
The new PM talks less about the continent than his predecessor, but his agenda is more closely aligned with the EU’s

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Europe’s leaders queued up this week to welcome Andy Burnham as Britain’s seventh prime minister since the Brexit vote – all expressing the hope that his tenure would continue the thaw in EU-UK relations initiated by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission chief, said she was looking forward to strengthening cross-Channel ties, adding that a “very good” first discussion had confirmed a common commitment to “bringing the EU and UK closer and closer”. France’s Emmanuel Macron said he hoped for a deeper relationship that gave “new momentum to the partnership” between the EU and the UK. Germany’s Friedrich Merz said he, too, was looking forward to forging an even closer bond.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Europe’s leaders queued up this week to welcome Andy Burnham as Britain’s seventh prime minister since the Brexit vote – all expressing the hope that his tenure would continue the thaw in EU-UK relations initiated by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission chief, said she was looking forward to strengthening cross-Channel ties, adding that a “very good” first discussion had confirmed a common commitment to “bringing the EU and UK closer and closer”. France’s Emmanuel Macron said he hoped for a deeper relationship that gave “new momentum to the partnership” between the EU and the UK. Germany’s Friedrich Merz said he, too, was looking forward to forging an even closer bond.
But what, realistically and concretely, can Europe expect from the Liverpudlian dubbed the “King of the North”? How might his approach to the bloc differ from Starmer’s much-trumpeted (and as often maligned) “reset” in post-Brexit relations?
We know practically nothing about what Burnham’s foreign policy might look like: his priorities, as Paul Taylor noted, are famously domestic. We do know his baseline instincts are pro-European: he argued against the “isolation” of Brexit in 2016.
Last year, he said he hoped Britain might rejoin the EU during his lifetime. This year, campaigning for the byelection he had to fight and win in order to become PM, in a constituency estimated to have voted 65% leave, he carefully clarified his position. Brexit “has been damaging”, he said, but, he added, “I also believe the last thing we should do right now is rerun those arguments.” His aim was to “unify the country”, not divide it further, so he was “not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU”.
But even if his headline focus is on the UK, Burnham knows Britain’s “economic stagnation, declining relative living standards and latent social discontent” are at least partly down to the huge Brexit hit to UK trade and investment, Taylor wrote. “Even without the compelling security and geopolitical reasons for rapprochement with the EU,” he argued, “closer engagement with Britain’s main export market would be a no-brainer to deliver healthier growth.”
But how exactly, given the immovable red lines laid down in the Labour party’s last election manifesto – no single market, no customs union, no freedom of movement – might Burnham go about it? Starmer’s longed-for “reset” was all about security cooperation and easing Brexit trade barriers. Ironically, Burnham’s focus on industrialisation, regionalism and economic sovereignty could ultimately bring the UK closer to the EU.
In a detailed analysis for the UK in a Changing Europe thinktank, Joël Reland argued that Burnham’s growth agenda, centred on domestic devolution rather than diplomacy, meant negotiations with the EU may drop down the list of UK priorities. But while the new prime minister may speak a lot less about trade access, his vision for building the UK’s “sovereign capabilities” – in fields such as AI, energy, digital infrastructure – closely mirrors the EU’s own “strategic autonomy” drive.
Burnham’s desire to reduce UK reliance on foreign-owned datacentres and US-centric tech policy aligns well with Brussels’ tech sovereignty package, perhaps leading to pragmatic UK-EU cooperation in areas such as critical minerals and cloud storage.
In short, argued Reland, Burnham may sound markedly less pro-European than his predecessor in 10 Downing St, “but he is formulating an economic and security agenda which could bring London into closer line with Brussels”. If this happens, UK-EU relations could see occasional leaders’ summits replaced, for example, with project-based re-engagement via platforms such as the EU’s committee of the Regions, and stronger support for the UK-EU joint parliamentary assembly.
At the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, senior policy fellow Anthony Dworkin likewise observed that Burnham was likely to ground foreign policy very much in local economic realities, in a way Starmer never did. In the short term, Dworkin argued, the new government’s focus will certainly be on completing the three EU-UK agreements that were due to signed at a UK-EU summit meeting on 22 July, but will now be held sometime in the autumn.
As Jennifer Rankin explained, the two sides are due to sign deals on reducing paperwork and certification for fresh food; linking emissions trading systems; and an exchange scheme allowing 18- to 30-year-olds to study and work in the EU and UK.
Longer term, the ECFR suggested, Burnham’s drive for regional regeneration – such as green manufacturing in the north – could connect directly to EU supply chain partnerships, structurally repositioning the UK alongside the EU in key sectors.
Jill Rutter at the Institute for Government observed that Starmer had spent substantial political capital on warm rhetoric toward the EU, but his intended reset had delivered only modest economic returns due to Labour’s structural red lines. Burnham would face an early choice, Rutter said, over “how much personal effort he puts into pulling this reset over the line – and what price he is prepared to pay for that – as well as how much emphasis he puts on further rounds”.
In short, Andy Burnham’s pragmatic domestic industrial goals naturally overlap with EU policy. Without shouting about it, by aligning the UK with the EU’s own priorities, he may just achieve a quieter, but far more effective UK-EU partnership.
We’ll see.
Call the Doctor
Turns out if you spend nearly four decades writing European allsorts from Athens to Aarhus and Prague to Poitiers, eventually someone gives you a strange-looking hat.
Last week, I was awarded an honorary doctorate by the University of London for my reporting on Europe. Personally, to be honoured for doing a job you love (well, most of the time) was, of course, doubly gratifying.
But 10 years after the UK voted to leave the EU, it was also, I like to think, a nod to history’s biggest ever experiment in cooperation over conflict.
Europe is, most certainly, not perfect. But the fact so many of you subscribe to this newsletter, and read the rest of the Guardian’s expanded European coverage, shows how much you think it matters – and never ceases to fascinate, surprise and frustrate.
Stick with it.

title: Food price fears after Europe’s heatwave destroys estimated €2bn of crops
summary:
Record June temperatures expected to cut grain harvest by 9m tonnes to its lowest level since 2018

The heatwave that swept across Europe in June is estimated to have cost the continent’s grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue and destroyed 9m tonnes of crops, sparking concern about the impact on the price of food.

Coceral, the European cereals and oilseeds trade association, made the estimate for the harvest of crops such as wheat, barley, maize and oats following the heatwave.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The heatwave that swept across Europe in June is estimated to have cost the continent’s grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue and destroyed 9m tonnes of crops, sparking concern about the impact on the price of food.
Coceral, the European cereals and oilseeds trade association, made the estimate for the harvest of crops such as wheat, barley, maize and oats following the heatwave.
The reduction of 9m tonnes would mean the 27 EU member states and the UK will record their smallest harvest since 2018, and represents lost crop production larger than the combined total forecast grain production of Austria, Ireland and the Netherlands.
Coceral has linked the crop losses to the hottest June on record in western Europe. Maize was affected during the crucial pollination period, while wheat was affected during the time known as “grain fill”, when cereals need moisture to fill out, a key stage of development for crop yield.
Based on current prices, the value of lost grain production is estimated by the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank to be about €2bn, although this figure does not include wider costs of the heatwave, such as lost vegetable crops and livestock.
Tom Lancaster, the ECIU’s land, food and farming analyst, said: “This will hit farmers in the pockets, reducing their income and undermining European food security at the same time. In the UK we have already seen three of the five worst harvests on record this decade, and recent heatwaves here will inevitably have cost British farmers again.”
France is expected to suffer reductions in grain production, where an estimated 3.4m tonnes of maize has been lost, with the cost of lost grains expected to reach €891m. The next biggest grain losses are expected in Hungary (2.4m tonnes) and Spain (1.4m tonnes).
Benoît Merlo, a farmer in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region of France, said a decade of adapting his farm to hotter and drier conditions had not helped this year: “With temperatures exceeding 38C for weeks on end, everything is breaking down. I’m expecting yield losses of at least 50%, or even 70%, for certain crops, such as soya.”
British farmers are reporting dry conditions across much of the UK following the June heatwave and a dry spring, although this has been felt most acutely in East Anglia and parts of south-east England, with regional variations expected.
Helen Plant, the lead analyst for cereals and oilseeds, at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), said: “The dry conditions through April and much of May have clearly taken a toll on crop development, particularly for spring crops and winter cereals with limited moisture reserves.”
The result of the UK harvest is uncertain, the AHDB said, while many farmers have had to bring forward harvesting as a result of the hot, dry weather.
Paul Tompkins, deputy president of the National Farmers’ Union, said: “Farmers and growers across the country are working around the clock to harvest crops which have come early, keep fruit and vegetables watered, and care for their livestock.
“For many arable farmers, this could be another difficult and expensive harvest after extreme weather impacts in both 2024 and 2025 which saw both drought and flood.”
The lost crops are expected to make Europe more dependent on grain imports, pushing global commodity prices higher, although this will also be affected by the southern hemisphere harvest in late 2026 and early 2027.
The shortfall in European grain production comes as global crop supplies are also tightening, as southern and western parts of the US are suffering from severe drought, affecting grain and meat production.

title: Mamdani says he can’t arrest Netanyahu as mayor and urges US to enforce ICC warrant
summary:
Mamdani admits he lacks power to arrest Israeli prime minister after saying he’s ‘not welcome’ in New York City

Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, doubled down on his support for the international criminal court on Wednesday, a day after calling on federal authorities to execute the court’s warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu’s arrest should he visit the city in the fall.

“I call on the federal government to join the international criminal court and to execute both this warrant as well as any warrant the international criminal court holds,” Mamdani told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday.

full_text:
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, doubled down on his support for the international criminal court on Wednesday, a day after calling on federal authorities to execute the court’s warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu’s arrest should he visit the city in the fall.
“I call on the federal government to join the international criminal court and to execute both this warrant as well as any warrant the international criminal court holds,” Mamdani told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday.
Those remarks came less than 24 hours after Mamdani called the Israeli prime minister a “war criminal” who is “not welcome in New York City” in a video statement posted on social media on Tuesday. The mayor admitted that he has no legal authority to direct New York police to arrest Netanyahu should he attend the United Nations general assembly in September. The mayor had previously said he was “in conversation” with city lawyers to determine whether his administration could arrest Netanyahu, as he had pledged to do during his mayoral campaign last year.
“I believe that Prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani told the New York Times last week, referring to the city in the Netherlands that is home to home to the court, known as the ICC, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
Neither the US nor Israel are members of the ICC, which the US government has long opposed and which Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, this month threatened to “dismantle” by pressuring other nations to abandon it.
The warrant, which the ICC issued for the arrest of Netanyahu and the former defence minister Yoav Gallant, accused them of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including “starvation as a method of warfare, and … murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts”.
Mamdani said he concluded his administration has no authority to execute the ICC arrest warrant, but shifted the burden on the Trump administration to do so. “It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant,” he said in Tuesday’s statement. “The federal government, however, does – and I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant.”
Trump has already said he will do no such thing.
Netanyahu “will not be arrested” on US soil, the president said in a social media post earlier this week, adding that the Israeli prime minister is “fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and “the only ones that should be arrested are the people that led Iran into this unprecedented spiral of death and destruction”.
Netanyahu had said in the past he was “not concerned” with Mamdani’s threat and his office said in a statement last week that the mayor “appears interested in diverting public attention from his follies and attacking the leader of the Jewish state and the only democracy in the Middle East”. It called the ICC a “kangaroo court”.
Other pro-Israel officials and legislators also slammed both Mamdani and the court. 
  “I think the mayor should stay in his lane,” Jonathan Harounoff, Israel’s former international spokesperson at the United Nations, told NY1, accusing him of “political theater”.
John Fetterman, one of the most staunchly pro-Israel Democrats in the Senate, called Mamdani a “clown” who should “sit down”.
“America’s not even part of that corrupt court,” Fetterman said in an interview with Fox News over the weekend. “That’s really not your purview.”
But at Wednesday’s press conference, Mamdani rejected suggestions that Israel’s war crimes in Gaza have nothing to do with New York City.
“This is something that has not only offended the conscience, the morals, the mere humanity of so many New Yorkers, but it has also ripped apart the lives of so many that have been affected by it as well,” he said. “I think that it is incredibly important that we ensure that we have done all of our due diligence when conducting a review.”

What are the proven health benefits of mushroom coffee?
Research hasn’t focused much on mushroom coffee itself. But there have been studies on some of the medicinal mushrooms—a fungi category
known for its health benefits
that’s used in traditional Chinese medicine and includes adaptogenic mushrooms—which these brews contain. For example, medicinal mushrooms such as lion’s mane, reishi, chaga, cordyceps, and turkey tail contain bioactive compounds that have demonstrated  anticancer, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and immune-modulating effects in laboratory and preclinical research, according to a 2023
published in the journal
It’s not yet known whether those translate into meaningful benefits for people.
And “mushroom coffee does include compounds like
that have been studied for their role in immune function and inflammation,” says Bazilian. Much of this research comes from lab or animal studies, she adds, or from human trials using controlled doses that may be different from what you’d get from a cup of mushroom coffee.
How does mushroom coffee compare to regular coffee?
“It’s not the same flavor as the mushrooms we’re sautéing and putting into a stir-fry,” says Marisa Moore, a registered dietitian-nutritionist based in Atlanta and author of
The Plant Love Kitchen
. Mushroom coffee doesn’t have the same taste as coffee, either. It’s more of an earthy or umami flavor, Ayoob says.
The effects of mushroom coffee are a bit different, too. “Because these are lower in caffeine—they contain about half of what’s in a cup of coffee—they will potentially give you less of that jittery feeling and they may be less harsh on the stomach,” says Dawn Jackson Blatner, a registered dietitian-nutritionist based in Chicago and author of
And because the caffeine content is lower than in coffee, there’s less of a spike-and-crash pattern with mushroom coffee.
Are there any drawbacks to mushroom coffee?
The price may be one of the biggest downsides, because mushroom coffee tends to be considerably more expensive than many bagged coffees, Ayoob says. “The more exotic the mushroom, the more likely it is to be costly.”
Another potential concern has to do with quality control. Many mushrooms “absorb compounds from their environment—so sourcing and cultivation practices matter,” says Toby Amidor, a registered dietitian based in New York. Look for products that have been tested for contaminants like lead, arsenic, and mercury.
While medicinal mushrooms are generally considered safe for many people, there are some exceptions. If you take prescription medications, it’s best to check with your doctor before trying mushroom coffee. “Some mushrooms like reishi may interact with medications such as blood thinners,” says Bazilian. And chaga is high in oxalates, so if you’re predisposed to kidney stones, mushroom coffee with chaga might be risky, Moore says.
As long as it’s safe for you, the decision is yours. Keep in mind: “This is not some magic bullet or upgrade,” says Blatner. “But if you like coffee and want a little less caffeine and the benefits of mushrooms, this could be a good thing to try out in your life.”
If you’re happy with your current java habit, there’s no reason to jump on the mushroom-coffee bandwagon. Your brew is already providing a lot more established benefits. “Coffee is one of the most well-studied beverages out there—it’s consistently associated with benefits like a reduced risk of
,” Bazilian says. “Mushroom coffee doesn’t have that depth of evidence yet.”

title: A Toxic Love Story Retraces the Bizarre Case of a Former U.S. Marshal Who Framed His Ex for a Crime
summary: The documentary focuses on the strange case of a former deputy U.S. marshal who tried to frame his ex for a crime
full_text:
On June 1, 2016, Ian and Angela Diaz approached local authorities in Anaheim, Calif. to report a case of
that seemed to have a clear culprit.
For weeks, Angela had been receiving emails from the address “Lilith is Truth.” In some folklore stories, Lilith is a woman who ran away from Adam in the Garden of Eden to live a more independent life. These emails called Angela a “sinner” and included statements like “Ian does not love you” and “you have stolen my life.”
Ian and Angela told police they believed “Lilith Is Truth” was really his ex, Michelle Hadley, saying the religious language and references to Lilith in the emails matched what she had written to Ian in the past. Later that month, Angela accused Michelle of posting photos of her in online ads soliciting men to rape her in Ian’s condo to fulfill a sexual fantasy. She
that men had come to her home in response to the ads and claimed that on one occasion, a man had attempted to attack her in her garage.
That July, police arrested Michelle on felony counts of stalking and attempted rape, among other charges. Michelle spent nearly three months in jail until authorities realized that she hadn’t been involved in the
at all. After tracing the IP address for “Lilith is Truth,” they found that all of it—the emails, the ads—had actually come from Ian and Angela’s home.
This strange and layered case is the subject of the
, which recounts the events that led to uncovering Ian and Angela as the true sources of the harassment. A former U.S. marshal, Diaz was
to 10 years in prison in 2023, for
Michelle to make it seem like she was going to harm his then-wife, Angela. Authorities first connected Angela to the emails, and in 2017, she was sentenced to five years in prison for framing Michelle. Neither Ian nor Angela participated in the documentary.
provides a timeline of the case using police interviews, bodycam footage, texts of the harassing emails, and interviews with Michelle Hadley. Here’s what to know about the twisty case.
Netflix's A Toxic Love Story features body cam footage of police questioning Ian Diaz and his wife Angela in their condo.
Tracing the harassing emails
In 2016, Angela and Ian were living together in a condo that Ian had owned with his ex-girlfriend Michelle. They told police that she would be the most logical sender of the
, painting her as a jilted lover.
But in the documentary, Michelle says she had been over him for a while. Michelle and Ian met in 2013, but she left him after two years because she said he became too controlling and tried to force his sexual fantasies onto her, like demanding she have
with a stranger on camera. Shortly after Michelle left him, Ian met Angela on a dating site, and they married in 2016.
Though it had been years since Michelle sent Ian the religious emails referencing Lilith when she was at her angriest after their breakup, they resembled the 2016 emails so much that she was arrested, accused of arranging for someone to come to the condo to
Michelle spent 88 days in prison before authorities traced the IP addresses from the emails back to her old condo, where she no longer lived. As the Washington Post
in 2017, authorities linked the emails to Angela, saying she sent them from the condo where she was living with Ian, her cellphone, and her father’s home in Arizona. In 2017, Angela pleaded guilty to charges including false imprisonment, falsely reporting crimes, and kidnapping—based on her attempt to send Michelle to prison. Michelle was completely exonerated of all charges.
It would be another four years until federal authorities discovered Angela had a co-conspirator: her own husband.
How Ian Diaz got caught
While the case started out with the Anaheim police department, the
Department of Justice
(DOJ) did their own investigation of the case because it involved a U.S. Marshal.
While Michelle was in prison, DOJ special agent Jason Higley examined police body cam footage and noticed that Ian sounded anxious and appeared to be coaching Angela on what to tell police.
In backups of Ian’s government-issued laptop, Higley found Ian’s personal email linked to correspondence between Lilith and the man who responded to the
rape fantasy ad. Higley found fragments of “Lilith is Truth” emails on the laptop, proving that Ian was behind these messages too.
“Michelle admits that she did send a couple religious emails with mention of Lilith,” says
director Alexandra Lacey, “And either Ian or Angela—and we'll never know who exactly did what—drew on that and was able to then create these hundreds of emails from this character called Lilith."
, and in 2023, he was convicted of cyberstalking, perjury, and obstruction of a federal matter and sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Angela and Ian Diaz, as pictured in Netflix's A Toxic Love Story
The mystery of Ian Diaz’s motivation
Why Ian wrote these emails, and why he harbored so much
towards his ex-girlfriend, is unclear.
“We will never know exactly what happened in the condo," Higley says in the documentary, arguing that only Ian and Angela know and “they’re not reliable witnesses.” However, Higley believes that Ian craved control: “It boils down to Ian wanting to control someone. He wanted to control Michelle, and she got away. And that made him angry, so he designed this scheme to frame his ex-girlfriend.”
Michelle explains that shortly after she and Ian bought a condo together, he installed security cameras so he could watch her in the kitchen. Whenever she was outside of the house, he’d repeatedly call her, asking where she was and what she was doing.
He also tried to change the way she looked, picking her outfits, plus making her wear fake nails and pierce her bellybutton.
As producer Emma Supple sums up the remaining questions in this case: “We will never really know who the puppet master is, who was doing exactly what, who sent which email at which time.”
Michelle Hadley in the Netflix documentary A Toxic Love Story
What happened to Michelle?
Michelle sued the Anaheim police department in 2021, arguing that the department didn’t prepare officers to adequately investigate the case, according to
“I’m on the other side of that journey,” Michelle says in
She gets the final word at the end of the documentary, talking about how she’s rebuilt her life as a mom of a young daughter, born the same day Ian was convicted.
“Raising this beautiful little girl is my fairy tale ending. I think it is ‘happily ever after.’ I’m not a princess but I get to be the hero in my own story.”

title: What Food Safety Experts Are Eating During the Cyclospora Outbreak
summary: The people who study foodborne illness for a living aren't panicking—but they are making a few targeted changes.
full_text:
If you've found yourself staring into your refrigerator wondering whether that bag of lettuce is safe to eat, you're in good company.
Many people are avoiding lettuce in the midst of the ongoing outbreak of
, a microscopic parasite that can contaminate fresh produce and cause days—or even weeks—of miserable gastrointestinal illness. It's unusually stubborn: Unlike many foodborne pathogens, it can't reliably be washed off at home.
, federal officials have linked 1,644 illnesses and 94 hospitalizations across five states to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell and traced to Taylor Farms de Mexico. Recalled products were distributed to 27 states.
Communication from public-health agencies has been
, and though investigations are ongoing, no further sources of the outbreak have been identified. So how are the people who study food safety making sense of it all?
None are panicking. But several have changed the way they shop and cook while the outbreak continues. Many of their habits are surprisingly easy to borrow.
They aren't avoiding lettuce altogether
If you expected food safety experts to swear off salads until the
outbreak is over, think again.
Donald Schaffner, a professor of food microbiology in the department of food science at Rutgers University, hasn't changed his eating habits at all. "I had a salad last night and the night before, and I'll have a salad tonight," he says. Rather than writing off an entire category of food because of an outbreak, he focuses on what's actually been recalled or linked to the current investigation. If a specific product is part of an active recall, he'll avoid it. Otherwise, "I don't worry about it,” he says.
Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute of Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, agrees that avoiding all lettuce isn't the answer. Instead, she encourages people to think about their own level of risk. She's comfortable ordering a salad at a restaurant, even knowing it's likely made with bagged lettuce, because she's healthy and not immunocompromised. "I know the risks I'm taking," she says. But she notes that the calculation is different for young children, pregnant women, older adults, and anyone with a weakened immune system, all of whom are more vulnerable to serious foodborne illness.
Frank Yiannas, who served as the FDA's deputy commissioner for food policy and response from 2018 to 2023 and is the author of
Food Safety Culture: Creating a Behavior-Based Food Safety Management System
, takes a similar approach. He'll avoid products that regulators have specifically identified or recalled—but not every food in that food group. "I'm still a big fan of eating fresh fruits and vegetables," he says. "Two days in a row, romaine salad." He notes that Americans safely consume more than 150 million servings of leafy greens every day, making it important to keep outbreaks in perspective.
They take more control over their lettuce
Some experts have changed one grocery-shopping habit over the years: They'd rather prepare their own lettuce than let someone else do it.
Bill Marler, an attorney who focuses on food-safety cases—and who
represents several people suing over the ongoing
—stopped buying prepared salads years ago. "I'm not a fan of bagged or boxed salads or pre-made kits," he says, which are usually made from greens from several different places. "You're ceding responsibility to somebody else in a large factory." Instead, he buys whole heads of lettuce, removes the outer leaves, and washes the rest himself under running water. That tactic is also recommended by the
Michigan Department of Health and Human Services
, the state most affected by the outbreak.
linked to bagged spinach, when contamination believed to have originated from wild pigs spread after spinach from across a field was harvested, chopped, washed, and packaged together. The pigs "didn't poop on everything," he says. But once the leaves were mixed, what might have remained a localized problem became a nationwide outbreak. "Convenience just isn't worth the risk."
Kowalcyk has reached a similar conclusion. She also buys whole heads of lettuce, washes them thoroughly under running water, and discards any bruised or damaged outer leaves before eating the rest. Broken leaves are more vulnerable because "that's how the bacteria gets inside," she says.
They don't take "pre-washed" at face value
For some experts, even "pre-washed" isn't enough. Gerardo Lopez, a food safety professor at the University of Arizona, still rinses bagged greens before serving them. "Just because something says pre-washed doesn't mean [it’s safe]," he says, noting there's still potential for cross-contamination. At home, he rinses leafy greens thoroughly under running water in a colander before serving them.
They pay attention to where their produce comes from
The outbreak has reinforced a lesson many food-safety experts learned long ago: where produce is grown matters.
Darin Detwiler, an associate teaching professor of food policy at Northeastern University and author of
Food Safety: Past, Present, and Predictions
, pays close attention to where his produce comes from. At farmers markets, he asks two questions before buying anything: Where was this grown? And how recently was it harvested?
If a vendor tells him the produce came from a wholesaler or middleman instead of a nearby farm, he keeps walking.
He brings that same curiosity to the grocery store. Detwiler encourages consumers to look beyond the brand name on the front of a package because it isn't always the company that actually grew the produce. During this outbreak, many people assumed they were unaffected because they didn't see "Taylor Farms" in their refrigerator—even though the same grower supplies produce sold under multiple labels.
For Detwiler, the broader point is to get as close to the source of your food as possible. "I would rather have an imperfect-looking tomato that was grown within 25 miles than a perfect tomato at the grocery store that I don't know where it came from," he says. And if you're ever unsure whether something is part of a recall, he adds, "If in doubt, throw it out. Your public health should take priority."
They lean into cooked vegetables
Some food-safety experts aren't avoiding vegetables—they're changing how they prepare them. Lopez says his family has been eating fewer salads during the outbreak and more grilled vegetables instead. Cooking vegetables to about 158°F (70°C) inactivates
, making grilled vegetables an appealing alternative while the investigation continues. His recent favorites include grilled zucchini, Brussels sprouts, corn on the cob, and tomatoes. He's also opting for cooked greens—like sautéed spinach—instead of raw salads.
They've built small habits into their kitchen routines
Years of studying foodborne illness have changed experts' routines.
Kowalcyk recommends using a digital, tip-sensitive meat thermometer because, she says, "color and texture is not a good indicator of doneness." She also skips old-fashioned dial thermometers, which need to be calibrated—and often aren't.
She has another kitchen habit that's easy to borrow. Any utensil that touches raw meat immediately goes into a designated cup on the counter. "Silverware in a cup in our family means: don't," she says. "It touched something that should not be used again." It's a simple way to prevent someone from accidentally grabbing the same tongs or spoon for ready-to-eat food.
She's equally careful at summer cookouts. Cooked food shouldn't sit out for more than two hours—and even less when temperatures are high. At a recent gathering, she nestled the hummus in a bowl of ice to keep it cold while people snacked. "Foodborne illness has a season," Kowalcyk says, which is why she's most vigilant in summer.

title: Advancing the next era of national science
summary: OpenAI outlines its commitment to advancing American science working with the U.S. Department of Energy and national labs to use frontier AI to accelerate discovery.
full_text:
Advancing the next era of national science
American leadership has always been driven by scientific leadership. The technologies behind economic growth, national security, and better lives—from energy and computing to medicine, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing—begin with the ability to discover, build, and deploy.
Frontier AI can expand that ability. It can help compress decades of scientific progress into years, strengthen the institutions behind American innovation, and give researchers new capacity to solve problems once considered out of reach.
OpenAI is committed to bringing these capabilities to American science. We are working with the U.S. government, National Laboratories, universities, and researchers to connect frontier models with the people, supercomputers, simulations, and facilities that make American science exceptional.
Our goal is to help scientists explore more ideas, test hypotheses faster, and move from insight to validated results more quickly. That requires pairing frontier models with the tools, workflows, expertise, and infrastructure of research environments, turning AI from tool to national strategic scientific infrastructure.
As part of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission(opens in a new window), OpenAI will support participating researchers through broad access, frontier capabilities, technical collaboration, and focused scientific campaigns. We will:
- Provide $4 million in Codex access to approximately 2,000 Genesis researchers at National Laboratories and universities, bringing advanced coding and reasoning capabilities into their daily work.
- Commit $3 million in API support to two large-scale scientific campaigns testing frontier models against major scientific challenges.
- Offer participating researchers up to $10 million in API usage for $2.5 million spent, expanding the work Genesis researchers can support.
- Provide selected national-laboratory researchers working on eligible biology projects access to GPT‑Rosalind’s specialized bioscience capabilities.
- Give trusted national-laboratory leaders early access to selected models and features so they can prepare the workflows, evaluations, and infrastructure needed to use them effectively.
- Expand trusted access to advanced cyber capabilities for selected national-laboratory cybersecurity researchers working to strengthen defensive research and protect critical systems.
These commitments build on our work across the national-laboratory system. In an AI Jam Session with nine National Laboratories, more than 1,000 scientists tested frontier models on domain-specific problems and provided structured feedback.
We also deployed advanced reasoning models on Venado, the supercomputer at Los Alamos National Laboratory, as a shared resource across the National Nuclear Security Administration laboratories. This work explores how frontier reasoning can support complex research alongside high-performance computing.
In bioscience, OpenAI and Los Alamos developed evaluations to study how multimodal AI systems can be used safely by scientists in realistic laboratory environments. This work can help researchers understand both the opportunities and the risks that emerge when increasingly capable systems are incorporated into consequential scientific work.
Last year, we launched our formal collaboration with Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission, which brings together DOE, its 17 National Laboratories, universities, and industry. Genesis aims to integrate AI with federal scientific data, advanced computing, experimental facilities, and expert teams—and double the productivity and impact of American research and innovation within a decade.
Our support will combine two complementary approaches: broad access, so researchers can develop practical uses for frontier models; and concentrated resources for a small number of ambitious challenges.
The initial large-scale campaigns are intended to include:
- Breakthroughs for high-temperature superconductors. This campaign would combine frontier AI, simulation, materials expertise, and experiments to pursue superconducting materials that operate at higher temperatures and practical pressures, with potential benefits across energy, transportation, medicine, scientific instrumentation, and national security.
- An Atlas of the Machine-Accessible Frontier. This campaign would examine where AI may already support meaningful scientific advances using existing knowledge, data, and computation—helping researchers and governments distinguish newly tractable problems from those that still require evidence from the physical world.
Together, these campaigns can help establish repeatable methods to apply AI to difficult national scientific challenges.
No single company, laboratory, university, or government agency can realize this opportunity alone.
Government can coordinate priorities and invest in shared infrastructure. Laboratories and universities can define important problems and uphold scientific standards. Industry can contribute frontier capabilities, engineering expertise, and deployment at scale. Researchers must remain at the center: defining the questions, choosing the methods, challenging the outputs, and validating the results.
The United States has repeatedly translated scientific leadership into national power. Frontier AI offers a chance to renew that model—and build an advantage grounded not in a single model or momentary lead, but in a deeper national capacity to apply frontier intelligence to important problems.
OpenAI is committed to working alongside scientists, National Laboratories, universities, and government to build that capability—and help turn frontier AI into sustained scientific and economic progress.

title: How the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 phones compare
summary: Samsung's latest round of folding Galaxy Z phones and updated smartwatches were announced at its July 2026 Unpacked event and set to launch on August 7th. The Galaxy Z Flip 8, Fold 8, and Fold 8 Ultra don't seem geared toward people who bought last year's model; Aside from a few design updates and AI […]
full_text:
Samsung’s latest round of folding Galaxy Z phones and updated smartwatches were announced at its July 2026 Unpacked event and set to launch on August 7th. The Galaxy Z Flip 8, Fold 8, and Fold 8 Ultra don’t seem geared toward people who bought last year’s model; Aside from a few design updates and AI features, there’s not a whole lot that’s new — unless we’re talking about the Z Fold 8.
How the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 phones compare
Not many surprises, but some welcome improvements if you know where to look.
Not many surprises, but some welcome improvements if you know where to look.
The Z Fold 8 is the foldable that will probably get the most attention in the US this year, that is, unless Apple’s rumored foldable arrives in the coming months. While its name makes it sound like the successor to last year’s Z Fold 7, it’s a new, shorter variation that starts at $1,899.99. It has a 7.6-inch main screen, and a 5.5-inch exterior screen — noticeably smaller than the new $2,099.99 Z Fold 8 Ultra. It’s nearly as feature-packed as the Ultra, with some exceptions, like having a 50-megapixel main camera instead of a 200-megapixel lens, and a slightly smaller 4,800mAh battery. There are three configurations, with the 256GB and 512GB models sporting 12GB of memory, and the 1TB model upgraded to 16GB of RAM.
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is, in a lot of ways, a direct follow-up to the Z Fold 7, but with a new name. It has a 8.0-inch main screen and a 6.5-inch cover screen that are the same size and resolution as the previous model, along with the aforementioned 200-megapixel camera with 3X telephoto optical zoom. It has the same storage and memory configurations of the smaller Fold 8.
Lastly, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 is the most affordable model starting at $1,199.99. Of the three foldables, the Flip 8 seems to have the fewest hardware updates. Its battery capacity is unchanged, as are its camera specs. However, it has the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 instead of the Exynos 2500 used in the Flip 7. We’ll have to wait until the review to see if that change will bring improvements; our review of last year’s flip phone didn’t highlight performance issues with the Samsung-made chip.
While that covers some of the surface-level changes, we have the full spec sheets below for your perusal.

full_text:
Samsung’s newest foldables are here. At Galaxy Unpacked, the company announced the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. All three devices will be available on August 7th, but you can preorder them now starting at $1,199.99, $1,899.99, and $2,099.99, respectively.
Preorders for Samsung’s new Z Fold and Flip 8 come with up to $350 in gift cards
The Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 are now available for preorder ahead of their August 7th launch.
The Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 are now available for preorder ahead of their August 7th launch.
You probably noticed that Samsung’s foldable lineup looks a little different this year. Rather than simply updating the Galaxy Z Fold 7, Samsung now has two book-style foldables: the productivity-focused Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and the shorter, wider (when folded) Galaxy Z Fold 8 that’s geared more toward entertainment. The Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is a touch thinner and lighter than its predecessor, but otherwise retains the same design as the Flip 7.
All three phones also feature Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy processor and ship with Android 17 and One UI 9, which add new AI features like Gemini Intelligence task automation and Now Nudge, which proactively surfaces helpful suggestions like an event to your calendar.
We’re still in the process of testing all three foldables, but after spending a few hours with them, we’ve shared our early hands-on impressions of the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Below, we’ve gathered everything you need to know about preordering Samsung’s new foldables, including pricing, carrier deals, and more.
Where to preorder the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99 when you buy the base model with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. If you want 512GB of storage, it costs $2,299.99, while 1TB of storage will set you back $2,699.99. The phone is available in violet shadow, graphite, cream, and shadow green, with the latter exclusive to Samsung’s online store.
In terms of deals, Amazon is including a $350 gift card with preorders of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, while Best Buy is offering a $200 gift card. Samsung, meanwhile, is throwing in $200 in Samsung credit, plus the $30 reservation credit for those who reserved, and you can also save $100 with code PAYPAL100. The company’s additionally offering up to $100 off on select Samsung products.
If you’re after Samsung’s most capable foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the one to preorder. It retains the design of the Z Fold 7 while adding a larger 5,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, plus faster 45W wired and 20W wireless charging. It offers up to 16GB of RAM and an upgraded camera system with a new 50-megapixel ultrawide sensor alongside its 200-megapixel main camera. Like the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8, it also features Samsung’s new Flex Titanium display technology, which makes the crease far less noticeable.
Where to preorder the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899 for the base model with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. You can also upgrade to 512GB of storage for $2,099.99 or 1TB of storage for $2,499.99. It’s available in lavender, graphite, cream, and a Samsung-online exclusive pistachio shade.
If you’re looking to save some money, Amazon is offering a $350 gift card when you preorder the Galaxy Z Fold 8, while Best Buy includes a $200 gift card. If you buy directly from Samsung, you’ll receive $200 in Samsung credit, along with the $30 reservation credit if you reserved ahead of time, and can save $100 with code PAYPAL100. Samsung will also take up to $100 off select Samsung products.
Unlike the larger, productivity-focused Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, the Z Fold 8 is designed more for entertainment, with a wider, shorter design that feels more like a small tablet when unfolded. The 4:3 inner display is better suited for reading and gaming than previous Fold models. It also shares many of the Ultra’s core features, including Samsung’s new Flex Titanium display technology so the crease is less noticeable, a bright 120Hz OLED display, and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy processor. Samsung has also upgraded the Fold 7’s 4,400mAh battery to a larger 4,800mAh silicon-carbon cell, though it drops the telephoto lens found on both the Fold 7 and Fold 8 Ultra in favor of a dual-camera system.
Where to preorder the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 starts at $1,199.99 for the phone with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, while the 512GB model costs $1,399.99. It’s available in pink, graphite, cream, or mint colorways, with the latter exclusive to Samsung’s online store.
If you preorder the Galaxy Z Flip 8 from Amazon, you’ll receive a $200 gift card, while Best Buy is including a $200 gift card as well. Samsung is offering $150 in Samsung credit, along with the $30 reservation credit if you reserved ahead of time for eligible customers. You also get up to $100 off on select Samsung products.
Like its predecessor, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 features a clamshell design with a 6.9-inch OLED main display and a 4.1-inch OLED cover screen that lets you check notifications, reply to messages, and access apps without unfolding the phone. It also retains a 50-megapixel main camera paired with a 12-megapixel ultrawide and a 4,300mAh battery.
The biggest changes are that it’s thinner and lighter, and now runs on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy processor. Samsung has also made the cover screen much more capable. You can now access notifications, quick settings, and a full app drawer with simple swipe gestures. You also no longer need Samsung’s Good Lock app to launch apps from the outer display.
Carrier offers and promotions
- T-Mobile is offering new and existing customers the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for free when you trade in an eligible device on an Experience Beyond or Go5G Next plan, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is available for $200 with the same qualifying trade-in and plan. The carrier is also offering the Galaxy Z Flip 8 for $100 when you add a new line or trade in an eligible device on an eligible Experience More, Experience Beyond, Go5G Plus, or Go5G Next plan.
- Verizon is taking up to $900 off the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or Galaxy Z Flip 8 with an eligible phone trade-in on the Unlimited Ultimate or Unlimited Plus plans. Meanwhile, customers on the Unlimited Welcome plan can save up to $360. All discounts are applied as 36 monthly bill credits.
- AT&T is offering up to $1,900 off the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra applied as monthly credits when you trade in an eligible phone on a Premium or higher-end plan. You can also get up to $1,000 off the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Galaxy Z Flip 8 with an eligible trade-in on qualifying plans. AT&T is also bundling the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Tab A11 5G for $1.99 per month each with Galaxy Z Fold 8 purchases.

title: Philips’ new smart toothbrush shows you where you didn’t properly brush
summary: The latest addition to Philips' Sonicare line of smart electric toothbrushes could take the guesswork out of your brushing routine. The Next-Generation DiamondClean 9900 Prestige uses a third-generation AI model to provide real-time feedback on how you're brushing through a glowing ring on its base, while a touchscreen highlights areas of your mouth that may […]
full_text:
The latest addition to Philips’ Sonicare line of smart electric toothbrushes could take the guesswork out of your brushing routine. The Next-Generation DiamondClean 9900 Prestige uses a third-generation AI model to provide real-time feedback on how you’re brushing through a glowing ring on its base, while a touchscreen highlights areas of your mouth that may need more attention when you think you’re done.
Philips’ new smart toothbrush shows you where you didn’t properly brush
The toothbrush uses AI to track its movements and suggest areas of your mouth that may need a do-over.
The toothbrush uses AI to track its movements and suggest areas of your mouth that may need a do-over.
The Sonicare Next-Generation DiamondClean 9900 Prestige is expected to launch in Europe and the US this fall, with a wider global rollout coming in 2027. Pricing hasn’t been announced, but previous versions sell for $430, and you can expect this new one to be even more expensive.
The toothbrush’s touchscreen lets you swipe through eight cleaning modes including gum health, max clean, and sensitive options. To help ensure you’re not pressing too hard while you brush, causing damage, the glowing ring on the base of the brush changes color to indicate when you should be a little gentler. But the 9900 Prestige also uses pressure sensors to adjust its intensity when you’re pressing too hard so the bristles go easier on your gums.
The touchscreen also displays what Philips calls a mouth map representing your teeth and gums in 12 different segments that are highlighted in blue or orange indicating how effective your brushing was. The 9900 Prestige tracks its movements in your mouth while you brush and areas it deems in need of a little more attention glow orange so you know exactly what areas you need to target during a second pass.

title: Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
summary: Microsoft is expanding its Xbox backward compatibility efforts today by bringing original Xbox games to PC. An early preview release will see four classic Xbox games available on PC today, as part of a bigger effort to bring more Xbox console games to PC in the future. The first four games are Blinx: The Time […]
full_text:
Microsoft is expanding its Xbox backward compatibility efforts today by bringing original Xbox games to PC. An early preview release will see four classic Xbox games available on PC today, as part of a bigger effort to bring more Xbox console games to PC in the future.
Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
The first four games are Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. You’ll be able to purchase and download each of these games on PC, and they’ll also be included with all Xbox Game Pass plans. If you already own a digital copy of these games, you can now play them on PC or handhelds like the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X.
Microsoft has also added a bunch of PC features to these games to make it easier to customize graphics settings while maintaining the original gameplay. VSync support has been added, alongside up to 4x resolution upscaling, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, fullscreen and windowed modes, and more.
Achievements are also coming to these four classic Xbox games in the coming months, a highly requested addition for both console and PC. All four titles will also include customizable language and audio settings.
Most modern PCs will be able to run these Xbox games comfortably, and Microsoft’s minimum system requirements include:
- GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310
- CPU: Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor
- RAM: 8GB
You will also need Windows 11 to run these original Xbox games, and Microsoft recommends a GTX 1070 Ti or equivalent on the GPU side and a six-core CPU like the Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 to get the best out of these games.
“This marks the beginning of a broader effort to preserve Xbox games from the past and bring them to PC over time,” says Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox. “Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC is another step toward preserving the games from the past and making it easier for you to enjoy and play more of the games you already own across the devices you use every day.”
Ronald first teased that classic Xbox games were coming to PC earlier this year, in a discussion about the next-generation Project Helix Xbox console. Microsoft’s next Xbox will also play PC games, and the company has been working on a disc-to-digital feature that will allow Xbox owners to digitize their existing physical game collections in preparation for future Xbox consoles.

summary: AMD says it's going to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, while helping to expand the AI company's computing power, according to an announcement on Wednesday. full_text:
AMD says it’s going to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, while helping to expand the AI company’s computing power, according to an announcement on Wednesday. As part of the new partnership, Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD’s Instinct MI450 AI GPUs using the chipmaker’s new Helios rack-scale system, as reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal.
AMD commits up to $5 billion to Anthropic
As part of the agreement, Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD’s AI GPUs.
As part of the agreement, Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD’s AI GPUs.
The companies plan to deploy the first gigawatt in the first half of 2027, building upon recent data center deals Anthropic has reached with SpaceX and TeraWulf. Anthropic has also signed AI infrastructure deals with Google, Broadcom, and Amazon, with rumors suggesting that it could reach an agreement with Meta as well.
AMD and Anthropic will also launch a “multi-year engineering collaboration,” where AMD will use Anthropic’s Claude across its software development, engineering, and product development. “By partnering with AMD across the stack, we are securing the capacity we need and optimizing it for training and serving Claude,” Tom Brown, Anthropic cofounder and chief compute officer, says in the press release.

title: Anthropic joins UK FCA’s AI regulatory sandbox as second cohort launches
summary: Anthropic will provide Claude AI models to companies participating in the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s next Supercharged Sandbox cohort, as the regulator pushes to test AI applications in financial services.
full_text:
Anthropic joins UK FCA’s AI regulatory sandbox as second cohort launches
Anthropic will provide Claude AI models to companies participating in the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s next Supercharged Sandbox cohort, as the regulator pushes to test AI applications in financial services.
Anthropic will provide its Claude AI models to firms participating in the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) second Supercharged Sandbox cohort, expanding the regulator’s effort to help financial companies test artificial intelligence applications in a controlled environment.
Participants will receive access to Claude, including Claude Code and Claude Cowork, to develop applications ranging from agent-led payments and fraud detection to compliance automation and AI governance. The second cohort includes 21 organizations, among them Scottish Widows, Money Advice Trust and TrueLayer.
The FCA said Wednesday it received 199 applications for the latest group, up 51% from the first round, reflecting growing demand for regulated environments where financial firms can experiment with AI systems.
The program builds on the FCA’s partnerships with NVIDIA and NayaOne, which provide participants with computing infrastructure and development tools. Alongside the second cohort, the regulator launched a 10-week Agentic Academy with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship to help firms develop and deploy AI agents in financial services.
The Supercharged Sandbox is aimed at firms in the discovery and experimentation phase of AI development, while the FCA’s separate AI Live Testing program supports firms that are ready to use AI in live markets.

title: SEC’s Peirce says crypto vaults and onchain lending may fall under securities laws
summary: The SEC commissioner said crypto vaults, onchain lending products and other asset management tools may trigger US securities laws depending on how they are structured and operated.
full_text:
SEC’s Peirce says crypto vaults and onchain lending may fall under securities laws
The SEC commissioner said crypto vaults, onchain lending products and other asset management tools may trigger US securities laws depending on how they are structured and operated.
SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce said crypto vaults and onchain lending products may fall under US securities laws, urging developers to assess whether products that actively manage user assets require regulatory compliance.
In a statement published Wednesday, Peirce said crypto vaults and lending strategies that involve discretionary decisions, including allocating assets, selecting yield-generating activities, setting lending terms and determining liquidation thresholds, may fall within the scope of federal securities laws depending on their structure and operation.
She said some vaults could be treated as securities offerings or investment companies, while parties managing vault allocations or lending parameters could also trigger investment adviser requirements.
Peirce said that some onchain loans may also qualify as securities depending on how they are structured, distributed and used.
“Moving activities that fall within the scope of the federal securities laws onchain, as a general matter, does not take those activities outside the scope of the laws the Commission administers,” Peirce said.
Peirce urged developers and operators to consult the SEC if their products may fall within its jurisdiction and invited feedback on how existing rules could better accommodate onchain finance.
Related: SEC sues Mining Automatic and founder over alleged $22M crypto mining scheme
Crypto vaults grow as regulators scrutinize onchain yield products
Crypto vaults pool user assets into onchain strategies designed to generate yield through lending markets, staking or liquidity pools. Their use has expanded this year as companies package sophisticated DeFi strategies into products aimed at both retail and institutional investors.
In April, Sentora opened its Smart Yield platform to the public, allowing users to compare and access DeFi vaults based on strategy, yield and risk metrics. Earlier, Wallet in Telegram launched self-custodial Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and USDT (USDT) vaults that provide automated yield generation without requiring users to transfer assets to a centralized custodian.
Kraken followed in May with a Bitcoin vault offering up to 2.5% variable APY by deploying wrapped Bitcoin across decentralized lending protocols including Aave and Morpho. Rewards are paid in Bitcoin and fluctuate based on borrowing demand in the underlying markets.
The products have also exposed users to technical risks. In December, decentralized finance protocol Yearn disclosed a roughly $9 million exploit affecting its legacy yETH yield vault, though the protocol said its V2 and V3 vaults were not effected.
If crypto vaults were to fall under federal securities laws, their operators could be required to register with the SEC or qualify for exemptions while complying with disclosure and other regulatory requirements.
Source: Yearnfi
