title: Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
summary: Athletes from 74 countries and territories will compete for 215 gold medals over 10 days of competition.
full_text:
Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
- Published
When the fastest man on the planet won Commonwealth relay gold for Jamaica in 2014, more than 50,000 fans cheered him home at Hampden.
But the athletes seeking to emulate Usain Bolt when the Games return to Glasgow - including mile world record holder Josh Kerr - will be competing at Scotstoun Stadium in front of 11,000 spectators.
This time round almost everything is on a smaller scale but organisers are confident fans will create a Tartan Army-style atmosphere for the 3,000 competitors who will be chasing glory.
From Friday until 2 August, 215 gold medals will be up for grabs - compared to 261 when Scotland last staged the Games - but Glasgow 2026 will see a record 47 para-sports events.
The action gets under way with bowls and para-bowls heats at 09:30, but the Games will be officially opened by King Charles during a ceremony at the Hydro later.
It will be attended by athletes from 74 nations and territories as well as dignitaries including Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and the First Minister of Wales Rhun ap Iorwerth.
Some of the 4,000 Games volunteers, aged 16 to 96, will also take part in the celebration.
Why is Glasgow hosting the Games?
Glasgow stepped in when the Australian state of Victoria pulled out of hosting the Games in July 2023.
It had only agreed to stage the event in April 2022 after the Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF) struggled to find a host.
Organisers had originally estimated the event would cost A$2.6bn (£1.35bn) and the state government had billed it as a boost for the regions.
But the projected bill soared to more than A$6 billion (£3.11bn).
Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews said the new figure was "more than twice the estimated economic benefit" it would bring to the state.
The decision not only plunged the future of the 2026 edition into doubt but the Games as whole.
But in September 2024 a deal, backed by the Scottish government, was agreed for Glasgow to host "a scaled back, but high-quality" event.
It will be staged across four venues along an eight-mile stretch - Scotstoun Stadium, Tollcross International Swimming Centre, Glasgow International Arena and the Scottish Event Campus (SEC).
In 2014 the budget for the Games was £543m but no public money has been spent on the 23rd edition, which will cost £150m in total.
The CGF is investing £100m of this, with the remainder coming from commercial revenue streams such as ticketing, sponsorship, broadcast rights and merchandise.
Athletics, cycling and swimming have proved the most popular but tickets are still available for many events.
Who is competing in Glasgow?
The triumphant 2012 London Olympics were still fresh in the mind when Glasgow last staged the Commonwealth Games.
Usain Bolt topped an athletics cast list which also included Olympic champions David Rudisha of Kenya (800m), Australia's Sally Pearson (100m hurdles) and Valerie Adams of New Zealand (shot put).
This year the most decorated track star is also a Jamaican sprinter.
Elaine Thompson-Herah made her Commonwealth debut in 2014 and went on to become the first woman in history to win back-to-back Olympic 100m and 200m titles in Rio and Tokyo.
She is aiming to defend the titles she won at Birmingham 2022.
Other big names include Canadian sprinter Andre De Grasse, who is a double Olympic champion, and two-time world 200m champion Shericka Jackson of Jamaica.
Meanwhile, Scotland's Eilish McColgan will be hoping to retain her Commonwealth title in the 10,000m.
Her triumph four years ago followed her mother Liz's victory in the same event at the 1986 Games in Edinburgh.
McColgan will line-up alongside compatriot Megan Keith, who broke the European 10k road record in Spain earlier this year.
Meanwhile, reigning 1500m Commonwealth champion Laura Muir will run the 5,000m.
In the pool, South Africa's Chad Le Clos was one of the biggest draws in 2014 after he defeated his hero, American legend Michael Phelps, in the 200m butterfly at the London Olympics.
Le Clos will return to Glasgow, where he won two golds in 2014, with the aim of becoming the most decorated male in the history of the Games by adding to his current haul of 18 medals.
- Is Glasgow ready for the Commonwealth Games - and does the city care? - Published5 days ago
 
- Hoy backs Glasgow 2026 for 'massive success' - Published5 days ago
 
Fellow Olympic champions competing at Tollcross include Mollie O'Callaghan of Australia, England's Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Daniel Wiffen of Northern Ireland.
Duncan Scott, Scotland's most successful Olympian, will hope to add to his collection of 13 Commonwealth medals.
But Archie Goodburn, who has terminal brain cancer, could provide one of the moments of the Games if he lands a podium finish in the 50m breaststroke.
Last month he told BBC Scotland: "I get goosebumps thinking about it."
Elsewhere, two five-time Commonwealth champions will be hoping to delight the home crowd.
Bowls great Alex "Tattie" Marshall will be making his eighth Games appearance and para-cycling star Neil Fachie will retire after riding both men's tandem events.
What's new for 2026?
The mile returns to the Games for the first time since the 1966 edition in Kingston, Jamaica.
The race on 1 August - which will replace the 1500m - will see a stellar line-up go head-to-head over the distance made famous by Sir Roger Bannister.
In May 1954 he became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes and later that summer won gold over the same distance at the 1954 Games.
Fast forward 72 years and the line-up will include three Scots with high hopes of a medal.
Josh Kerr, fresh from breaking the 27-year-old mile world record in London, will be a favourite to top the podium.
But the former 1500m world champion will face competition from 2022 world champion Jake Wightman and Neil Gourley, who has world and European indoor 1500m medals to his name.
Australian track sensation Cameron Myers - who ran the fastest 1500m by an under-21, external in July - will also compete in the event.
In the women's mile race Scotland will be represented by Jemma Reekie.
The decision to scale back the Games meant there was some disappointment when the final schedule was announced.
Hockey was dropped despite a £5m national hockey centre being built for Glasgow 2014.
The cycling programme, which previously included mountain biking and road races, will be confined to the track.
In gymnastics, there is no room for any rhythmic events, with only artistic gymnastics being included.
Bowls, which were last time held at Kelvingrove, will be staged indoors at the SEC.
Badminton and squash were also scrapped and there will be no diving competitions.
What happened with the baton relay?
In 2014 the baton relay visited 70 Commonwealth nations and territories over 248 days, covering a distance of 190,000km (118,060 miles).
The epic journey concluded with a 40-day trip across Scotland involving 4,000 baton bearers.
They included actor Brian Cox, Scotland manager Gordon Strachan, singer Susan Boyle, broadcaster Kirsty Wark and cycling legend Sir Chris Hoy.
This time round each competing team was given its own baton to decorate rather than transporting one across the Commonwealth.
The Scottish leg of the relay was launched on 1 July when swimmer Duncan Scott sailed up the River Clyde on a power boat.
Since then the baton has travelled to communities, events, and festivals across the country's 32 local authorities.
Who will perform at the opening ceremony?
Celtic Park staged a spectacular opening ceremony in 2014 which featured Rod Stewart, dancing Tunnock's Tea Cakes and a Red Arrows fly over.
This year the event will be staged at the Hydro and will feature performances by headliner KT Tunstall, Callum Beattie, Nathan Evans, Tom Walker and Saint Phnx.
Inspiration for the opening ceremony has come from a variety of sources, including Bad Bunny's half-time show at this year's Supe

title: Most sewage spills in England may be illegal, new research suggests
summary: The new analysis from a prominent water campaigner emerged after secret court documents were leaked.
full_text:
Most sewage spills in England may be illegal, new research suggests
- Published
Most of the sewage spills into England's waterways in the last two years may have been illegal but gone unpunished, according to new analysis.
UK law states that raw sewage should not be released during "normal" weather conditions, yet until now the regulator has not clarified exactly what that means.
But campaigner Prof Peter Hammond obtained a definition in secret court papers, and said it shows that for more than 80% of the time sewage was being spilled, the weather was "normal" - making the spills possibly illegal.
The water companies and the regulator, the Environment Agency (EA), rejected the analysis and said they were working to reduce spill numbers.
- Failing water sector needs stronger regulation, says damning review - Published3 June 2025
 
- Record number of illegal sewage spills in Windermere last year - Published31 March 2025
 
The last few years have seen growing awareness and mounting public anger at the amount of raw sewage that is being discharged into England's rivers, lakes and seas.
The country's sewage issues are, in large part, caused by the fact that drains usually take rainfall into the same network of pipes that remove waste from homes.
This means that when it rains, if there is not enough spare capacity, the system and sewage treatment works can be quickly overwhelmed.
But until now, it has not been clear what amount of rainfall there must be before water companies can legally spill raw sewage into waterways. Campaigners have said this has allowed the industry to spill routinely with no consequences.
Secret court documents
Earlier this year, a source at the EA sent Prof Hammond undisclosed documents from a court case against Southern Water for illegal sewage spilling in 2021.
It included a previously undisclosed definition of "heavy rain" conditions. And accompanying internal EA documents confirmed that water companies can spill sewage when there is "heavy" rain i.e. beyond the "normal" weather conditions.
Prof Hammond, a retired academic and campaigner whose work on sewage spills has been cited in Parliament and in economic regulator Ofwat's enforcement decisions, used the definition to run an analysis of water company spill data.
He looked at more than 350 storm overflow outlets in England and whether there had been heavy rain when they were spilling sewage.
The outlets include all of the largest sewage treatment works and a representative selection of smaller ones, across all England's nine water companies serving more than 30m people.
Hammond said he found about 86% of the raw sewage spilling hours took place when there had not been heavy rain, meaning those discharges could be potentially illegal.
None of England's water companies did well in Hammond's analysis, with even the best having a potential illegality rate of over 70% for the last two years.
"It's totally outrageous, both from the point of the water companies who are exploiting the weak regulation but also from the Environment Agency's point of view, where they've not been doing their job properly," Prof Hammond told BBC News.
The EA told BBC News that the "heavy rain" definition Hammond was using was only for the Southern Water sites and that different parts of England had different levels of rainfall, so different thresholds.
Hammond said he had also run his analysis taking into account regional variations in rainfall and it had not significantly changed the level of possible illegality, because most of the spills took place at relatively low levels of rain.
EA inaction
It is not the first time the Environment Agency's enforcement regime has been called into question.
In 2024, the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP), an independent public body, ruled that the EA was not applying legislation properly as to when sewage could be legally discharged. It said the EA was allowing water companies to spill in "normal" weather rather than "exceptional circumstances" - as the law states.
In light of the OEP report the EA issued new guidance last year, external making it clear that spills should not take place during normal weather.
But in an email exchange with the BBC the EA refused to confirm that spills should only take place during "exceptional circumstances", but said it would "always take action" if there had been a breach of the law.
"However, to meet the strict legal requirements needed to pursue a criminal conviction we must consider a wide range of factors including specific site and permit conditions, as well as rainfall totals," its spokesperson said.
Asked to provide details of completed or ongoing enforcement action related to spills in "normal" weather a spokesperson for the EA said they could not, citing "ongoing legal proceedings".
In response to Prof Hammond's analysis, a spokesperson for Water UK, which represents the water companies, told the BBC: "As confirmed by the High Court and the Office for Environmental Protection, discharges should only occur in 'exceptional circumstances' or if preventing them is technically possible but would involve excessive cost.
"In any case, we want to end all discharges and are working to end them as fast as we physically can."

title: Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
summary: The cost of parking closest to the terminal just for a few minutes has hit £10 at two of the UK's busiest airports.
full_text:
Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
- Published
Drop-off fees at the UK's major airports have risen by a third on average since last summer, new analysis has found.
The RAC looked at the cost of pulling up at the closest point to terminals at the 20 busiest airports - 16 had put up their fees since last year.
Two London airports, Gatwick and Stansted, topped the price table at £10.
Trade body Airports UK said free drop-offs were available and fees were part of airports' business models and climate change objectives.
London Gatwick's is the highest "farewell fee", charging £10 for 10 minutes on the forecourt outside either of its terminals. At Stansted, £10 buys a more generous 15 minutes, at "Express Set Down" outside departures.
London City Airport, which only started making people pay this year, is the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute.
In contrast, none of the top 10 airports in the EU charge for drop-offs, according to RAC research.
The RAC acknowledged UK airports generally offered other options for dropping people off at locations further from the terminal, sometimes with free shuttle buses.
But the motoring organisation's senior policy officer Rod Dennis said "having a captive audience should be no excuse for these 'farewell fees' – especially when they're completely at odds with how major airports around the world operate."
He said drivers needed to be especially careful of barrierless 'park now, pay later' drop-off zones, as they could face a parking charge notice if they failed to pay online or by phone within a certain period of time.
Gatwick's price hike comes as the airport tries to get more people arriving by trains and buses.
When the Transport Secretary approved the airport's plans for a second runway, one of the requirements was to have 54% of passengers using public transport.
Heathrow may also have to act to try and put people off driving to get a third runway.
A London Gatwick spokesperson said drop-off charges were aimed at disincentivising 'kiss and fly' trips and data indicated it was "influencing passengers to seek alternative options".
The airport links to 120 train stations across London and the South East, with eight local bus routes running 24/7, they said.
Passengers can still be dropped off for free at long-stay car parks, with a free shuttle bus to the terminal and Blue Badge holders are exempt from the charge, they said.
A spokesperson for Airports UK said where drop off fees are charged they are "necessary to manage congestion, and the traffic and air pollution concerns of our local communities, as well as our climate change objectives".
"These are issues that airports are mandated to manage by the government and local authorities," they said.
But Clive Wratten, CEO of the Business Travel Association, said fees were adding to businesses' costs.
"First it was environmental [reasons]. Then congestion management. Then funding new routes. Now apparently it is about offsetting tax rises," he said.
"The goalposts have moved so many times now that the credibility of any justification has long since gone."
How to avoid unexpected charges
- Check fees and how to pay them before setting off. Blue Badge holders are sometimes exempt. 
- Look for cheaper or free alternatives, for example car parks slightly further away which have shuttle buses to the terminal. 
- Research possible public transport alternatives. 
- Keep an eye on the time; make your goodbyes quick to avoid over-staying the limit. 
- Check where a taxi will drop you and whether they include the fee in their fare.

title: Why the UK is dithering over what to do about e-scooters
summary: Why is it taking so long for the government to regulate them, and what are the consequences of delay?
full_text:
When I step out of Southampton Central railway station, it takes me just seconds to spot an e-scooter. In this city, these devices have become a normal part of the transport ecosystem, along with e-bikes.
"It's just the most convenient way to commute from home to the station and back," says Keith Reed, who I speak to as he arrives at the station to catch a train to London. Keith says uses rental e-scooters twice a week. His alternative option would be his bike, but he'd then have to worry about where to leave it.
Around the city, there are parking areas for bright orange rental devices everywhere - but they're not necessarily a permanent feature. Southampton hosts one of the numerous government-backed trials around England. This one has been going on since 2021.
It also doesn't take long to find e-scooters which aren't part of the trial, but instead are owned by individuals. I see a man riding one along the pavement outside a parade of shops. He doesn't want to stop and talk.
These privately owned e-scooters are illegal to ride on public roads across the UK, but they've proliferated regardless. One expert told me the situation was a "Wild West".
Among people I spoke to in Southampton, the same concerns came up time and time again: "They're a blinking nuisance," says elderly pedestrian Fred. Another shopper, Martin, says he's "very concerned" whenever he sees them racing through precincts: "An accident's almost inevitable."
The endgame of the trials is to reach a decision on whether to make permanent hired e-scooter schemes such as the one Keith uses - and whether to bring in legislation that would legalise and regulate privately owned e-scooters too.
But six years since the trials started around England, there's still no conclusion - and as the UK government has responsibility for road traffic legislation across Great Britain, officials in Scotland and Wales say they are waiting on Westminster to act.
So why is it taking so long for the government to decide what to do, and what are the consequences of delay? What does the evidence tell us about how safe these things are?
And why are people using them in the first place - are they here to stay as a useful part of the transport offer, or will they end up being viewed as a pest on our streets?
What are e-scooters - and who rides them?
You'd recognise an e-scooter if you saw one. The Department for Transport's (DfT's) definition of an e-scooter includes no pedals, two wheels and a maximum continuous power rating of 500W.
And so far, the trials around England appear to have proved popular. According to DfT research, fom January 2022 to May 2024, 36.9 million trips were made across 30 trial areas outside of London. On average, nearly 19,500 e-scooters were available to hire every day.
Dr Yasir Ali, a reader in Transport Modelling at Loughborough University, says e-scooters are "complementary" to other modes of transport, rather than replacing them. Due to factors such as range and being exposed to the elements, they are less suitable for longer trips, rural areas with less infrastructure or in bad weather. They work best as "a first- and last-mile solution" in urban areas, to reduce reliance on cars for short trips.
Shared mobility charity CoMoUK's 2025 report suggests that for more than half of the people using rental e-scooters, the most common use was travelling to work or school. Its analysis of DfT data suggests the majority of people using hired e-scooters are male and under 35.
"Sometimes it's a bit difficult to take the bus from dot to dot", says Yan Zhang, who works at Southampton university and doesn't drive, "so for shorter distances, I'll take the scooter."
Around half of respondents to CoMoUK's online survey used it in conjunction with another mode of transport - such as riding to a railway station, like Keith.
Earlier evidence from a national evaluation of the trials published in 2022 found that although some users would have driven instead had they not had access to an e-scooter, the biggest "modal shift" - meaning switch in ways of getting around - to e-scooters was from walking. Given walking is an active mode of travel, this has raised questions over how significant the public health impact of e-scooter use really is.
And the usage of privately owned e-scooters isn't reflected in this research. The DfT has said between 760,000 and 1.2 million people in England aged 16 and over own one - despite the fact that it remains illegal to ride them in public.
In the eyes of the law, e-scooters are classed as motor vehicles. Outside of the trials, they can't be insured, and thus can only legally be ridden on private land, with the owner's permission.
The trials themselves are bound by strict rules. The devices' top speed is limited. Businesses who operate the pilots must insure them. Users must have a full or provisional driving licence, and they must not ride on the pavement. Helmets are recommended but not mandatory.
Richard Dilks, CEO of CoMoUK says "mass-scale use of something that is inherently low-carbon, low-impact, low-cost" is a "good thing" but "we also don't have rules of engagement about how they should be ridden".
And as a result of the delays in introducing regulation, Loughborogh University's Yasir Ali says "we are increasingly in a situation where the law and reality have diverged", with "the disadvantages of e-scooter use without securing the full benefits of regulation".
Against the law
Back in Southampton, I meet a lady pushing a black e-scooter, who doesn't want to give her name. She says nobody told her when she bought it that it was illegal to ride on the streets.
The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency has a unit that carries out surveillance of retailers to check they're complying with the law. But earlier this month, an investigation by the Press Association news agency discovered some retailers were advertising them for commuting purposes.
Police tell me they regularly see children illegally riding private e-scooters. Margaret Winchcomb, deputy executive director at the Parliamentary Advisory Council for Transport Safety (PACTS), says some are being specifically marketed at kids.
So what can police do? Forces regularly launch crackdowns where they seize illegally used devices, and often crush them. Each year, awareness campaigns run urging parents not to buy their kids an e-scooter for Christmas. But enforcement is a challenge.
Insp Matt Boiles from Avon and Somerset's road policing team says problems arise even with the legal trial devices - for example, people riding them after drinking alcohol, which counts as drink-driving. Riding with another person on the back is another common issue.
But officers see private e-scooters being illegally ridden in public places "all the time, every single day" and they can be really hard to catch - it isn't always safe for police in a car to pursue someone on an e-scooter, he says.
Insp Boiles despairs over parents buying them for children: "We do have parents attend a police station quite a lot, getting very, very upset that their child's £500 e-scooter has been seized." But "the legislation is really, really clear that you can't have it back".
How safe are they?
For many the biggest concern is safety.
There's a potential risk of fire if unregulated devices with lithium batteries are left to charge unattended. Most train operators have banned e-scooters on board for this reason.
But there's also the fact that riders are unprotected in the case of falling off or being hit by motorised vehicles. And - along with e-bikes - they can end up involved in collisions where pedestrians are hurt. Many trial e-scooters in the UK are restricted to 12.5mph, but privately owned scooters' speeds aren't.
Some coroners have even raised concerns. In 2022, a coroner in London called for action after the death of 14-year-old Fatima Abukah on a privately owned scooter.

title: Even camels can't cope: Africa's ships of the desert hit by rising temperatures
summary: Herders and experts tell the BBC how Africa's camels are suffering because of extreme heat.
full_text:
Even camels can't cope: Africa's ships of the desert hit by rising temperatures
- Published
Camels are famously known as the ships of the desert, but even these hardy animals are not being spared from the extremes of rising temperatures in Africa.
The Afar region of north-eastern Ethiopia is one of the hottest and driest places on Earth, where nomads often lead camel caravans carrying salt through the desert.
"I can see my camels suffering from extreme heat," Ali Umer, a camel herder from Semera in Afar, told the BBC.
"They get blisters on their feet, their eyes become watery and the hot sand burns their skin and eats up their hair when they are sitting," said the 40-year-old who owns around 500 camels.
"Within the past one month I have lost eight camel calves because of the extreme heat, it has become much more intense and difficult.
"Even the wind, which used to bring cool air, now carries heat," he said, adding he had noticed these drastic changes in the temperature in recent years.
He is not alone in his observations: scientists, animal welfare workers and various studies all mention stress, fatigue, dehydration, disease prevalence as direct impacts of extreme heat.
The higher temperatures also indirectly make camels suffer by causing severe loss of water, vegetation, and reduced shaded areas.
North Africa and the Horn of Africa host around 80% of the world's largest population of dromedary camels - those with one hump.
Over the years, farmers and cattle herders in these regions have switched to these animals because of their resilience to harsh heat and drought conditions.
But a study based on the perception of camel herders in southern Ethiopia, published in 2025, , externalshowed that high temperatures and climate variability had had a detrimental impact on camel herd health.
"Respondents reported that climate change and variability have affected camels' health, productivity, and reproductive performance," it said.
In neighbouring Somalia, the situation appears to be more serious. Research published in June, external has shown that drought-related camel mortality is a widespread crisis, affecting nearly 46% of camel-owning households.
The study included nearly 6,000 pastoral households and showed that the mortality was concentrated in northern regions, with Sool reporting a "staggering mortality rate of nearly 73%".
Extreme heat is the main cause behind the drought in the region although other factors like inadequate veterinary services and animal management make things worse, experts say.
An analysis by atmospheric scientists, external found that high temperatures in the region were behind the 2021-22 drought, as extreme heat makes water from soil and water bodies turn into vapour and plants release water in them into air as vapour.
Veterinarians say they are treating more sick camels and are seeing more deaths due to extreme heat and drought.
"We are seeing significant increase in cases of hyperthermia in camels as a result of which they get multiple infections," Hassan Nuya Guyo, a veterinary officer in Marsabit county in north-eastern Kenya bordering Ethiopia, told the BBC.
"In the last two years, we have seen a more than 15% increase in camel deaths in our county due to extreme heat."
Disease prevalence among camels and reduced milk yield from them are as a result of climate change impacts including heat stress, according to another study conducted in the Horn of Africa, external.
A similar story is playing out in North Africa. A study in Algeria, external, published this year, has shown a significant increase in camel deaths during summer heatwaves.
"Time series analysis highlights significant seasonal mortality patterns, underscoring the need for targeted interventions during high-risk periods like peak summer months; such as strategic water provisioning, supplemental feeding, and enhanced disease monitoring," it said.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says extreme heat events have become a common phenomenon in several North African countries with heatwaves having increased with a clear upward trend since 1981.
It said a number of countries in the region and the Middle East reported temperatures above 50C in 2024.
WMO's State of the Climate in Africa 2025 report, external said North Africa recorded the most rapid warming of the six subregions - 0.43C per decade - between 1991 and 2025.
Experts say camels comfortably beat the heat up to around 40C by mainly allowing their body temperature to fluctuate by several degrees throughout the day to deal with outside temperature.
By doing that they avoid sweating and, combined with concentrated urine and dry faeces, it helps them minimise water loss, while their thick skin coat helps them ward off solar radiation.
"But camels can also experience heat stress when temperatures rise beyond their comfort range," said Dr Mohammed Bengoumi, a scientist with the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), who specialises in camel health and works in North Africa.
"In many parts of the Sahara, summer temperatures now frequently exceed 50C, increasing the risk of severe heat stress, particularly when accompanied by reduced vegetation cover, water scarcity, and limited access to shade," he told the BBC.
Professor Abdelmadjid Chehma at the University of Ghardaia in Algeria, who has conducted experimental works on camels in the Sahara Desert, has a similar conclusion.
"Our works show that prolonged day-and-night heat above 41 to 45C directly attack their cells," he told the BBC.
"Their immune system suffers because such heat levels damage their white blood cells and other cells because of stress, they [the cells] struggle to repair themselves and end up destroying themselves."
For camels this means when heat stress sets in, their metabolism slows down to limit internal heat production leading to sharp reduction in food intake resulting in lethargy and generalised fatigue.
That leads to drop in milk production and also causes reproductive disorders.
Professor Mohammed el Khasmi, animal hydrobiology expert at the University of Casablanca in Morocco, has a long list of effects of heat stress he and his team have observed on camels.
Weight loss, inflammation, muscle and bone related illnesses, chemical imbalance due to kidney malfunction, infectious diseases caused by parasites were a few among them, he said.
While extreme heat is the primary culprit, its impacts become severe when other factors like loss of vegetation and water, lack of shaded areas and inadequate veterinary services add up, experts say.
This is why many herders in Ethiopia have moved their camels from the northern region, where the animals were found historically, to the south where water and vegetation are relatively available, experts there say.
"And this is not the seasonal movement of the herders," said Daniel Gelan, professor and pastoralist development researcher with Vision University in Ethiopia.
"They are leaving the northern region for good because they can no longer sustain camel herding there because of extreme heat and drought," he told the BBC.
The Horn of Africa has been recovering from the longest and most severe recorded drought spanning from 2020 to 2023, but now it is seeing another round of the harsh condition, according to charity organisation Oxfam.
It said water prices in some parts of Somalia had risen by more than 2,000% because of the drought.
Umer, the cattle herder in Afar, said he was worried that an outbreak of disease could start killing his adult camels anytime now.
His concern is valid, according to Prof Chehma.
"While camels remain the livestock herders' last line of defence against the desert, the unprecedented intensity of current heatwaves directly threatens their vital functions, turning this historically resilient animal into a climate victim," he said.
Additional reporting by BBC Amharic's Firehiwot Kassa

title: Scottish Labour at a crossroads again as Sarwar jumps ship
summary: Anas Sarwar has never made a secret of his desire to hold high office, but where does it leave Scottish Labour?
full_text:
Scottish Labour at a crossroads again as Sarwar jumps ship
- Published
Anas Sarwar has never made a secret of his desire to hold high office.
It's only a matter of weeks since he offered himself to Scottish voters as a candidate to replace John Swinney as first minister.
That went spectacularly wrong. The SNP held power for a fifth consecutive term and Labour recorded their worst Holyrood result since devolution.
While the performance of the UK government under Sir Keir Starmer gets much of the blame, there is now a live debate in the party about Sarwar's strategy.
Questions are also being asked of Scottish Labour's campaign co-directors Jackie Baillie and Douglas Alexander.
Sarwar had said he would stick around as leader to steady the ship, but his swift exit contradicts that position and is a source of controversy for some.
There are those who see it as a reward for failure given the Holyrood defeat, even if Labour was able to beat the SNP in Scotland at the UK general election two years earlier.
There are those who see it as a reward for treachery given that Sarwar was the first senior Labour figure to call for Starmer to quit - a move that undermined the then prime minister, to the eventual benefit of Andy Burnham.
- Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar set to become a minister in Burnham's government - Published14 hours ago
 
- Who is Anas Sarwar? The Scottish Labour leader returning to UK politics - Published12 hours ago
 
- Who could be the new Scottish Labour leader? - Published10 hours ago
 
The prime minister's cabinet includes a number of those who took a stand against Starmer, so perhaps it should be no surprise that Burnham would want to make Sarwar a minister too.
There are also those who see Sarwar's appointment to the Lords in order to take up his government position as hypocritical.
Sarwar previously said he would not take a peerage, and both he and Andy Burnham have expressed support for replacing the Lords with a senate of the nations and regions.
By appointing another life peer within his first few days in office, is the new PM not sending out a completely contradictory signal?
I suppose he could argue that Sarwar is an ally on his agenda to rewire how British politics works and can now agitate for change from within.
As an experienced Labour leader in a devolved parliament with previous service as a Westminster MP, Sarwar might be particularly well placed to back up Burnham's case for devolving power from parliaments into cities and communities.
Their argument is that this could be a potential driver of economic growth.
Who could replace Sarwar?
Where does all this leave Scottish Labour? At yet another crossroads.
Sarwar was the party's tenth leader since the creation of the Scottish Parliament. They are now looking for number eleven.
The current deputy leader Jackie Baillie is in acting charge as she has been on a number of occasions in the past. She has always resisted running for the top job and will almost certainly do so again.
More likely candidates include MSP Michael Marra and Sarwar's probable replacement at Holyrood Monica Lennon - if the rules of the contest allow her to run.
The snag is that you have to be an MSP to stand for the leadership and she will not be able to take her seat until the Scottish Parliament returns in September.
My gut feeling - and it is only that - is that the party's ruling body, the Scottish Executive Committee, would want to accommodate her candidacy if she would like to run.
Other names that have been mentioned include MSPs Daniel Johnson and Paul Sweeney.
As I mentioned, there is already an internal debate about what went wrong in the 2026 Holyrood campaign and what the party needs to change. These conversations would fold in to any leadership contest.
The choice of personality is obviously important as is the party's future policy offer.
There's also likely to be discussion about whether or not Scottish Labour should split from the UK party.
Others might want to revisit their opposition to another independence referendum.
Huge questions for a party that used to dominate Scottish politics and hungers for a way back to power at Holyrood.

title: Indian police cracked down on 'cockroach' protesters. They went home and made memes about it
summary: For 'cockroach' protesters, reels and memes became a way of documenting fear, making sense of violence and refusing to let it have the last word.
full_text:
Indian police cracked down on 'cockroach' protesters. They went home and made memes about it
- Published
On Monday, 20-year-old Chhavi (name changed) paused outside a Delhi metro station on her way to what would become one of the largest anti-government demonstrations against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in the Indian capital in recent years.
She balanced her phone against a railing, stepped back and filmed a quick "fit check" - a video showing off her outfit before the protest.
"Going to get beaten by cops, guys," she smiled into the camera.
Hours later, police fired tear gas and charged demonstrators with batons as tens of thousands of supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – a youth-led movement that grew from protests over exam irregularities into a broader campaign for government accountability – marched towards parliament.
They demanded the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam paper leaks and recruitment scandals. Pradhan has refused to resign, accusing the opposition of exploiting students for political gain.
Authorities suspended mobile internet around the protest site. By evening, protesters said scores had been beaten by police, while police said several officers had also been injured.
When Chhavi finally uploaded the videos that evening, one thing stood out. Before the march, she joked about being beaten by police. Hours later, she was still smiling - posing beside riot officers, flashing victory signs, filming through crowds and even interviewing an injured protester.
The clips were among thousands of reels, memes and first-person dispatches that flooded Instagram once protesters regained internet access. Some were raw with anger. Others were breathless, frightened or quietly defiant. Yet it was often the sardonic humour that drew the eye.
One young woman calmly reapplied her lipstick in front of a line of riot police. Another joked she was "serving face at the protest because the government couldn't serve justice".
One reel began as a routine outfit reveal before abruptly cutting to protesters fleeing tear gas. Another gave a deadpan "review" of tear gas, rating its smell and sting like a new restaurant.
To many watching online, the humour seemed strangely at odds with the violence. For the young people making the videos, there was no contradiction.
None of the protesters interviewed for this story spoke about algorithms, engagement or going viral. They described filming as almost inseparable from protesting itself.
And when they turned to humour, it was almost always self-directed: joking about the kilometres logged fleeing baton charges or the absurdity of filming an outfit reveal moments before running into tear gas. The jokes did not erase the fear. They coexisted with it.
Experts say the trend hints at a broader shift in how a generation raised online experiences protest.
"Older generations separated political life from everyday life," said Joyojeet Pal, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies technology and society.
"Younger generations grow up with politics alongside their memes, their family pictures and their daily commutes."
For Chhavi, documenting the protest continued once the crackdown began. Some commenters later accused her of treating the violence as content.
"But I was adrenaline-soaked, scared, petrified," she said. "It was either laugh in the face of fear or cry."
That instinct to keep filming, even as the situation turned violent, is one that Payal Arora, a digital anthropologist at Utrecht University, says has become increasingly common around the world. Smartphones have turned ordinary people into chroniclers of political upheaval, recording moments that might otherwise disappear.
"The act of capturing a protest is often an end in itself," she said. "Their message is more like: 'This happened. We were there. We will remember.'"
The humour, too, followed a pattern. No young protester described the day as funny. They spoke instead of tear gas, baton charges and the confusion of watching a peaceful march descend into chaos.
- India's 'cockroach' protest continues a day after police crackdown - Published1 day ago
 
- India has a new political superstar - a cockroach - Published21 May
 
- Why are thousands protesting for education reform in India? - Published12 hours ago
 
- The hunger-striking engineer demanding education reforms in India - Published2 days ago
 
People often mistake that humour for detachment, says Nishant Shah, director of Digital Narratives Center at School of Journalism & Communication at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. In reality, he argues, it serves almost the opposite purpose.
"Politics is everyday, emotional and experiential," he said.
Humour has long been part of protest movements. It can create solidarity, ease tension and help people endure moments of fear.
"Even when the cause is brutal and the fight fierce," Shah said, "there is joy, laughter, songs and hope. Without those things, protests don't sustain themselves."
Ishaan (name changed), 21, came to Delhi for his first protest. When tear gas landed nearby, he reached for his phone instead of leaving.
The reel he posted later showed white smoke drifting across the street beneath a simple caption: "Delhi Police doesn't realise I'm from Jamuna Paar."
For most Delhiites, the joke needed little explanation. Jamuna Paar - literally "across the Yamuna" - is shorthand for the city's eastern neighbourhoods and the subject of endless teasing over their neglected civic infrastructure.
"The smell there is worse than the tear gas," Ishan said, laughing.
He told the BBC the joke was never about pretending nothing had happened.
"It was about refusing to let fear dictate the memory of the day," he said.
Protest movements have always developed their own emotional vocabulary to help people endure moments of fear together.
India's freedom movement had songs and speeches. Trade unions marched behind banners. Student movements embraced posters and street theatre. More recently, the anti-citizenship protests were marked by murals and public readings of the Constitution, while the farmers' movement became synonymous with tractor rallies and livestreams from Delhi's borders.
The CJP protests spoke in the idiom of a generation raised online. To dismiss that language as frivolous, Shah argues, is to misunderstand what it is doing.
"We often make the mistake of trying to understand new technologies through older ways of thinking," Shah said.
But a meme is not simply today's version of a political poster, he said. It gathers meaning as people remake it, parody it and pass it on. Sharing it becomes another way of participating in the protest.
That was true for Manit, an 18-year-old engineering student. It was his first protest, and he had almost decided not to film.
"I was scared," he said. Then he looked around. "Everyone was recording, talking to the camera, just being themselves. So I asked my friend to record me."
At first glance, the reel resembled the workout videos he usually posted. Only the final frame revealed the distance on his fitness app had been logged while fleeing police baton charges.
"I escaped the lathi charge," he laughed. "I ran and ran and ended up completing my workout too."
For Manit, that was precisely the point.
"Not all young people read the news," he said. "If humour can make important conversations accessible, why wouldn't we use it?"

title: Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries
summary: Ukrainian drones have hit several retail warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries in a matter of days.
full_text:
Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries
- Published
Ukrainian drones have hit several retail warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, in a matter of days, dealing a blow to a large number of small and medium-sized businesses.
After months of drone attacks on oil depots and refineries, Kyiv says it is now targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.
But it has also frustrated hundreds of Russian sellers who depend on online marketplaces for their livelihoods, making the war feel closer to home after almost four and a half years.
"I am a mother of a disabled child, I've built the business myself," one woman complained on an expletive-laden social media post that went viral.
"I've lost 1m roubles (£9,500; $12,700)... We're already getting screwed over from every direction as it is."
In Ukraine's first attack on Wildberries at the weekend, two warehouses were hit, at Elektrostal east of Moscow and in Kotovsk in the Tambov region, some 400km (250 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Seven workers on a nightshift were killed in Kotovsk and one was fatally wounded at Elektrostal. Dozens more were injured and goods worth an estimated at £750m ($1bn) were destroyed.
Kyiv said it had struck "major logistics facilities" used to "supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment".
Further attacks overnight into Wednesday hit Wildberries logistic hubs at Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.
The company's owner Tatiana Kim said further casualties had been reported.
"We are, quite justly, bringing the war back home - to Russia," said Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals.
Sorting terminals for Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta, have come under attack, so too have warehouses owned by retail chain ATB and confectionery group Roshen.
- Ukrainian drones hit Russian online giant retailer Wildberries for second time - Published9 hours ago
 
- Who is Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ukraine's new commander-in-chief? - Published8 hours ago
 
With the situation on the front line now close to a stalemate, Ukraine's long-distance drone campaign has hit supply routes and energy facilities, in effect cutting off annexed Crimea and leading to fuel shortages across Russia.
Businesses had already been disrupted before the warehouse attacks, but now some have lost much of their stock overnight.
Wildberries and its rival Ozon are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population, it is estimated. In many remote places lacking accessible stores, Russians depend on them for much of their shopping, from clothes to household appliances.
The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies, but a variety of military-related goods such as body armour are on sale, alongside items with both civilian and drone-production applications.
Pro-war bloggers say the platforms are routinely relied on by volunteers to buy kit that is then sent to the front.
There is, however, no independent confirmation that the warehouses targeted in the attacks stored these supplies.
Unlike Western retail giant Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.
This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by businesses.
For one woman, who sells stationery items, Wildberries is the only distribution channel. The day after she delivered her goods to the Elektrostal warehouse near Moscow last Friday, she learned that it had all gone up in flames.
She still has other inventory left, but this time of the year is important for her business, as parents and students stock up for the new autumn term.
Another Wildberries trader who sells teenage clothing, told the BBC she had lost about 1.4m roubles (£13,300) worth of stock. She is halting new supplies for a few weeks.
"The outlook for working with Wildberries is very murky," she said. "Right now I have enough of a safety cushion to survive the current losses, but if there are more strikes, I probably won't manage."
Neither woman expects compensation. Earlier this month, less than two weeks before the attacks, a clause was added to their contracts, including drone attacks in the list of "force majeure events" for which Wildberries is not liable.
Company owner Tatiana Kim has promised "not to abandon" the sellers, and she has offered temporary discounts and waived shipment fees, but this has done little to calm fears of further attacks.
Supporting small and medium-sized businesses has been among Vladimir Putin's declared priorities even in wartime, and framed as a backbone of resilience in the face of Western sanctions.
But the Russian state has been unable to shield the sector from the war's impact, and there have been several shocks to businesses since the start of the year.
VAT went up from 20% to 22% in January, with extra funding earmarked for defence, and tax breaks for some businesses were scrapped.
Some 209,000 small and medium-sized companies closed in the first quarter of 2026, according to business intelligence platform Kontur.Fokus. That is 9% more than in the first three months of 2025.
Widespread internet shutdowns and a crackdown on popular messaging apps led to further troubles, and Moscow businesses lost tens of millions of dollars in one week in March, according to some estimates.
And then came the fuel crisis, triggered by Ukrainian strikes on oil depots, refineries and supply routes.
"There are already a lot of nails, and they keep hammering them in. Is [the attack on Wildberries warehouses] another nail in the coffin? Well, yes, of course," Prof Ruben Eniklopov of Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona told the BBC.
Small businesses in Russia have proved resilient in the past, but inflation is high, the budget deficit is widening, and oil and gas revenues are 23% lower than in the first six months of last year.
Russia has vast financial reserves, accumulated in peacetime, but its war in Ukraine is increasingly swallowing resources, starving the civilian economy of growth.
Additional reporting by Olga Shamina.

title: Blocked by censors, China's animal lovers take fight against abuse offline and overseas
summary: The killing of a dog and her puppies in Guangdong has sparked outrage inside and outside the country.
full_text:
Blocked by censors, China's animal lovers take fight against abuse offline and overseas
- Published
When videos showing the horrific killing of a stray dog and her puppies sparked outrage on the Chinese internet in June, Beijing's censorship machine kicked into action.
But what was unusual this time was that it pitted the shocked and angry voices against authorities who said they were concerned about the four boys involved, all of them younger than 14.
China's Communist Party regime tightly controls media and the internet to suppress criticism of the state and to manage public anger. But in this case authorities cited the age of the boys as they urged people to withhold their comments and scrubbed social media posts about the incident.
"We urge the public not to disseminate related information, to reject cyberbullying, and to work together to create a good environment for the growth of minors," reads an official statement.
But the restrictions only seemed to spur the outcry. China's animal lovers have now taken their fight offline and abroad, even putting up billboards in New York to drum up support.
In China, posts about the incident are still drawing thousands of comments across social media, three weeks after the incident. There is shock, anger and sorrow, as well as demands for laws against animal cruelty, which China currently does not have.
Disturbing footage showing the boys in the city of Jieyang, Guangdong province, hitting three puppies with sticks before setting their mother on fire emerged online at the end of June. The boys were seen laughing as the dog, named Wang Wang, burned.
Jieyang authorities said last month that the boys would not face criminal charges and would instead be sent to a "specialised school", but did not elaborate.
Some reports suggest the boys filmed themselves and uploaded the video online, but police have not commented on that. Censors have tried to block the video to protect the boys' identity, although some people argue that it should stay.
Their identities have not been revealed, but snippets of the video with their faces visible continue to circulate online. There are also unverified posts claiming to be close-ups of the boys' faces, raising the risk of other children being wrongly identified.
Countries around the world restrict information about child offenders or set a high bar for identifying them.
For instance, media coverage and public access to juvenile court documents are often restricted to minimise psychological harm caused by undue publicity.
In this case, Chinese authorities have not completely banned the discussion – keywords such as "Wang Wang" and "animal protection" still come up as trending search terms. Many are still posting about it, and even raising awareness offline.
Still, users have also reported that their posts have been removed, or their ability to share others' posts has been restricted. It is hard to say if the deleted or restricted content had named or identified any of the four boys. Officials have not said anything more on the matter.
Posts by several celebrities, including Chinese actor Du Jiang and Taiwanese actress Joe Chen, who had called for China to strengthen protection for animals also disappeared. But it's unclear if these were taken down by the celebrities themselves.
Chinese users have refused to back down though, with some turning to advocates abroad to air Wang Wang's plight.
It is hard to say why this, of all the sensitive issues that are censored in China, has galvanised such pushback.
Part of the reason could be that it's the latest in a string of animal abuse cases that have made headlines recently. And the footage seems to have had a visceral impact. Animal lover PL tells BBC Chinese she found it "affecting in a particularly severe way".
"We can't make our voices heard, so many people [outside China] are actively helping us to share this message," the woman in eastern China says.
The International Organisation for Animal Protection based in Italy says it has received more than 100 reports from people across the world, calling for the organisation to intervene. It added that it had sought more information from Chinese authorities.
In New York City's Times Square, one of the busiest pedestrian intersections in the world, photographs of Wang Wang come up on a gigantic digital screen every 35 minutes.
One of the captions reads: "She was loved. She wanted to live. She should still be here." Similar billboards have been put up on a building near Taipei 101, an iconic 101-floor skyscraper in Taiwan. This one includes a picture of Wang Wang nursing her puppies. "This planet is their home too. Justice for Wang Wang," the caption reads.
CK, a Taiwanese woman who spent NT$30,000 ($930; £692) putting up the billboard, says she hopes it can foster "a sense of unity".
"It makes everyone feel like we're speaking out together on this issue, rather than airing our individual opinions online," she tells BBC Chinese. CK has also set up accounts on platforms like Reddit and X to share the animals' plight.
"The world need to know about the cruelty these dogs have been subject to," CK says, adding that she couldn't sleep or eat properly for days after seeing a clip of the brutal killing.
Elara, another Taiwanese woman, used AI to translate a summary of the incident into more than 10 languages, such as Japanese, Portuguese and Russian, which have been circulated online.
Residents in Hong Kong and Macau have raised funds to put up posters on buses and trains.
Within mainland China, the debate continues, with much of the conversation centred around creating awareness to demand laws against animal cruelty.
A striking cartoon of Wang Wang and her puppies caught the eye of many football fans during a domestic game at a stadium in Dalian on Saturday. "Every life deserves respect and kindness," read the cartoon that was displayed on a huge screen before the game.
Homegrown businesses, such as beauty brand Amortals and streetwear label Wah Yan Ching Nin, have also placed ads outside shopping malls across the country, calling for an end to animal abuse.
Stickers and car decals featuring Wang Wang and her puppies have also been put up for sale on China's largest e-commerce platform Taobao.
And people have continued to rally online.
"Let's keep posting. Don't let the heat of discussion cool down," reads a comment on Weibo.
"Constantly speaking up does not mean disturbing social order. [We're doing this] to let more people see it and realise it's such an important thing that we do not mistreat animals," reads another.

title: A year after deadly jet crash at Bangladesh school, families demand answers
summary: This week marks one year since a military jet struck a school in Dhaka, killing 36, most of them children.
full_text:
A year after deadly jet crash at Bangladesh school, families demand answers
- Published
It was a normal day for sixth-grade student Nure Jannat Yusha when suddenly, a Bangladeshi air force jet crashed into her school in the capital, Dhaka, killing 36 people - most of them children.
Within minutes, Milestone School and College, a private institution buzzing with student activity, was transformed into a scene of chaos and raging flames.
It was the deadliest aviation disaster the country had seen in decades.
Earlier this week, families and survivors gathered to mark one year since the incident - many of them students who say they are struggling to return to normal life, Yusha among them.
"Even now, if I go to school and see a plane, I feel afraid. I can't sleep at night. In my dreams, someone is throwing me into the fire," she told BBC Bengali.
She was one of more than 160 people who were injured in the crash at Milestone School - and among those at the memorial held at a hospital in Dhaka on Tuesday, where the families of some victims say they are still waiting for answers about the deadly crash.
Yusha's mother Yasin Akter says her child had once dreamt of becoming a dancer - an aspiration that has since faded.
"My daughter screams all day and is afraid," she says, adding that Yusha has become paranoid about planes falling from the sky.
"Earlier she was interested in studies. Now she does not want to study any more."
'No one can guarantee another plane will not fall'
On 21 July 2025, a training aircraft took off from a Bangladesh Air Force Base in Dhaka at around 13:00 local time (07:00 GMT) and crashed soon after in the Uttara neighbourhood.
Images from the scene hours after the crash showed scores of emergency service workers sorting through charred rubble in an attempt to find survivors.
Authorities announced that an investigation commission had been formed to investigate the crash, but in the days that followed, hundreds of student protesters took to the streets, clashing with police as they demanded accountability over the disaster and changes to training flights regulations.
The committee's findings, which it reportedly submitted to the government last November, have not yet been made public.
According to a copy of the full report obtained by BBC Bengali, it highlighted issues like Milestone School's lack of compliance with building codes. It also found more than 600 buildings - including schools and hospitals - located near Dhaka's international airport that had violated height restrictions.
The report also found that the pilot lacked sufficient flight training and proper ground supervision. And there was no technical fault with the aircraft, the report said - contradicting an early statement by the Bangladeshi Armed Forces that the jet had experienced a mechanical fault after taking off.
The Bangladesh Armed Forces did not respond to a request for comment.
"No one can give a guarantee that another plane will not fall onto this school in the future," Mansur Helal, the husband of one victim, told the crowd during the memorial, referencing a recent BBC documentary on the committee report.
"This is truly a horrific situation. Every day around 2,500-3,000 students go to that school."
Helal's wife, schoolteacher Mahreen Chowdhury, had died in hospital from extensive burns she had suffered while rescuing students.
"The building in which this accident happened had only one door. How can there be only one door for 800-900 students?" Helal added.
Helal and others are calling for the government to release the full report.
They are also urging better government support for survivors undergoing treatment, as well as compensation for them and victims' families - which was recommended in the investigative committee report but yet to be implemented.
Health Minister Sardar Sakhawat Hossain, who was at the event on Tuesday, said the government would support survivors who require further medical treatment. And Zubaida Rahman, the wife of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, hailed the courage shown by survivors as "a source of inspiration for the nation".
But many of the students who attended the memorial this week, sporting burn scars, are still grappling with their new reality.
Mehreen, who's in the fifth grade, says she is no longer able to go to school because of her injuries.
"If I get a little sunlight, my whole body burns. For that reason, I do not go to school any more."
It has also affected her sleep and learning ability: "Earlier, if I read something, I would memorise it in two minutes. Now I can't memorise a line in two hours.
"I can't sleep at night. When I do sleep, I often have strange dreams. I still can't forget that incident."

title: Google burning through cash with spiralling AI costs
summary: The company said earlier this year it expected to spend as much as $190bn on AI investments.
full_text:
Google burning through cash with spiralling AI costs
- Published
Google parent Alphabet saw its business continue to grow in recent months, yet growing spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure put its leftover cash into negative territory.
The company's free cash flow, the cash it maintained after paying for operations and investments, came in at negative $5.9bn (£4.3bn) for the first time in at least a decade, according to its past financial records.
Alphabet's spending on AI is now expected to hit as much as $205bn this year, an increase from $190bn, as major tech companies race to build around a new wave of the technology.
Meanwhile, Alphabet's combined quarterly revenue hit $119.8bn, up 23% compared with the same time last year.
But the company's stock fell 4% in after hours trading.
Anat Ashkanazi, Google's chief financial officer, noted on a call with financial analysts that the company had shown negative free cash flow due to growing capital expenditures, essentially all of which was related to AI spending.
She said the company spent $45bn in the second quarter, with 60% of the cost going towards servers and the remaining 40% going towards data centres.
Alphabet's capital spending was $36bn in the first quarter of this year.
Ashkanazi said on the call that when it comes to AI, "the demand still outpaces that investment".
"As long as we see these attractive opportunities to invest, we will continue to invest."
Sundar Pichai, Google's chief executive, said that the technological shift to AI tools and capabilities still "feels like early innings in a shift across multiple areas" and that the company's plans around generating financial returns on its spending were "disciplined".
"What I see with what you can do with frontier capabilities, there is still a lot of work left to do to translate that into experiences for our users. So that looks like extraordinary opportunities with extraordinary returns."
Tesla, the electric vehicle company controlled by Elon Musk, also reported negative free cash flow on Wednesday of $1.1bn for the second quarter due to its own increasing investment costs.
It was the company's first negative showing of leftover cash in two years, according to its financial records.
Vaibhav Taneja, Tesla's chief financial officer, said during a call with analysts that the company will spend as much as $25bn this year, more than double its capital spending in 2025.
He added that Tesla was in "a big investment cycle" and that its spending would probably increase further over the next three years.
Tesla's stock also dropped by 4% in after hours trading.

summary: Claimed attacks come days after Houthis announced naval embargo on Saudi vessels
full_text:
Yemen’s Houthis claim attack on two Saudi oil tankers
Claimed attacks come days after Houthis announced naval embargo on Saudi vessels.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have claimed an attack on two Saudi oil tankers transiting through the Red Sea.
“We targeted two Saudi oil tankers, named ENCELA and LAYLIA, for their violation of the blockade decision issued by the armed forces,” Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Wednesday.

Saree added that the attacks were carried out, “using a number of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones”, and led to fires on the ships.
The Houthis had also forced “nearly ten ships… to abandon their routes, and turn back”, Saree said.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the claims, but the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said it had received reports that a tanker has been struck.
“The master of a tanker reports being struck by an unknown projectile which has caused a fire onboard that the crew are currently fighting,” UKMTO, which monitors shipping in the region, said.
Yemen’s Houthi group, which has fought the Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition that backs it for more than a decade, imposed a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia on July 20. That followed some of the worst violence Yemen has seen for four years, after the Yemeni government bombed the Houthi-controlled Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane from landing.
The Houthis said the declaration of the maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia was “based on the equation of ‘an eye for an eye’ and affirmed “the right of our great people to respond to the blockade with a blockade”.
The group, which seized Sanaa in 2014, accused Saudi leaders of imposing “an unjust and oppressive siege” for nearly 12 years, “plundering our resources and imposing a comprehensive blockade on our ports and airports by land, sea, and air”.
Riyadh has rejected claims that it was imposing a siege on the Yemeni people, and the group’s critics point out that they have rejected a proposal from Jordan to resume flights between Amman and Sanaa.
Amid the disruption in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Israel war on Iran, Saudi Arabia has been attempting to facilitate oil flow through alternative routes through the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. But that route is now under threat from the Houthis.
The Houthis disrupted global commerce when they began attacking ships around the Bab al-Mandeb after the launch of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. The attacks ended with the announcement of a “ceasefire” in Gaza in October 2025.
The Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden is one of the world’s most important shipping routes, including for oil exports.
Between Yemen to the northeast and Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa to the southwest, the strait is just 29km (18 miles) wide at its narrowest point, limiting traffic to two channels for inbound and outbound vessels using the Suez Canal.
In 2024, about 4.1 billion barrels of crude oil and refined petroleum products passed through the strait – about 5 percent of the global total.
With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed since Israel and the US launched their war on Iran in late February, shutting down Bab al-Mandeb as well could block 25 percent of the world’s oil and gas supply.

title: Rubio says US, China must ‘work through’ big differences at ASEAN meeting
summary: Rubio met his Chinese counterpart to discuss managing tensions ahead of President Xi Jinping's upcoming US visit.
full_text:
Rubio says US, China must ‘work through’ big differences at ASEAN meeting
Rubio met his Chinese counterpart to discuss managing tensions ahead of President Xi Jinping’s upcoming US visit.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi at a gathering of southeast Asian foreign ministers, to discuss how to manage bilateral tensions ahead of a planned summit between US President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping.
The meeting on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gathering of foreign ministers in Manila on Wednesday came amid tensions over China’s conduct in the disputed South China Sea and the US war against Iran. ASEAN countries have expressed concerns about both issues at the meeting.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3US targets China in move to ban military-grade drone imports
- list 2 of 3Trump imposes 50% US tariffs on some Canadian goods, citing discrimination
- list 3 of 3China and Philippines trade accusations after sailor injured at sea
Relations between Washington and Beijing have also been complicated by Trump’s accusations that China meddled in US elections, allegations Beijing has dismissed as “pure fabrication”.
Rubio said the US and China have “great differences” that are likely to persist “for the foreseeable future”, but that he and Wang discussed the need to manage those disagreements to ensure Xi has a “very positive visit” to the US. Xi is expected to visit in September.
Wang said the US must “respect China’s core interests … effectively manage differences and disagreements, and address China’s legitimate concerns”, according to an official Chinese summary of their meeting. It described the talks as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”.
The two sides agreed to “make sound preparations for the next stage of high-level exchanges,” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
‘Commerce as geopolitical weapon’
Wednesday’s meeting came two days after a confrontation between Chinese and Philippine vessels in the South China Sea left a Philippine sailor injured, leading both countries to summon each other’s ambassador.
The incident this week took place on Monday at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal. The Philippines said Chinese coastguard struck one of the Philippine navy staff on the head with a wooden baton, while China said the Philippine personnel were the first to attack and accused Philippine vessels of ramming a Chinese patrol boat.
Rubio said the altercation benefited nobody, adding that Washington had reiterated in all its meetings that it was bound by a defence treaty to stand up for Manila.
“We intend to live up to our treaty obligations, and I think we’ve done so, and will continue to do so,” he said.
Rubio’s remarks echo an opinion piece he published in Philippine media on Tuesday about Beijing’s conduct in the South China Sea. Rubio warned of “dire new threats” if those waters were to “fall under the control of a power willing to use commerce as a geopolitical weapon”.
Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea via a line on its maps that cuts into the exclusive economic zones of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, and is at the centre of long-running disputes over a multitude of islands.
Disputes between the Philippines and China have increased in recent years as Manila takes a bolder stance while pursuing closer defence ties with the US, Australia and Japan.
The US has increased military financing for the Philippines to $100mn for the 2026 fiscal year and is providing an additional $9mn to expand a coastguard pier on the island of Palawan “to enhance Philippine maritime law enforcement presence and sustain operations in the South China Sea”, the State Department said in a fact sheet.
Discussing the US relationship with ASEAN member states, Rubio said the security and prosperity of the US and southeast Asia were closely interconnected.
“I believe very much that the future and the story of the 21st century will be written in this region and by how events unfold here,” he said.
Iran ‘not serious about talks’, says Rubio
Rubio also addressed the situation with Iran in a meeting with ASEAN foreign ministers, claiming that Tehran was responsible for the latest escalation.
“The problem we’re having right now is that they’re not serious about talks,” Rubio said. “If they’re serious, we’re serious. If they’re not, then we will do what’s necessary to protect our interests, and also the interests of our allies.”
The US has carried out strikes on Iran for eleven consecutive nights, including targeting roads, bridges and power plants in recent attacks, all but shattering an interim peace deal agreed by the two sides last month.
Rubio stressed that Iran could not be allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz, as it could set a dangerous precedent for other parts of the world.

title: Iranian missiles show deadly precision amid US-Iran war escalation
summary: Killing of three US soldiers at Jordan base shows Iran maintains the ability to exact deadly toll in grinding conflict.
full_text:
Iranian missiles show deadly precision amid US-Iran war escalation
The killing of three US soldiers at a Jordan base shows Iran maintains the ability to exact a deadly toll in grinding conflict.
An Iranian attack on a United States military site in Jordan that killed three US soldiers has shown the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) ability to inflict a deadly toll five months into the US-Israel war on Iran.
The strikes on Friday were the first time US soldiers have been killed by Iranian attacks on US military installations since March 1, just hours after the US and Israel launched the war.
