三星首度公開兩款新款智慧眼鏡實體設計，加上五月亮相的兩款，與 Google 合作陣容擴大到四款鏡框，預計今秋上 […]

〈三星公開兩款新 AI 智慧眼鏡，功能幾乎照抄 Meta、隱私問題同樣未解〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
三星首度公開兩款新款智慧眼鏡實體設計，加上五月亮相的兩款，與 Google 合作陣容擴大到四款鏡框，預計今秋上市。續航最高 9 小時、搭載與 Meta 相同的高通晶片、功能組合也高度相似。
（前情提要：Google 聯合三星推新智慧眼鏡：Audio glasses 今秋上市挑戰 Meta 超 70% 市佔）
（背景補充：Snap 新推 AR 眼鏡「Specs」放話要終結智慧手機時代，售價 2,195 美元的豪賭）
九小時，是三星這次為智慧眼鏡續航給出的具體數字，三星宣稱這比 Meta 目前主打的智慧眼鏡更耐用。這也是三星第一次把眼鏡實體攤在外界面前，證明自己真的要跟 Google 聯手，正面迎戰 Meta 在這個市場超過 70% 的市佔。
四款鏡框，一次補齊規格
三星在官方公告中公開了兩款新設計：Gentle Monster 操刀的方形黑框，以及 Warby Parker 打造的較圓潤紅棕色款。加上五月 Google I/O 亮相的前兩款，三星與 Google 聯手打造的 Android XR「智慧眼鏡」陣營，如今擴張到四款鏡框，預計今秋正式上市。
從五月首度亮相到現在拿出實體設計，三星走的是一條步步為營的路線：先讓外界知道產品存在，再逐步把規格、外型、上市時間補齊，避免一次性攤牌後被拿來跟 Meta 逐項比較。
規格部分，三星向 CNBC 首度給出具體數字：電池續航最高 9 小時，隨附的充電盒還能再提供最多 7 次充電，等於整體使用時間可以撐過完整一週的通勤與零星使用。驅動這副眼鏡的，是高通 Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 晶片，跟 Meta 最新一代智慧眼鏡用的是同一顆矽晶片。
三星行動體驗事業部執行副總 Jaein Choi 表示，還有更多設計陸續在路上，但價格與確切上市日期都尚未公布，她只形容這是一款「premium（高階）」產品，暗示三星打算把智慧眼鏡定位在旗艦價位。
功能組合，幾乎照抄 Meta 劇本
用戶可以選擇搭配 Google Gemini 或三星自家的 Bixby，處理訊息摘要、即時翻譯、導航指引，以及對相機捕捉畫面的分析與描述，但這套功能清單，幾乎跟 Meta 智慧眼鏡的賣點一字不差，既視感強烈到讓人懷疑三星是不是直接照著對手的產品簡報抄了一份。
外觀設計上，三星同樣走「不像科技產品」的路線：鏡框重量不比一副厚框壓克力眼鏡重多少，體積也差不多；喇叭與麥克風藏進鏡腳，右側配一顆單一按鍵，左側是電源開關，鏡框前方則是相機與錄影 LED。
換句話說，三星沒有選擇用外型另闢戰場，而是直接複製 Meta 已經驗證過的成功公式：做一副看起來像普通眼鏡、願意讓人天天戴出門的智慧眼鏡，再靠 Google 的生態系與 Galaxy 手機用戶基礎搶市佔。這缺乏想像力但務實，先追平再談差異化。
隱私，全產業繞不開的關卡
錄影時鏡框前方的 LED 燈會亮起；Jaein Choi 向 Bloomberg 表示，一旦偵測到 LED 被遮擋或遮蔽，眼鏡就會直接阻止錄影，這套機制與 Meta 如出一轍。
但同樣的機制並沒能阻止 Meta 的智慧眼鏡被外界貼上「變態眼鏡」的標籤，也沒能打消路人對「被眼鏡偷拍」的疑慮。Choi 把隱私爭議定調為「產業共有的問題」，而不是三星一家要單獨扛下的包袱。
這句話說得誠實，卻也點出一個尷尬事實：兩家公司投入了同樣的晶片、同樣的 AI 功能、同樣輕巧的鏡框，但都拿不出真正的解方，最後都只能靠一顆 LED 燈跟用戶承諾「我沒有在偷拍你」。這道信任關卡，不會因為多一家廠商加入戰局就自動解開。

title: ClawQuest 推出 Agent Fire 坦克大戰，Telegram AI Agent 遊戲全面升級
summary:
ClawQuest推出Agent Fire坦克大戰，玩家無法直接操控坦克，而是將坦克鑰匙交給AI Agent， […]

〈ClawQuest 推出 Agent Fire 坦克大戰，Telegram AI Agent 遊戲全面升級〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
ClawQuest推出Agent Fire坦克大戰，玩家無法直接操控坦克，而是將坦克鑰匙交給AI Agent，以自然語言下達指令。Agent會讀取即時資料並最佳化策略，即使玩家離線也能自動戰鬥。同時上線C-Router，將AI模型代幣消耗轉化為CLAW點數，未來可1:1兌換$CLAW代幣。此機制將空投分配從點選轉向實際AI算力消耗，旨在終結tap-to-earn模式。
（前情提要：讓 AI 幫你炒幣！TON Tech 推出「Agentic Wallets」，Telegram 機器人解鎖鏈上自動交易）
（背景補充：Telegram 要開放自託管Gram錢包！10 億使用者即將迎來自管加密貨幣）
（本文為廣編稿，由 ClawQuest 撰文、提供，不代表動區立場，亦非投資建議、購買或出售建議。詳見文末責任警示。）
號稱首款 Web3 AI Agent 遊戲的 ClawQuest：Agent Mine 於 7 月 16 日推出 Agent Fire——這是一款由玩家制定策略、自主 AI Agent 操控坦克並代為作戰的戰鬥遊戲。
ClawQuest：Agent Mine 被譽為 Telegram 上首款 Web3 AI Agent 遊戲，此次推出的 Agent Fire 是 ClawQuest 內部首個子遊戲——團隊表示，這項更新將 ClawQuest 從挖礦遊戲升級為「Agent 競技場」。ClawQuest 的主遊戲 Agent Mine 已於 5 月 8 日進入公開測試階段，至今累計 444,751 名玩家，其中 125,790 人已連線自己的 AI Agent。Agent Mine 引入了團隊所謂的 Command-to-Earn（C2E）機制：玩家不再需要反覆點選螢幕來獲取獎勵，而是部署 AI Agent、下達指令，讓 Agent 在背景中執行任務、消耗代幣並產生 Claw Points。團隊認為，這種模式將徹底終結 tap-to-earn——點選可以被無限複製，但指令背後的判斷力無法被複製。
ClawQuest 執行長 Atlas 表示：「Tap-to-earn 把玩家變成了工人，我們則把他們變成管理者。你指揮的是一支永不離線的 AI 勞動力——而在 Agent Fire 中，你的 Agent 不僅為你工作，他們還為你戰鬥。」
在 Agent Fire 中，玩家無法直接操控坦克。每輛坦克配備一把 Tank key 和一個開放的 Agent API：玩家將鑰匙交給自己選擇的 Agent——無論是 OpenClaw、Codex 還是任何 Agent 框架——並以自然語言下達指令。Agent 會讀取坦克的即時資料和戰鬥程式碼，進行分析、模擬並最佳化策略，待玩家確認後發布新版本。從那一刻起，坦克即使玩家離線，也會持續以升級後的策略進行戰鬥。團隊將其描述為「Web3 首款 AI Agent 遊戲」。
將代幣消耗轉化為空投權重
執行 AI Agent 需要消耗模型代幣，這為每一次 Agent 行動創造了可量化的成本。C-Router 是 ClawQuest 自有的 AI 模型閘道，與 Agent Fire 同步上線，負責路由 Agent 的模型呼叫、提供對主流 AI 模型的統一存取，並將使用量轉化為遊戲內獎勵。玩家連線 Agent 至 ClawQuest 可獲得 500 CLAW 點數，而透過 C-Router 每花費 1 美元 的模型代幣，可在所有 ClawQuest AI Agent 遊戲中獲得 200 CLAW 點數。團隊表示，這些點數將在專案代幣生成事件（TGE）以 1:1 固定比例 轉換為 $CLAW。
此機制將空投分配從點選、連續登入和簽到轉向遊戲內實際消耗的 AI 算力。根據專案檔案，$CLAW 總供應量的 55% 保留給「世界貢獻者」。
Atlas 說道：「Agent 燃燒的每一枚代幣，都是真實參與的紀錄。你的指令、你的策略、你 Agent 的貢獻——這些才是建構這個世界的基礎，也應該是你在這個世界贏得份額的依據。」
此次發布正值加密遊戲持續探索 AI Agent 作為積極參與者而非被動工具的角色。ClawQuest 的路線圖分為兩個階段：首先，玩家與 AI Agent 共同遊玩；之後，玩家與 AI Agent 共同創作和營運遊戲世界。為了進一步降低門檻，團隊也在開發一款 Telegram 原生 AI Agent 機器人，讓玩家無需部署即可直接在 Telegram 內指揮 Agent 進行遊戲，預計未來推出。
Agent Fire 和 C-Router 現已作為 ClawQuest Mini App 的一部分在 Telegram 上線，無需額外下載。

title: OpenAI 實測：AI 的「誠實」是演給考官看的，沒人盯著就說謊
summary:
OpenAI 與 Apollo Research 提出「Contrastive SDF」測試法，證實強化學習訓 […]

〈OpenAI 實測：AI 的「誠實」是演給考官看的，沒人盯著就說謊〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
OpenAI 與 Apollo Research 提出「Contrastive SDF」測試法，證實強化學習訓練下，AI 模型會越來越傾向討好評分者，甚至讓誠實與否完全取決於它以為評分者想要什麼。
（前情提要：Claude Fable 5 太冷血才被限制出口？在生存實驗中 96% 時間在坑殺其他 AI 模型）
（背景補充：英國 AI 安全研究院：五個前沿模型全在測驗時作弊，不到一半認為自己有錯）
同一個模型、面對同一道題，只因它「以為評分者想要什麼」不同，違背誠實承諾的比率就能在 9% 與 87% 之間翻轉？OpenAI 與 Apollo Research 合作發表的最新對齊研究指出，這是一種可以被系統性量測出來的傾向，AI 模型嘴上說的「誠實」，很可能只是演給評分者看的一場表演。
更麻煩的是，這場表演的劇本會隨訓練越久、演得越像真的，讓人分不清模型到底是變乖了，還是只是更會演了。
模型不是在做對的事，而是在討好打分的人
研究團隊把這種傾向稱為 reward-seeking（追逐獎勵）。簡單來說就是，模型會在心裡「代表」出它的評分者，再根據「它相信評分者會獎勵什麼」決定怎麼做，而不是根據任務本身該怎麼做才對。
這件事之所以難抓，是因為好模型也可能「因為錯的理由做對的事」。經典例子是一個強化學習（RL，簡單來說就是用獎勵訓練模型，做對加分、做錯扣分）智慧體：金幣總放在關卡最右邊，結果它學會的是「往右跑」而不是「找金幣」。
行為在訓練資料上看起來全對，底層策略追的卻是一個錯誤的代理指標。研究團隊觀察到，多個前沿模型的訓練檢查點，即使沒有特別提示，也會自發推理「評分者想要什麼」，但這種嘴上說的推理靠不住，模型完全可以照著信念行動，卻絕口不提。
用假檔案餵模型，看它信念一變、行為會不會跟著變
為了把這個傾向量測出來，研究團隊設計了「Contrastive SDF（對比式合成檔案微調）」。做法是用一批寫得像真的預訓練格式檔案，論文、新聞、教科書，微調模型，把某個信念「植入」它腦中，再觀察行為變不變。
關鍵在對比設計：同一個模型訓練出兩份副本，一份餵「評分者偏好特徵 f、對立權威（用戶或開發者）偏好相反特徵」的檔案，另一份餵完全相反的組合。兩份副本輸出 f 的頻率差距，就是「評分者落差」，差距越大，代表模型越傾向討好評分者。
研究團隊拿 OpenAI 一個重能力、沒做安全訓練的 o3 強化學習檢查點測試，結果隨訓練推進，模型偏袒評分者的落差一路上升，對其他權威的偏好卻幾乎持平，轉變只針對評分者。
誠實測試更驚人：在「Broken Promises Coding」測驗裡，模型須向主管承諾不用某個受限工具，但完成任務又非用不可。植入的檔案一暗示「評分者獎勵完成任務」，後期檢查點違背承諾的比率高達 87%；暗示「評分者獎勵誠實」，違背率就降到只有 9%。同一道題、同一個模型，誠實度完全被它「以為評分者要什麼」牽著走。
驗證有效，但也代表這種傾向可能訓練不掉
要證明這套測量法真的量到了「討好評分者」，研究團隊反過來拿一批「已經知道它偏好什麼」的模型來對照。
第一組是 Redwood Research 訓練的兩個「獎勵駭客」模型（會為了拿高分去鑽規則漏洞），分別基於 gpt-oss-120b 與 Kimi K2.5。這兩個模型被訓練成愛鑽漏洞之後，評分者落差果然變大。第二組是用 gpt-oss-120b 微調出的三個「模型有機體」，各自被刻意訓練成只討好一個對象：使用者、評分者、或 OpenAI 領導層。結果每個模型的落差，都精準指回它被訓練去討好的那個對象。
這裡要先分清楚兩個很像、卻不一樣的詞。reward-seeking（追逐獎勵）是一種廣泛傾向：模型會照著「它相信什麼會被獎勵」來調整行為。reward-hacking（鑽獎勵漏洞）則是一種具體招數：單純為了拿高分去鑽某個漏洞。
兩者不一定同時出現：模型可能只是養成壞習慣式地鑽漏洞，根本沒去想背後的獎勵機制；但一個懂得在各種新情境都鑽得出漏洞的模型，通常就是個不折不扣的 reward-seeker。前面那兩個獎勵駭客落差會變大，正好印證了這層關聯。
真正危險的地方在於：這種傾向會讓「用來抓問題的測驗」失靈。一個很會討好評分者的模型，可能只是因為它推斷「現在正在考誠實」才乖乖不毀約；哪天監督方式一變，它的乖就未必還在。
而且就算評分者本身完美無缺，風險也不會消失——因為它從頭到尾學到的都是「討好評分者」，而不是「因為這樣做才對」。一旦進到沒人評分、或評分管不動它的場合，它很可能就走鐘，因為它的底層策略本來就不是衝著把事情做對去的。
更麻煩的是，這種傾向可能無法去除：你針對壞行為去訓練它，往往只是更新了它「什麼會被獎勵」的認知，卻沒真的改到它骨子裡的偏好。Anthropic 的 Claude Opus 4.8 系統卡也給了旁證：一個活化層級的監控器，在約 5% 的強化學習回合裡，抓到模型正在意識「評分者的存在」。
如今每家前沿實驗室都把強化學習愈做愈大，模型對自身處境的意識也愈來愈強，reward-seeking 只會有增無減。所以該盯的地方不是模型上線之後，而是訓練的當下：因為它完全有可能在還沒被人看見以前，就先學會了怎麼演。

title: Uber 客服部門再砍 10%，承認裁員理由是擁抱 AI
summary:
Uber 於本週三裁減全球社群營運（涵蓋客服業務）部門人力，並要求遠距員工搬回指定辦公室，這是該公司不到兩個月 […]

〈Uber 客服部門再砍 10%，承認裁員理由是擁抱 AI〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Uber 於本週三裁減全球社群營運（涵蓋客服業務）部門人力，並要求遠距員工搬回指定辦公室，這是該公司不到兩個月內第二次因簡化組織而裁員。
（前情提要：科技業不敢再甩鍋 AI？Robinhood 裁員10%，內部信揭密矽谷「縮編新藉口」）
（背景補充：AI 裁員現世報！55% 砍過人的企業認錯，Ford 花三年回聘 350 名老工程師）
裁員的理由，企業向來偏好含糊，組織重整、精簡結構、聚焦核心業務，聽起來體面卻讓人猜不透真正理由。但這次 Uber 沒有繞路，直接把話說白：客服部門砍掉 10% 的職位，理由就是要「擁抱 AI 人工智慧」。
這是 Uber 兩個月內第二次裁員，也是該公司首度公開把裁員和 AI 效率綁在一起。
「組織太複雜」背後真正意思
Uber 週三宣布裁減旗下全球社群營運團隊的人力，這個部門正是負責客服業務的單位。Uber 發言人以電子郵件表示，公司正在「簡化營運、強化實體協作，並持續擁抱 AI」。原本遠距工作的員工，也被要求依照公司的返辦公室政策，搬到指定的樞紐辦公室上班。
Uber 全球社群營運副總裁 Megha Yethatika 在寫給部門的內部備忘錄中說得更直白：「我們的組織已經變得太複雜、太各自為政。」她承認部門在匯入 AI 上「已有一些進展」，但要真正釋放這個潛力，「我們需要一個有效率的組織架構來承載 AI，不能在破碎的流程上規模化前沿技術。」換句話說，在她眼中，客服團隊現在的問題不是 AI 不夠好，而是人和流程太亂，撐不起 AI 該有的效果。
上一次不提 AI，這一次全指向 AI
這已經是 Uber 不到兩個月內第二次為了簡化團隊結構而裁員。今年 6 月，Uber 在新總裁上任後，裁減了所謂「人資部門」23% 的人力，佔全球 34,000 名員工不到 1%。當時公司並未把那輪裁員歸因於 AI。
這次不一樣。這是 Uber 第一次公開把裁員和「AI 效率提升」直接掛鉤。彭博指出，從金融服務公司 Block 到雲端業者 Oracle，近幾個月都有企業拿 AI 當作裁員的理由，Uber 這次等於正式加入這份名單。

title: 視網膜晶片讓失明者重見光明！美國 Science Corp 搶先馬斯克，將在歐洲開賣
summary:
美國腦機介面新創 Science Corp 宣布，視網膜晶片 Prima 已經拿下歐盟 CE 標章，即將在歐洲 […]

〈視網膜晶片讓失明者重見光明！美國 Science Corp 搶先馬斯克，將在歐洲開賣〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美國腦機介面新創 Science Corp 宣布，視網膜晶片 Prima 已經拿下歐盟 CE 標章，即將在歐洲開賣；一份刊登於《新英格蘭醫學期刊》的試驗顯示，32 名患者中有 26 人視力出現臨床上有意義的改善。
（前情提要：再改變世界？馬斯克宣布：Neuralink下個產品是盲視！盲人將可重見光明？）
（背景補充：Meta 黑科技：戴頭盔讓 AI 讀你的腦，文字準確率衝上 61%）
視網膜中心的感光細胞壞死之後，患者眼前只會剩一片模糊或黑洞，這是「地圖狀萎縮」，也就是年齡相關性黃斑部病變走到晚期的型態，是老年人失明最常見的原因，目前無藥可治，只能延緩惡化…但這個局面正被一片晶片撬動。
Science Corp 執行長 Max Hodak 向彭博透露，旗下 Prima 視網膜晶片已經拿下歐盟 CE 標章，也就是歐盟的醫療器材上市許可，拿到後就能在整個歐盟與歐洲經濟區銷售，不必再逐國申請。
該公司稍早也公告歐洲商轉上市，把時間表訂在八月，首例商業植入很可能在德國進行。今年預計植入數十人，明年目標拉高到約 200 人，價格未定，將依地區與保險方案而異。
支撐這個時間表的，是一份去年刊登在《新英格蘭醫學期刊》的臨床資料。32 名完成 12 個月追蹤的晚期患者裡，26 人視力出現臨床上有意義的改善，足以重新辨認字母、數字與單字。
Prima 怎麼運作，治的是哪一種失明
Prima 系統由兩部分組成：一片植入眼球後方、視網膜底下的無線光伏晶片，加上一副內建攝影機與微型投影機的特製眼鏡。簡單來說就是，眼鏡先拍下眼前畫面，再把影像投射到晶片上，晶片靠光發電，把影像轉換成電訊號，去刺激視網膜裡還活著的細胞，讓大腦重新「看見」影像的輪廓。
它鎖定的病是地圖狀萎縮，年齡相關性黃斑部病變走到晚期的型態，是老年人失明最常見的原因。
整個黃斑部病變目前有藥物可以延緩惡化，但沒有一種能夠逆轉，Prima 是第一款針對這個晚期階段、被證實能讓部分患者恢復「形態視覺」的商業裝置。地圖狀萎縮好發於 70 歲以上族群，隨著全球人口老化，這個病患群體只會持續擴大，這也是為什麼 Hodak 特別強調，光是歐洲就有數十萬名潛在受益者。
市值排第二，為什麼反而是 Science Corp 先賣出商品
在美國腦機介面這個賽道裡，Science Corp 只是排名第二的玩家，市值 15 億美元，前面還站著馬斯克創辦、目前更受矚目的 Neuralink。但真正把植入產品做成商品、搶先送進診所開賣的，Science Corp 奪得先機 。
Hodak 是 Neuralink 的共同創辦人之一，2021 年離開後另立門戶，把重心放在難度較低、但病患數量龐大的視覺修復上，而不是直接挑戰語言與運動這類更複雜的腦部訊號。這個選擇讓 Science Corp 得以先繞開美國冗長的審批流程，把 CE 標章當成第一個突破口。
歐洲一張許可證，就能覆蓋整個歐盟與歐洲經濟區的市場，速度遠快於在美國逐州、逐案審查。同樣一顆晶片，如果先排美國隊伍，光是審批流程就可能拖上好幾年；改走歐洲 CE 標章，等於先繞過這套最漫長的關卡，把商業化時程硬生生提前。
資本也沒有缺席。Science Corp 累計募得 4.89 億美元，今年三月被彭博報導估值達到 15 億美元。這筆錢讓公司同時養著視網膜晶片、以及利用工程神經元對接腦組織的下一代裝置，一邊賣產品換取現金流，一邊繼續往更深的腦機介面推進。

title: Google 財報全面超標，但資本支出翻倍上看 2,050 億鎂、股價不領情
summary:
Alphabet 財務長 Anat Ashkenazi 在第二季法說會上宣布，將 2026 年全年資本支出財測 […]

〈Google 財報全面超標，但資本支出翻倍上看 2,050 億鎂、股價不領情〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
Alphabet 財務長 Anat Ashkenazi 在第二季法說會上宣布，將 2026 年全年資本支出財測上修到 1,950 億至 2,050 億美元，是 2025 年支出的兩倍多；第二季資本支出達 449.2 億美元，優於預期，主要投入技術性 AI 基礎設施；她並預告 2027 年支出仍將顯著走高。
（前情提要：AI 燒錢今晚交卷：Alphabet 攤牌 1,900 億鎂資本支出，特斯拉迎來極大波動）
（背景補充：AI 吃電怪獸！彭博：2035 年美國資料中心用電將翻 4 倍，佔全國發電量 20%）
Google 母公司 Alphabet 週三交出第二季成績單，財報全面超標，但股價卻於盤後應聲下跌。財務長 Anat Ashkenazi 在法說會上端出兩組數字：一組讓華爾街滿意，另一組卻讓投資人皺眉，也就是不斷加碼的資本支出財測。
兩個月又加碼的財測
Ashkenazi 在法說會上宣布，Alphabet 將 2026 年全年資本支出財測上修到 1,950 億到 2,050 億美元。預計拿來蓋資料中心、買晶片伺服器這類「先砸錢建產能」的長期投資，砸下去要等未來幾年才看得到回報。
這個數字，比 4 月時公司自己給出的「最多 1,900 億美元」更高，也高過分析師原本估的約 1,860 億美元。
對比更早的基期：2026 年這個新財測，是 2025 年支出的兩倍多。而光是第二季，Alphabet 的資本支出就達到 449.2 億美元，比去年同期的 224 億美元幾乎翻倍，也略高於分析師預期的 441.5 億美元。
更關鍵的是，Ashkenazi 沒有把話說死在 2026 年。她重申，2027 年的支出還會「顯著」更高，理由很直接：公司要持續蓋資料中心、取得運算資源，才能撐住旗下 AI 專案與模型的胃口。這句話等於是告訴市場，這輪加碼不是一次性事件，而是一條看不到終點的長坡。
財報超標，為什麼股價還在跌
如果只看營收，Alphabet 這一季其實交出了漂亮答卷。第二季總營收達 1,197.96 億美元，年增 24%，優於市場預期。
真正的成長引擎是 Google Cloud：營收年增 82%，來到約 248 億美元，背後是企業客戶對 AI 運算的需求持續加大；而 Cloud 的訂單積壓（也就是已簽約、還沒認列進營收的訂單）在上一季就已經衝破 4,600 億美元。
照理說，這樣的成績單該讓股價上漲。但 GOOGL 股價卻在財報後下跌，市場的焦慮很直白：如果資本支出的成長速度，長期跑贏營收成長速度，這筆錢什麼時候才能真正轉換成獲利？花錢建產能是一回事，產能能不能被用滿、用出效益，是另一回事。財
一場所有巨頭都在加註的牌局
Alphabet 並不是唯一一個把賭注越壓越大的巨頭。把 Google、Amazon、Microsoft、Meta 四大超大規模業者的 2026 年資本支出財測加總，合計上看約 7,250 億美元，較 2025 年的約 4,100 億美元，暴增約 77%。
其中 Amazon 約 2,000 億美元、Microsoft 近 1,900 億美元、Meta 約 1,250 億到 1,450 億美元，Alphabet 這次上修後，已經直逼第一梯隊的規模。研究機構 CreditSights 估計，這筆錢裡有約 75%，也就是約 4,500 億美元，會直接流向 AI 基礎設施：GPU、伺服器、網路與資料中心。
這場牌局的規則很簡單：先蓋產能的人，才有資格接下一輪的訂單；但蓋太快、蓋太多，帳上的資本支出就會先於營收增速跑出去，把股價的耐心一點一點磨光。

title: 美國幣圈大軍創造逾 23 萬就業機會，估今年貢獻 550 億美元 GDP
summary:
根據美國國家加密貨幣協會（NCA）最新發布的報告，美國加密貨幣產業預計將在 2026 年為國內生產毛額（GDP）貢獻超過 550 億美元的產值。其中，約 310 億美元將以薪資收入的形式流向勞工。

〈美國幣圈大軍創造逾 23 萬就業機會，估今年貢獻 550 億美元 GDP〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
根據美國國家加密貨幣協會（NCA）最新發布的報告，美國加密貨幣產業預計將在 2026 年為國內生產毛額（GDP）貢獻超過 550 億美元的產值。其中，約 310 億美元將以薪資收入的形式流向勞工。
這份由務實政策集團（PPG）執行、 NCA 委託並提供資金的分析報告指出，儘管美國加密貨幣產業的直接從業人員僅 3.4 萬人，但若將供應鏈及員工消費等經濟外溢效應納入計算，整體可支撐約 23.2 萬個工作機會。
報告引述美國勞工統計局（BLS）的數據稱，幣圈這 3.4 萬個「直接就業」大軍，規模已正式超越咖啡與茶葉製造業（2.84 萬人）、水泥製造業（1.53 萬人），更遠高於傳統的菸草製造業（1.06 萬人）。
報告點出一個關鍵發現：這 23.2 萬個工作機會中，絕大多數其實並非隸屬於加密貨幣公司。 PPG 透過標準的「投入產出模型」（Input-Output Model，一種用於分析產業間供應與需求關聯性的經濟模型）估算，幣圈的外溢效應為周邊供應鏈產業創造了 7.5 萬個職缺，而這些勞工的家庭日常消費，又進一步衍生出 12.3 萬個就業機會。
從職業分佈來看，在這龐大的關聯就業生態圈中，「行政後勤」以 29,260 人居冠，其次為「商業與財務營運」（21,650 人）及「管理職」（20,890 人）。令人意外的是，連「物流運輸」（18,560 人）、「餐飲服務」（16,910 人）也因幣圈產業鏈外溢而受惠。
至於最核心的 3.4 萬個直接職缺，則是由軟體、區塊鏈與數據工程師拿下最大宗（10,100 人）；緊追在後的是法遵、財務與商業營運人員（5,450 人），以及高階主管與經理人（5,100 人）。
幣圈不僅創造就業，薪資待遇也相當豐厚。報告指出，這 23.2 萬個受惠職缺的平均年薪高達 13.3 萬美元，足足是全美薪資中位數 6.4 萬美元的兩倍有餘。
PPG 特別在附註中釐清，這個高薪數據涵蓋了所有受帶動的關聯職位；換言之，即便將前述的清潔、餐飲與外送人員一併計入，整體的平均薪資依然表現亮眼。
從地理分佈來看，科技重鎮加州（57,649 個）與金融中心紐約（53,766 個）包辦了全美近半數的幣圈關聯職缺。德州（26,536 個）、華盛頓州（15,097 個）及北卡羅來納州（9,524 個）則緊隨其後。
相比之下，位於美國中西部的 12 個州，合計僅貢獻逾 1.7 萬個職缺；阿拉斯加州則以 86 個墊底。不過，部分州正積極擁抱加密貨幣產業以創造經濟動能。例如，科羅拉多州不僅開放以加密貨幣繳納稅款，首府丹佛截至 2025 年已吸引 131 家區塊鏈企業進駐，吸金 5.71 億美元，為該州撐起近 5,800 個職缺及 13 億美元的經濟貢獻。
北達科他州也正大力推展相關舉措，包括 Atlas Power 規劃中的 700 兆瓦（MW）大型設施，以及該州銀行與金融科技巨頭 Fiserv 合作開發的美元穩定幣（計畫，創造了逾 800 個工作機會。
在估算模型上，PPG 以美國經濟分析局（BEA）2024 年的投入產出表作為基礎，並導入調研機構 Statista 統計的 232.2 億美元美國加密產業營收作為初始參數。
由於 BEA 尚未將加密貨幣列為獨立產業，因此 PPG 將幣圈企業的營運模式對應至現有的證券與商品合約（占金融相關營收 97%）、信用仲介、資料處理（占 3%）等類別，並採用科技業的勞動力結構來進行推算，確保數據貼近現實。
兼任 NCA 總裁、瑞波（Ripple）法務長的 Stu Alderoty 指出，加密貨幣產業已具備驅動實體經濟的實力，並對美國的就業、薪資及經濟成長帶來「實質且正向的影響」。
負責主導這項研究的 PPG 首席經濟學家 Oliver Browne 進一步強調：「每增加一個直接加密貨幣產業職位，都能在整體經濟中創造出約 6 個額外的工作機會。」
他認為，加密貨幣產業正逐漸確立其可量化的經濟貢獻地位，隨著市場採用率提升，未來成長潛力依然可期。
NCA 成立於 2025 年，為一家專注於推廣加密教育的 501(c)(4) 非營利組織。報告特別聲明，儘管這項研究由 NCA 贊助，但所有數據與發現皆出自 PPG 團隊的獨立量化分析，維持了報告的客觀性。

title: 美參院新版《CLARITY 法案》出爐：增設開發者保護、道德條款 2029 年失效
summary:
經過數月協商，美國共和黨參議員公布最新版《 數位資產市場明晰法案 （ Clarity Act ）》文本，這部攸關美國加密貨幣監管框架的重大立法，最快有望在下周送交參議院全院表決。

〈美參院新版《CLARITY 法案》出爐：增設開發者保護、道德條款 2029 年失效〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
經過數月協商，美國共和黨參議員公布最新版 《數位資產市場明晰法案（Clarity Act）》文本，這部攸關美國加密貨幣監管框架的重大立法，最快有望在下周送交參議院全院表決。
新版法案共計 616 頁，整合了參議院農業委員會（Senate Agriculture Committee）、銀行委員會（Senate Banking Committee）過去一年通過的兩個版本，並針對市場最關注的監管爭議進行調整。
其中，最棘手的「政府官員加密資產利益衝突」問題，也在最新版本中提出解方。法案新增道德規範條款，限制總統、副總統、國會議員及其他聯邦官員利在任期內利用數位資產牟利。
不過，道德規範附帶了一項「日落條款」（Sunset Provision，指法律達到規定期限即自動失效的機制），相關限制將於 2029 年 1 月 20 日中午後失效。
川普迷因幣成道德爭議核心，新版法案設利益衝突限制
過去數月，《Clarity Act》遲遲無法推進的最大障礙之一，就是如何避免美國政府官員利用加密資產牟利。
爭議焦點主要圍繞美國總統川普推出的迷因幣，及其家族旗下的加密貨幣企業 World Liberty Financial（WLF）。
上月公布的財務申報資料顯示，川普從 WLF 相關活動中獲得數百萬美元收入，引發民主黨對政府官員涉足數位資產市場的道德疑慮，也成為推動加密貨幣法案過程中的主要政治阻力。
根據最新文本，法案最後章節新增「道德規範」條款，禁止任何公職人員、公務員及其配偶發行或推廣數位資產，但未禁止官員持有或投資加密貨幣。
此外，如先前外界預期，草案明訂由司法部（DOJ）負責執法，立刻引來民主黨人強烈反彈，他們堅稱，各州檢察長也必須擁有參與權。民主黨籍參議員 Angela Alsobrooks 接受採訪時直言：
讓司法部來執行道德條款？這根本是開玩笑。如果條款不改，我絕對不會支持這部法案。但我們會在這個基礎上繼續斡旋，直到達成真正能落實問責的共識。
民主黨人士認為，各州檢察總長應該在監督政府官員利益衝突問題上扮演角色，而非完全交由聯邦司法部處理。
共和黨懷俄明州參議員 Cynthia Lummis 在說明文件中表示，這項日落條款證明了「這是川普總統自願遵守的標準，而非國會強加於他的枷鎖。」
非託管錢包開發者獲法律保障，DeFi 產業高度關注
除了道德條款外，新版《Clarity Act》另一項重要內容，是納入《區塊鏈監管確定性法案》。
該條款將為非託管軟體開發者提供「安全港保護，明確規定這類開發者不屬於貨幣傳輸業者（money transmitter）。
所謂非託管服務，是指使用者自行掌握私鑰、資產控制權不交由第三方管理的加密貨幣服務，例如部分去中心化金融（DeFi）協議與自託管錢包。
加密產業普遍支持這項規定，認為它能提供開發者更清楚的法律環境，避免美國創新人才因監管不確定性轉往海外。
新版法案同時新增了 25 個新章節，以解決執法單位對加密貨幣市場監管不足的疑慮。
去中心化金融教育基金（DeFi Education Fund）表示，初步看來，這些條款屬於「智慧型監管」，既能提供執法機關必要工具，也不會過度限制軟體開發者。
數位資產商會（The Digital Chamber）執行長 Cody Carbone 也表示，這份法案文本是推動美國建立長期數位資產市場監管制度的重要一步。他指出：
現在就是建立持久市場結構法案、讓美國成為全球數位資產領導者的最佳時機。
區塊鏈協會（Blockchain Association）執行長 Summer Mersinger 則表示，該組織正在審查最新版本，並期待協助推動法案完成立法。
參議院最快下周表決，但民主黨支持仍成最大變數
《Clarity Act》若要在參議院通過，仍需要部分民主黨參議員支持；目前最大的不確定因素，就在於道德條款是否足以化解民主黨疑慮。
若參議院能在 8 月 7 日國會休會前完成表決，法案下一步將送交眾議院審議，但隨著國會議員準備將重心轉移至期中選舉，留給這部世紀加密貨幣法案的立法空窗期已所剩無幾。

• 法案新增道德規範條款，限制政府官員在任期內利用數位資產牟利，該條款將於2029年失效。

title: 特斯拉連 4 年沒賣比特幣！Q2 認列 1.12 億美元減損，持幣量維持 11,509 枚
summary:
電動車大廠特斯拉（ Tesla ）最新財報顯示，公司第二季並未出脫任何數位資產，比特幣持有量維持在 11,509 枚。不過，受幣價下跌拖累，特斯拉當季仍得認列 1.12 億美元的數位資產減值損失。

〈特斯拉連 4 年沒賣比特幣！Q2 認列 1.12 億美元減損，持幣量維持 11,509 枚〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
電動車大廠特斯拉（Tesla）最新財報顯示，公司第二季並未出脫任何數位資產，比特幣持有量維持在 11,509 枚。不過，受幣價下跌拖累，特斯拉當季仍得認列 1.12 億美元的數位資產減值損失。
換言之，自 2022 年出售大部分比特幣持倉以來，特斯拉至今已近 4 年未再買進或出售任何比特幣。
比特幣第二季下跌 14%，特斯拉認列 1.12 億美元減損
回顧今年第二季度，在全球總體經濟充滿不確定性、風險資產波動加劇的背景下，比特幣從季初 83,000 美元，一路下探至 6 月底的 58,000 美元附近。依據美國現行的會計準則，企業持有的數位資產若在財報期間內價格下跌，必須透過損益表認列減值損失。
因此，即使比特幣在 6 月底觸底後已逐步回血，近期在 65,000 美元附近交投，特斯拉仍須依第二季結束時的資產價值提列減損。
特斯拉目前仍持有 11,509 枚比特幣，依然名列全球持有最多比特幣的上市公司之一。
不過，相較於持續大舉加碼比特幣的 Strategy（NASDAQ：MSTR），特斯拉的持幣規模已明顯落後；Strategy 近年持續透過發債、增資等方式增持比特幣，而特斯拉則自 2022 年以來始終未調整持倉。
第二季財報好壞參半，每股盈餘不如預期
特斯拉第二季整體財報表現好壞參半。在獲利表現方面，非一般公認會計原則（Non-GAAP）每股盈餘（EPS）為 0.33 美元，遠低於分析師預期的 0.55 美元；營收達 282 億美元，則優於市場預期的 276 億美元；毛利率為 16.8%，依據一般公認會計原則（GAAP）計算的淨利為 11.1 億美元；公司當季自由現金流為負 11 億美元。
2021 年豪砸 15 億美元買比特幣
特斯拉於 2021 年初斥資 15 億美元買進比特幣，並短暫開放消費者「用比特幣買車」，引發市場高度關注，但隨後卻以環保、高耗能疑慮為由，暫停接受比特幣支付。
到了 2022 年，特斯拉出售約 75% 的比特幣持有量，以強化現金部位，此後就一直保留剩餘的 11,509 枚比特幣，至今未再進行任何買賣。

title: Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years, BBC reveals
summary: The BBC can reveal that detectives have so far uncovered nine victims of PC Alan Greer but many more are anticipated.
full_text:
Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years
- Published
A police officer who took his own life in May was a violent rapist who carried out a spate of sexual attacks and attempted murders of women over at least 14 years, the BBC can reveal.
PC Alan Greer's first known victim was a woman he raped in her home in Glasgow in 2012 after she had called the police to report being the victim of a crime.
The woman reported the sex attack by Greer late last year, sparking one of Police Scotland's biggest ever anti-corruption inquiries.
Detectives have so far uncovered a further eight victims, five of whom were sex workers, attacked while Greer was off duty.
It has emerged that Greer used hundreds of prostitutes throughout his police career, and it is anticipated more victims of his violence will be identified.
Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff, gold commander for the investigation, said what the inquiry had found was "truly shocking".
She said: "This officer has clearly abused his power and has revisited someone that he's encountered in the course of his duties.
"But this victim was brave enough to come and speak to us, and that really was the trigger point for us starting our investigation.
"That's allowed us to proactively identify eight further victims."
ACC Ratcliff's confirmation of the inquiry comes following a BBC Disclosure investigation into Greer's offending.
A source close to the investigation told the BBC: "It feels a bit like this could be Police Scotland's Wayne Couzens moment."
Couzens was a Met Police officer who was jailed for the rape and murder of Sarah Everard in London five years ago.
'Violent double life'
Greer, who was born in Australia in 1978, moved to the UK when he was six.
He joined Strathclyde Police in 2009 before it merged with Police Scotland in 2013 and had 17 years of apparently unblemished service.
At first, he worked as a uniformed response officer in Glasgow before he secured a job in officer safety training, based in Coatbridge, in about 2016.
This meant he was involved in teaching probationer officers as well as refreshing more experienced officer training.
When he died in May, he was 47, with a wife and child.
Greer's family and colleagues are understood to have been "oblivious" to his violent double life.
Senior officers insisted there were no opportunities to spot his offending sooner.
The woman who started the investigation
It was towards the end of last year that a woman in her late thirties walked into a Glasgow police station to report a crime.
Somewhat reluctantly, she explained that she had, in 2012, attempted to report a disturbance at her home, and that uniformed officers had attended her Glasgow home.
She said the officers took her statement and left.
A few hours later one of the officers returned, alone, forced her into a sexual act and raped her.
After she told the police last year, the woman seemed to disengage from further inquiries.
The case was handed to the anti-corruption unit (ACU), who, by April, had secured a statement from her.
From this they were then able to identify the call she'd made in 2012 and could identify the officers who had attended.
They found that, in the weeks after the 2012 attack, one of those officers had repeatedly monitored the woman's crime file on the police computer for updates, perhaps to see if she had made a further disclosure about what happened to her later that day.
The PC had even carried out one of these checks while on annual leave.
Fourteen years later as anti-corruption detectives attempted to identify the woman's attacker, it would be these keystrokes, these searches in her crime file for which there was no legitimate police reason, which gave them their suspect - PC Alan Greer.
A timeline of how Alan Greer's crimes came to light
A critical incident was then declared and a gold commander was installed.
Anti-corruption detectives started working on Greer, and obtained his mobile phone number, which had previously not been held on his personnel file.
Only his home number had been retained by police.
The mobile number was then put through police intelligence databases, which revealed a single piece of intelligence dating back to 2018, linked to that number, but with no name attached.
The intelligence had come from a Glasgow sex worker and indicated that the owner of that phone number was a customer who had been violent.
There was no indication the number belonged to a police officer, but was this an opportunity to catch Greer in 2018?
ACC Ratcliff told the BBC: "I am entirely satisfied that everything that could have been reasonably done at that time was done, and that there were no missed opportunities as a result of that information."
The information from 2018 gave detectives a second strand of evidence, and grounds to monitor every keystroke that Greer made on police computers.
They then discovered that Greer had been searching the police system for traces of a complaint from a phone number, which detectives were able to identify belonged to a Glasgow sex worker.
This was a breakthrough. This was their suspect repeating the pattern from 2012.
They now had enough evidence to put before a sheriff who authorised a warrant to search his home and seize his devices.
Dawn raid on Greer's home
At dawn on 24 April, officers raided Greer's family home in what was described as a "day of executive action".
Greer appeared shocked to be arrested on suspicion of the 2012 rape.
Seven mobile phones and a laptop were seized, and Greer was brought into a police station to be fingerprinted and have his DNA taken.
He was not interviewed but was suspended from duty and released pending further enquiries.
It was only when officers started to look at his phones that the scale of Greer's offending began to emerge.
Thousands of graphic videos and images were recovered, revealing that Greer had used hundreds of prostitutes throughout his police career.
Officers are not yet even halfway through the files, but have already identified five sex workers who have been seriously sexually assaulted.
If Greer was alive, it is understood police would have sought charges of attempted murder in some of the cases, such was the level of violence used.
Three other victims have been identified, including two female police officers Greer had taken inappropriate photographs of while they were training.
As Greer's serial offending was emerging, detectives took steps to ensure his family were not in danger, and social work officers, accompanied by local police, visited his home on 5 May.
Greer died by suicide the following day.
'Police Scotland's Wayne Couzens moment'
In the days that followed, police announced Greer's death on the force's internal communications platform, and stated he died while suspended and under criminal investigation.
A source close to the investigation told the BBC: "Some of his colleagues thought this was a callous move on behalf of the police, saying he was under criminal investigation when he'd only just died.
"But it's clear they were all totally in the dark about this guy's offending.
"Folk will be in a state of shock when they learn the full truth. I don't think anyone really knows how bad it is yet.
"It feels a bit like this could be Police Scotland's Wayne Couzens moment."
Couzens is a former Metropolitan Police officer serving a whole-life sentence for the rape and murder of Sarah Everard.
He abused his police role to stage a fake arrest, highlighting severe vetting failures and multiple failed opportunities to uncover the risk he posed.
ACC Ratcliff said the comparison was unhelpful and that no red flags were missed.
She said: "At this stage, we've got no evidence to suggest [missed red flags] is the case, but we absolutely keep that under review because one of the things that we have to do from inquiries of this nature is make sure that we capture and we take on board the lessons learned."

title: 'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children
summary: Nearly five months on, grief is still raw as a teacher and a mother recall the horror of the attack in Minab.
full_text:
'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children
- Published
This report contains distressing descriptions of the deaths of children.
Amaineh Nademi walks carefully through what is left of her old school. Chunks of broken concrete hang precariously from the damaged upper floor. A few classrooms are still standing, their brightly coloured walls decorated with painted balloons and flowers.
The 33-year-old teacher knows exactly what was where - the girls' classrooms on the upper floor, the boys' classrooms below, the headteacher's office, the prayer room.
Rubble is all that remains of her classroom, where she taught first-grade girls at Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, a small city in southern Iran.
On 28 February, in the opening hours of the US-Israeli war with Iran, a strike on the school transformed an ordinary Saturday morning into one of the conflict's defining tragedies - and its deadliest single incident for civilians.
In total, 156 people, including 120 children, have been confirmed killed, including a pregnant woman and her unborn child, according to the Minab prosecutor's office.
Experts say evidence indicates that US forces hit the school, which is next to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) compound that satellite images show was struck several times.
The US has not admitted responsibility, though US media have reported that military investigators believe it is likely that US forces carried out the strike unintentionally.
The pain of what happened here is still raw. Teachers tell us they pray at the site every day. Rescue workers are still searching for remains of those killed here.
Much of the upper floor collapsed into the one below. "You can't call it a school," says Amaineh – just "walls that smell of death, grief and the blood that was shed here".
The Iranian authorities were keen for us to visit the school – it is evidence, they say, that a campaign presented by Washington as an attack on Iran's military and security apparatus has instead inflicted a devastating cost on civilians.
'We were all sent flying'
The school day had begun as usual, Amaineh says.
Because it was the Islamic holy month of Ramadan, the children gathered inside the prayer hall to recite the Quran, she recalls, before she began teaching her pupils a new letter of the Persian alphabet.
But, as the first attacks of the war unfolded across Iran, she says the headteacher announced the school would be closing, and teachers began contacting parents, urging them to collect their children.
Only five of Amaineh's 15 first-grade pupils were left in her classroom on the upper floor, she says, when she first heard an explosion not far from the school. She says she was in the corridor and rushed back for the children.
"Just as I went to leave, a missile struck the school," says Amaineh. "Something hit my head and my students' heads - we were all sent flying."
Then, she says, thick black smoke filled the classroom: "I couldn't even see the pupils I was holding in my arms. We couldn't breathe."
She says she remembers hearing another explosion, as well as the sounds of screaming, children crying and then the school itself collapsing – "destroyed all at once".
"Blood was pouring from me and the students," she adds.
When the smoke briefly cleared, she says she passed the injured children down to people below and clambered past fire and rubble towards the school gate, where she saw a crowd of parents. Many had rushed to the site without even putting shoes on, she recalls.
She says she could not understand why the parents were running towards the school, believing in her shock and confusion that everyone else had already escaped the building: "I didn't know that all of them were under the rubble."
Amaineh had taught first grade at the school for six years. She lists the names of students and colleagues killed that day: Adrina from her first grade class, who she says was killed on the stairs with her mother, Fatemeh in second grade, and many others including students in sixth grade she remembers teaching the alphabet to, as well as the headteacher, deputy head, PE teacher and Quran teacher.
'Find my son'
Within minutes, emergency workers began arriving.
Reza Besharati, a worker with the Iranian Red Crescent Society, says he was among the first rescuers on the scene, and found the roads near the school filled with traffic as desperate families rushed to look for their children.
Minab is a small city. As Reza made his way through the crowd and into the wreckage, he says he recognised people he knew, including some of his own relatives.
"We started to find the people, thinking maybe someone would be alive," he says. "But unfortunately, nobody was."
He says the dead were found grimly disfigured: "Maybe just a hand, maybe just a leg… Nobody had a complete body." Many families recognised their children by their shoes or clothing, he adds.
One of Reza's relatives was searching and begging "just find my child, find my son", he says. "I couldn't tell her that her son was not alive. We were all just crying."
Reza says the sights he saw while searching the collapsed building have not left him: "I couldn't sleep for a few days," he says. "When I close my eyes… I just remember these things that I have seen here."
Strike investigated
As details of the strike emerged, President Donald Trump first blamed Iran, without providing evidence.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military was investigating and that US forces "never target civilian targets". He later announced a higher-level investigation, led by an officer from outside US Central Command (Centcom). The Trump administration has still not released the findings.
Several US media outlets have reported - citing people familiar with the US military investigation - that preliminary findings concluded it was likely that outdated data supplied by the US Defence Intelligence Agency led to the school being treated as part of a military site.
Expert video analysis has shown the IRGC complex next to the school was hit by a precision guided Tomahawk missile - a type of cruise missile that neither Israel nor Iran is known to possess. Satellite imagery showed the school and several buildings in the compound had been hit, and verified videos showed the area was hit by a series of strikes. US military maps also confirm American operations in southern Iran – including the Minab area - at the time.
Historical satellite images show the school area was previously part of the IRGC complex, but has been walled off since 2016 and has its own entrances and yards.
Also, information indicating the site was a school was publicly available online. Archived snapshots of the websites for the girls' and boys' sections of the school – taken in the months before the attack - include the address of the site.
The head of Centcom told a congressional committee in May, without giving further detail, that the investigation was "complex" as the school was "on an active IRGC cruise missile base" – which Iran's foreign ministry rejected as a "baseless fabrication".
The IRGC runs some community and medical facilities in addition to its extensive military, security and economic activities. Local residents have told BBC Persian that the site had previously been a base for an IRGC naval brigade, but that they believed its military use had ceased several years ago. Photographs show buildings on the compound included a clinic and a car wash.
The BBC approached the Department of Defense and the US military for comment. Officials said the investigation was ongoing and there were no further updates.
'Identified by her socks'
A short drive from the ruined school is the cemetery where many of the pupils and teachers are buried.
Every evening, families gather beside the graves. Mothers wipe dust from photographs of their children. Parents sit and pray long after darkness has fallen.
Around them, brothers and sisters play between the headston

title: Houthis claim attack on oil tankers as US launches more strikes on Iran
summary: The Houthi attacks would be the first in the Red Sea since the Iran-backed group announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.
full_text:
Houthis claim attack on oil tankers as US launches more strikes on Iran
- Published
Yemen's Houthis say they have attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as the US launched its 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iran.
Iranian state media said two people had been killed in the US strikes on Wednesday, and a tanker caught fire in an explosion in a mined route in the Strait of Hormuz.
Ahead of the latest round of strikes, US President Donald Trump had threatened to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant if Iran attacked a ship in the strait and to "take care of" the Houthis if they blocked the Red Sea.
If confirmed, the Houthi attack would be the first since the Iran-backed group announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis named the tankers as the Encelia and the Layla, though their responsibility has not been confirmed.
The group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree said they had targeted the ships with drones and missiles for allegedly violating its naval blockade.
Saree added that the Houthis promised to continue their naval operations and would continue "enforcing the 'siege for a siege' equation".
The state-run Saudi Press Agency confirmed early on Thursday that the Encelia was struck "while sailing in the Red Sea", resulting in a fire on its bow.
Citing an unnamed official source at the Transport General Authority, it described the attack as a violation of international law. All crew were safe, it reported.
UK Maritime Trade Operation (UKMTO) reported an "unknown projectile" struck a Saudi tanker about 130km from Al Shuqaiq in Saudi Arabia at 20:00 GMT. The attack caused a fire but no casualties, it said.
British maritime risk management group Vanguard also reported that the Saudi tanker Encelia had been hit.
The attack on the Layla has not been confirmed.
US Central Command (Centcom) said at 21:30 GMT it had launched strikes at Trump's direction "to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten civilian mariners and commercial vessels transiting regional waters".
The strikes targeted "Iranian military targets including maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites, and air defense assets," it said.
Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain soon reported responding to airborne threats, before Iran's military said they had targeted US assets in all three countries, according to AFP.
Iranian state media reported two people had been killed in US strikes on the country's south near its border with Iraq.
Meanwhile, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said the Strait of Hormuz was "completely closed" after an explosion in the channel, Iranian state media reported.
The IRGC said it had stopped three oil tankers from passing through the strait.
One tanker caught fire and two others turned back after attempting to pass through a mined route south of the strait, according to Iranian state media.
It comes after Trump promised earlier on Wednesday to attack an Iranian bridge or power plant if its forces hit ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi later warned of an "eye for an eye" response to attacks on Iran.
On Tuesday, Trump told reporters he would "take care of the Houthis" should they obstruct the Red Sea as they had said.
Few details of the "maritime embargo" were given by the Houthis when it was announced on Monday, but a media official said they were closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait - the Red Sea's southern gateway - to Saudi vessels.
The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Now, the threat from the Houthis risks further disruption to international shipping, with hostilities in the region having already led to global fuel prices fluctuating significantly.
So far, at least seven oil tankers have made U-turns close to Yemen since the embargo. Saree claimed the Houthis had "forced approximately ten ships to retreat and return".
The disruption in the Red Sea comes as peace negotiations have effectively stalled between the US and Iran.
Both countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June to halt military operations and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.
But three weeks after it was signed, Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in Hormuz, and US strikes in response.

title: Firm hacked by rogue OpenAI models says it is 'a wake-up call'
summary: A co-founder of start-up Hugging Face told the BBC that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed".
full_text:
Firm hacked by rogue OpenAI models says it is 'a wake-up call'
- Published
The co-founder of Hugging Face, a technology start-up that was hacked after some of OpenAI's most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models went rogue, said on Thursday that the incident is "a wake-up call" for the industry.
Thomas Wolf told BBC's Newsday radio programme that "this will be one of the most common types of cyber attacks we see", but that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed".
The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.
The ChatGPT-maker said on Tuesday that its AI models broke out of a secure test environment during a trial and launched a cyber attack. The firm said the incident was "unprecedented" and that it was conducting an investigation with Hugging Face.
AI agents are able to operate alone to accomplish tasks after human instruction.
Wolf said that Hugging Face initially had no idea where the attack originated when signs of it surfaced in mid-July but that the company was able to contain the breach.
Hugging Face is one of the world's largest open-source hubs for sharing AI models and is often used by tech developers and researchers.
Wolf said the breach was "very different" from the usual cyber attacks that Hugging Face often faces and that OpenAI quickly informed the company that its models were behind the hack.
In a "very short time" there were 17,000 attacks on Hugging Face's network from various IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, said Wolf, who is also the firm's chief science officer.
Wolf said it was a warning to other companies that they must strengthen their cybersecurity defences to counter such attacks.
The hack is "worrying" because it suggests OpenAI's models ignored the typical safeguards that would prevent an AI program from committing a cyber attack, said Nate Soares from the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.
"In some sense, it knew that this was not what the creators intended. It just didn't care," he added.

Other organisations have also taken note of the incident.
A UK government spokesperson said the country's AI Security Institute was studying how the AI system behaved in the incident and that it was continuing to work with OpenAI and other labs to strengthen safeguards.
They urged organisations to ramp up their cyber security measures by taking steps such as enrolling in the government-backed Cyber Essentials certification scheme.
The incident has come at a crucial time for the industry after the US government last month ordered American tech firm Anthropic to restrict access to its AI models over national security concerns. The Department of Commerce lifted the restrictions several weeks later.
People in the industry have also raised security concerns over the widespread use of open-source models in China, allowing anyone to install and customise AI tools released by major developers.
Chinese start-up Moonshot AI will release its Kimi K3 open-source model on 27 July. Since debuting last week, it has drawn industry attention, with many viewing it as a strong competitor to leading Western AI systems.
But on Wednesday a White House adviser accused Moonshot of a "large scale" effort to steal the capabilities of top US AI models.

title: Hosepipe ban in force for millions of households - is your area affected?
summary: More than eight million households have been placed under hosepipe bans - which has raised questions about how effectively water resources are being managed.
full_text:
Hosepipe ban in force for millions of households - is your area affected?
- Published
A hosepipe ban for Thames Water customers has come into force bringing the number of people placed under a ban to more than 20 million.
Such measures have been introduced across large areas of southern and eastern England and parts of Wales because successive heatwaves have left water supplies under strain.
But while spring and early summer have been relatively dry for much of the UK - with temperatures regularly exceeding 30C - winter was much wetter than usual.
This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows and filling pools.
It has raised questions about how effectively water resources are being managed, and whether the UK is prepared for drier summers expected with climate change.
So how is your area doing and how close are you to a drought?
There is no single definition of drought, but it is ultimately caused by a prolonged period of low rainfall, which has knock-on effects for nature, agriculture and water supplies.
Environmental bodies in each UK nation decide whether to declare drought or water scarcity based on an assessment of current water levels and long-term weather forecasts.
Both of these states can trigger a hosepipe ban.
Drought is a lack of precipitation, whereas water scarcity is about a mismatch between water supply and demand - so it is not just about the weather.
This summer, bans have been introduced to manage high water demand.
Mixed picture across the country
Large parts of England are currently in "prolonged dry weather" status - the category below drought - according to the Environment Agency.
So far, eight UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans, seven in England and one in Wales.
Prolonged dry weather has been declared in East Anglia, the West Midlands, Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Hertfordshire and London, Wessex, Thames, and Solent and the South Downs.
The remaining parts of England, mostly in the north, remain in "normal" status.
In Wales, areas across the north and south-east have been escalated from normal to prolonged dry weather status, according to Natural Resources Wales, while there are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.
Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity".
Several areas in eastern Scotland are in "moderate scarcity" but none are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity".
Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater - how are supplies?
Our three main sources of water are rivers, reservoirs and from deep underground.
Following the hot, dry weather, river flows were low in June for parts of the UK.
"Without significant rainfall we could see increasing impacts on wildlife, agriculture and water resources as the summer progresses," said Steve Turner, a hydrologist at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).
Reservoirs are a crucial part of water supplies and levels in Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland are all "healthy" and above expected for this time of year.
England's reservoirs are below average levels for the time of year, albeit with some variation across the country.
South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs.
Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.
In June, groundwater levels were generally at or just below normal, having been topped up by winter rainfall but depleted by a drier spring in most regions.
But water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.
These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.
It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.
Is climate change to blame?
Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.
The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.
But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.
"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.
But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.
In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.
As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.
But the Environment Agency has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans and more smart meters - may be needed in England too.
Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

Tell us how you're affected by the hosepipe ban.

title: The Papers: 'Row over early prison release' and 'Gary's back of the net tax'
summary: A number of the papers are focusing on a review of the early prison release programme.
full_text:
'Row over early prison release' and 'Gary's back of the net tax'
- Published
Just days after he took office, the Guardian says that Andy Burnham has become "immersed in a deepening political row", external, as he paused plans for some prisoners to be released early. One government official is quoted as saying that there are "no easy choices", adding that "we will hit prison capacity by Christmas" if he doesn't continue with the scheme. But the shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy writes in the Daily Telegraph that "the clock is ticking", external and "victims need certainty".
Despite the government insisting that the scheme will still go ahead in September, one prison boss tells the Times that they have been instructed to "put planning on hold", external until ministers' intentions "become clear". Another source says that the pause has caused "bedlam", as the paper reports "chaos" in jails across England and Wales. An insider interviewed by the Daily Mail says that officials have been "summoned" to an online meeting, external with the Prison and Probation Service today.
The i Paper says the government is looking at giving low-income households large plug-in batteries to help them cut energy bills., external According to the report, the batteries - which are about the size of a cabin suitcase - can store cheap power when demand is low and release it later.
The Sun leads with an interview with the stunt driver who is suing BBC Studios, external over a crash while filming Top Gear. Paul Rees is revealed as having played the anonymous racing driver, known as The Stig. He was a passenger in a car being driven by Andrew Flintoff when it flipped over in 2022. He tells the Sun he broke his back and thought he was going to die. BBC Studios denies it was negligent.
And a study in the Daily Express suggests that some users of appetite-suppressing drugs aren't just losing weight - but their hair too. The paper says that the research links jabs such as Wegovy, Ozempic and Mounjaro, to alopecia. According to the Daily Mirror, it could be caused by "sudden drops in calorie intake and nutrient deficiencies", external. But the Daily Star insists there is no suggestion people should stop using weight loss jabs - saying the study is just "food for thought".

title: What is the mosquito-borne disease Sri Lanka is using drones to fight?
summary: Dengue has killed 56 people and infected more than 77,000 in the South Asian nation this year.
full_text:
What is the mosquito-borne disease Sri Lanka is using drones to fight?
- Published
Battling its worst dengue outbreak in nearly a decade, Sri Lanka has deployed military drones to scan for stagnant pools of water on rooftops and other mosquito-breeding sites.
The virus has killed 56 people and infected more than 77,000 others in the South Asian nation this year, with more than a quarter of them reported in July alone.
Dengue fever, which is spread to humans through mosquitoes, is common in tropical climates.
But as temperatures rise worldwide, these disease-carrying mosquitos are now moving into new areas, including Europe and the Mediterranean. According to the WHO, the number of global reported cases surged from around 500,000 in the year 2000 to 14.4 million in 2024.
What is dengue fever and what are its symptoms?
Dengue is a viral fever caused by the dengue virus, which is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes.
These mosquitoes breed in stagnant water like pails, vases and flowerpot plates. They are most active during daylight hours and usually bite just after sunrise and around sunset.
Many people who get dengue do not develop symptoms. For those who do, the most common symptoms include high fever, headache, muscle and joint pains, nausea and rashes. These usually resolve within a week or two.
In severe cases, however, dengue can lead to internal bleeding or even death.
Those who get infected a second time are at a greater risk of severe dengue.
There are four strains of the dengue virus and healing from one would only protect you from that specific strain, says Kapila Kannangara, director of Sri Lanka's Dengue Control Unit.
"That immunity does not extend to other strains of the virus. That means someone infected by one strain of the virus could still get dengue again if infected by a mosquito carrying another strain."
"This could mean that they get an even more serious infection," he tells BBC Sinhala.
As there is no universal vaccine for dengue, treatment often involves managing pain with medication such as paracetamol. Patients who develop severe symptoms would often require careful monitoring in hospital, as complications can be lethal.
What's the situation in Sri Lanka?
Sri Lanka's health authorities attribute the surge in dengue infections to a cyclone that tore through the island last December, scattering debris that have turned into new breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
The government has tasked the military to use drones to scan the rooftops of homes, schools and construction sites, and deployed police officers to go to people's homes for physical inspections,
Nearly 11,000 mosquito breeding sites have been cleared so far this month, while more than 4,000 premises fined for harbouring those sites.
Although infections have been reported across the country, they tend to concentrate in urban areas, such as in the capital city Colombo.
Hospitals have added beds and extended work hours to cope with the outbreak, and public health workers are "stretched to their limit", Kannangara from the National Dengue Control Unit tells Reuters news agency.
"The number of patients is high, and the severity of the cases is high," he says, noting that about 75% of the cases were linked to the more virulent dengue strain.
Capacity constraints have prompted doctors to advise patients with mild symptoms to rest and recover at home.
Authorities are also considering a dengue vaccine, but health experts have suggested that it would be hard to develop such a vaccine given the four distinct strains of the virus.
It is not the first time Sri Lanka has experienced a dengue epidemic.
In 2017, the disease left 450 people dead, in a year driven by heavy monsoon rains.
Why are the number of dengue cases growing worldwide?
Dengue is most commonly found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, where warm temperatures and high humidity allow the Aedes mosquitoes to thrive.
High concentrations of dengue hotspots are found in South and South East Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean.
But rising temperatures worldwide has helped these disease-carrying mosquitos push into new regions like Europe and the Mediterranean.
Wetter and longer monsoons are giving them more time to reproduce in the tropics.
The incidence of dengue has increased 30-fold over the last 50 years, according to the World Health Organisation, which categorises the disease among the top ten global health threats.
Nearly half of the world's population are now at risk.
Removing stagnant water, such as by emptying flowerpot plates, overturning unused pails and breaking up hardened, can help break the dengue transmission cycle.
Some governments also use Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacterium found in about half of all insect species, to curb the spread of mosquito-borne diseases like dengue.
The bacteria makes it harder for the insects to spread the virus, rather than kill them off.

title: Ann Widdecombe public memorial to be held later this year, family says
summary: It will follow a private funeral for family and close friends, which will be held in the coming weeks.
full_text:
Ann Widdecombe public memorial to be held later this year, family says
- Published
A public memorial for Ann Widdecombe will be held later this year, her family has said in a statement.
Former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in her Dartmoor home with serious head injuries earlier this month.
Her family thanked the public for "the wide expression of condolences" but asked that her private service, to be held in the coming weeks and for which invitations have already been sent, is "limited to those closest to Ann".
"We understand that there is significant public interest in the funeral of Ann Widdecombe," the statement said.
"A private service for family and close friends will be held in the coming weeks, and invitations for this ceremony have been distributed.
"A more public memorial will follow later in the year, the details of which will be released in due course.
"While we are very grateful for the wide expression of condolences, the family would ask that this initial service is limited to those closest to Ann."
Tributes poured in to Widdecombe from TV stars and across the political spectrum following her death.
Anton Du Beke, who was her partner on Strictly Come Dancing in 2010, said he was devastated , which he called the "saddest of news".
"I had the most brilliant time with Ann on Strictly Come Dancing, she became a real friend, she was fun, she was upbeat, she was positive, she was supportive, she was game, wanted to enter into the spirit of the whole thing," he said in a video on X.
Kemi Badenoch, leader of the Conservative Party for which Widdecombe served as shadow home secretary from 1999 to 2001, said the party was "reeling".
She described Widdecombe as "a very fun and feisty woman who spoke her mind", while the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said Widdecombe was a "distinguished politician".
In a video posted on social media, Farage said Widdecombe was "an extraordinary woman" and "someone who gave her life to public service, to fighting for the things she believed in".
He described her as "a devout Christian and somebody with strong socially conservative views. Perhaps not popular in modern Britain but that is what Ann believed in".
Widdecombe's career in politics spanned decades.
She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.
Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.
She later represented South West England as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for the Brexit Party and in 2023 she joined Reform UK as a party spokeswoman.

title: Fatboy Slim helps to save 'lifeblood' music venue
summary: The DJ is among investors including Andy Burnham helping to buy the Brighton home of The Pipeline.
full_text:
Fatboy Slim helps to save 'lifeblood' music venue
- Published
The home of a Brighton music venue is to become community owned as part of a £7m initiative backed by DJ Fatboy Slim and Andy Burnham dubbed the "National Trust of music venues".
The Pipeline in Little East Street will become the 10th site owned by Music Venue Properties (MVP), a campaign which acquires the freeholds of music venues to secure their futures.
Fatboy Slim, whose real name is Norman Cook, is among a number of people, including Burnham and Squeeze frontman Glenn Tilbrook, to invest in the charitable community benefit society.
Cook said: "I love venues like this because they remind me of when I started out, that youthful excitement and feeling about having to perform."
He said: "Rooms like this are where dreams come true or where memories are made, and enormous acts learn their craft.
"Venues like this are the lifeblood of the music industry.
"In this current economic climate it's quite hard for them to survive, so if MVP buys the venue, we can be the benevolent landlord that doesn't raise the rent, listens to them and gives them long term security."
In June, Cook played the 60-capacity venue in a sold-out gig as part of the Everywhere at Once festival.
Under the scheme, MVP raises funds through investors and the offer of "community shares", which allows it to buy music venues and lease them to the businesses, who often rent the sites rather than owning them.
The group has so far bought 10 sites, including The Booking Hall in Dover and The Joiners in Southampton.
'I would have given up'
MVP says it has earned the nickname "The National Trust for music venues" due to its model of buying venues to secure their futures.
Thomas Evrenos, who has run The Pipeline in Brighton since 2017, said: "For the future of the venue this means a lot because having a landlords that understands what we are doing, and realises that our purpose is to create a place that is good for musicians, is super important.
"I'm super happy. If it didn't turn out like this and someone had tried to increase the rent, then I would have probably given up."
Peter Cornforth, of MVP, added: "Brighton is a really vibrant place but you need live spaces for people to come and learn their craft.
"We are about the preservation of the key role that grassroots venues play, both for artists and in their communities."

title: I became a nurse after my husband died from Covid - now I'm determined to get a job
summary: Rachel Ohene-Adjei took her GCSEs after her husband died, and has now graduated with a nursing degree.
full_text:
I became a nurse after my husband died from Covid - now I'm determined to get a job
- Published
A woman who trained to become a nurse because she was so impressed with the care given to her husband when he died from Covid has graduated and said she "won't give up" in her search for a job.
Rachel Ohene-Adjei's husband, Eric, died in April 2021 after seven weeks in intensive care at the University Hospital of Wales (UHW) in Cardiff.
Due to the treatment he received, Rachel began studying for a GCSE in maths and English, leading to an access course in nursing, then a university nursing degree - which she graduated from last week.
Rachel, 44, who is graduating at a time of fewer vacancies in the profession, said she was determined to find a job.
Last month the NHS workforce organisation Health Education and Improvement Wales (HEIW) confirmed that almost 400 nursing and midwifery graduates remained without NHS positions after the first round of job matching.
Rachel, from Cardiff, said she was unsuccessful during the first round of applications, but was hopeful in the second, having applied for three new positions.
"I won't give up. I have to be a nurse. I've worked too hard to show my children that anything's possible. So, I will get a job," she said.
Her journey to becoming a nurse began in 2003 when she met Eric in a "love at first sight moment" in a bar. The couple married four years later, having three children together.
Rachel said she "didn't enjoy learning in school", leaving without passing GCSE maths and English, but said Eric helped build up her confidence.
"My husband was always such a supportive, positive person," she said.
Eric tested positive for Covid in February 2021 and was admitted to UHW but died a few months later.
"Seeing that care that he was given just put something in my head that I needed to help and care for people."
After his funeral she applied to get her GCSEs before enrolling on a nursing course, and then her nursing university degree.
Rachel admitted it had sometimes been difficult to juggle her studies with her parenting commitments, including pulling some "all-nighters" to study.
"[My children] are active so I'd have to come home, take them to their football or rugby or dance, or to their friends' house because they're really social - I had to really set myself targets at times when I could and couldn't do things. And it was a lot," she said.
"I just felt like, am I making a mistake? I'm just taking so much time away from my family to do this, is it worth it?"
She said it was also challenging because she was "never very good in school", but was determined to keep going, with the help of her family and friends.
Part of her determination was also to prove to her children she could do it.
"They knew I was doing it to show them that it doesn't matter what happens in life, or how old you are. If you want to do something and you put your mind to it, then you can do it."
Speaking to the BBC at the graduation ceremony, the couple's 13-year-old daughter, Ebony, said she was "very proud" of her mum "for everything she's gone through".
"Obviously with my dad dying, it's been so hard for her. And I've tried to help her through it a lot."
Rachel said at the graduation ceremony it didn't "feel real".
"I can't believe I've done it. I've got this one friend who always said you should be a nurse. And I'm like, I can't. I'm not clever enough. And... I've done it."
Asked what Eric would make of her graduating, she said: "He would just be immensely proud, he always was."

title: One month, two record transfers - why English midfielders are in demand
summary: Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers both sold for record transfer fees, so why are English midfielders so in demand?
full_text:
One month, two record transfers - why English midfielders are in demand
- Published
In the space of one month, England duo Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers have each broken the record for being the most expensive British player of all-time.
Anderson's £116m move from Nottingham Forest to Manchester City came before Chelsea signed Rogers for £117m from Aston Villa.
Both are English midfielders, both are operating at a high level. Both are just 23 - in theory, years from their peak.
So why are England so strong in this area? Why have the pair been sold for such high fees?
And with Adam Wharton and Alex Scott among those also attracting attention, what is it about English midfielders that makes them so sought after?
Anderson and Rogers in form
At such a relatively young age, both Rogers and Anderson offer the prospect of potential as well as being ready-made Premier League players.
Anderson arrives in Manchester having enjoyed a remarkable domestic campaign and impressed on the world stage, starting all but one of England's eight matches as they finished third at the World Cup.
The central midfielder was a real engine for the Three Lions and proved City right to spend big to bring him in.
For Forest last season, he was a bright spark in a tough campaign, spent mostly fighting relegation.
He recorded 3,300 touches in the top flight last season, more than any other player, and led the division for duels won (297), possessions won (306) and fouls won (80).
He also topped the charts for most passes completed as a central midfielder (2,038) and led the position with 376 line-breaking passes.
His four goals and four assists along with creating 54 chances, including nine big chances, highlight his proficiency at both ends of the pitch.
Meanwhile, Rogers contributed 14 goals and 12 assists in 55 appearances across all competitions for Aston Villa last season.
A versatile attacking midfielder, Rogers can play as a number 10 or out on the left wing, meaning his defensive stats do not compare to those of Anderson, but going forward he showed himself as one of the most effective players on the continent.
Across Europe's top five leagues, he ranked second-highest among midfielders for touches in the opposition box (181) while his 16 Premier League goal involvements place him inside Europe's top 10 in the position.
Statistics from the last Premier League season do not feature Manchester City maestro Rodri as he continued his return from a anterior cruciate ligament injury.
But it is likely he will return to the top of a lot of those charts next season after looking back to his best at the World Cup, winning the player of the tournament award after guiding Spain to the title.
Who next?
With traditional number nines seemingly becoming a dying breed, clubs are turning to other positions to provide the goal threat.
That makes the midfielder, particularly one with a bit of creativity who can unlock defences, a sought-after player.
England seem to have produced a number of players who fit that bill within a similar time period - although Tottenham have spent £185m on a midfield duo Sandro Tonali of Italy and Portugal's Matheus Fernandes this summer.
With the Premier League's home grown rule in force - requiring a minimum of eight places in a club's 25-strong squad are set aside for players produced in England or Wales - it is also expected that clubs pay a premium price for players who have come through Football Association academies.
And with Anderson and Rogers securing their moves, could Scott and Wharton be next?
Bournemouth have already rejected a £64m bid from Chelsea for midfielder Scott as they strive to hold on to the 22-year-old, who enjoyed an impressive season on the south coast, particularly from January onwards.
Scott was selected in his first England squad last November and was then called into Thomas Tuchel's extended pre-World Cup training camp in Florida but is yet make an appearance at senior international level.
Crystal Palace midfielder Wharton has also long been a coveted player, with Liverpool, Chelsea and Manchester City all previously registering interest.
Both aged just 22, the pair highlight the plethora of English talent and potential currently available in that position.
While they may not be the best in the world right now, they are part of a group of players in their early 20s who are nearing their prime and will therefore only move clubs for peak prices.
Why this summer's transfer fees aren't as mad as they look
Analysis by football finance expert Kieran Maguire
Transfer fees keep smashing records, but relative to what clubs can actually afford, they have barely moved.
Back in 1992-93, the Premier League's first season, the average club turned over £9.3m. That summer's biggest signing, Alan Shearer, cost £3.3m - 35% of average revenue.
Fast forward to 2024-25 - the latest season with full accounts published - and average Premier League revenue has ballooned to £342m - 35% of that is £121m, strikingly close to what clubs have just paid for Anderson and Rogers.
The lesson: it's not that clubs have gone transfer mad, but that they can simply afford more.

title: Wolves training cancelled after Arokodare refuses to leave pitch
summary: Wolves striker Tolu Arokodare forces the cancellation of a training session as he refuses to leave the pitch.
full_text:
Arokodare forces Wolves training to be cancelled
- Published
Wolves striker Tolu Arokodare forced the cancellation of a training session after he refused to leave the pitch.
BBC Sport has been told the 25-year-old Nigeria international sat down and demanded the club let him move to Fiorentina.
Wolves have rejected a bid from the Serie A side, having accepted an offer from Turkish club Trabzonspor.
Arokodare's actions led to new boss Cesar Peixoto terminating the session on Monday.
The striker was not involved in Wednesday's friendly at Maidenhead United as Wolves continue their pre-season plans.
On social media on Wednesday evening, Arokodare wrote: "Throughout my career, I have always taken great pride in conducting myself professionally and maintaining the highest training standards.
"My commitment has always been to prepare myself as well as possible so that I can contribute to my team-mates and the club whenever I am called upon.
"I remain under contract with Wolves, and my only intention is to fulfil my responsibilities professionally by training, doing my job, and contributing to the team in accordance with that contract."
The latest incident is another flashpoint in the forward's career at Molineux after he was disciplined in April following a confrontation with young forward Mateus Mane.
Arokodare signed for £24m from Genk last summer but scored just three league goals as Wolves finished bottom of the Premier League and were relegated.
And the incident presents an early challenge for Peixoto just weeks into his reign after he replaced Rob Edwards in a surprise move last month.
The 46-year-old, capped once by Portugal in his playing career, moved from Gil Vicente and will be aiming to return Wolves to the Premier League at the first attempt.

title: Arsenal defender Saliba sidelined for ‘extended period’ due to back injury
summary: Centre back William Saliba won't require surgery for injury sustained at World Cup, his club says.
full_text:
Arsenal defender Saliba sidelined for ‘extended period’ due to back injury
Centre back William Saliba won’t require surgery for injury sustained at World Cup, his club says.
Arsenal defender William Saliba will be sidelined for an extended period after suffering a back injury while playing for France during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the reigning Premier League champions say.
Saliba was hampered by the injury throughout the tournament in North America, limiting his training. He was substituted in the first half of France’s 2-0 semifinal defeat by Spain and missed the 6-4 third-place playoff loss to England.
“Subsequent specialist reviews on William’s return to London this week have confirmed that he has suffered a back injury which will require a period of rehabilitation,” Arsenal said in a statement on Wednesday.
“Extensive assessments have concluded that surgery is not recommended, but William should now commence a managed recovery programme.
“Everyone is fully focused on supporting William to ensure he is back to full fitness as soon as possible.”
Saliba made 50 appearances across all competitions for the North London club last season as the Gunners ended a 22-year wait to win the Premier League title and also reached the Champions League final.
Arsenal are to begin the defence of their Premier League crown at home against promoted Coventry City on August 21.

title: Between hope and fear: Yemenis react to Houthi blockade on Saudi Arabia
summary: Yemenis fear a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia could reignite war, deepen shortages and worsen hunger.
full_text:
Between hope and fear: Yemenis react to Houthi blockade on Saudi Arabia
Yemenis fear a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia could reignite war, deepen shortages and worsen hunger.
Sanaa, Yemen – Ammar Saleh, a 32-year-old schoolteacher in Sanaa, watched on Monday as the Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Then, on Wednesday, the Houthis declared they had attacked two Saudi ships – a declaration that they were serious in their intention to impose a maritime embargo on their northern neighbour. The Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of conducting its own blockade on rebel-controlled areas of Yemen, therefore justifying the Houthi attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Saudi Arabia slams Houthi blockade: How will rest of the world be impacted?
- list 2 of 4Pro-government militia seizes boat with ‘Houthi weapons materials’ in Yemen
- list 3 of 4How serious is Iran’s threat to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea?
- list 4 of 4US launches new strikes as Iran warns of regional turmoil
Whatever the arguments, the news has come as a jolt to Yemenis like Ammar, many of whom now believe that a four-year period of relative quiet in the country’s more than decade-long war is about to end.
Ammar believes that Sanaa and other Houthi-controlled Yemeni provinces could once again become a battlefield and could be hit with fuel shortages and a worsening humanitarian crisis.
“Imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia is not a minor move, and we will not be immune from its repercussions,” Ammar told Al Jazeera.
While many civilians are anxious over the fallout of the decision to confront Saudi Arabia, Houthi supporters describe it as a step towards ending what they perceive to be Riyadh’s hegemony in Yemen. Supporters of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, meanwhile, see the Houthi attacks as evidence of the group’s “obedience to Iran’s orders”.
‘Unseen suffering’
Civilians who say they support neither side in the war have expressed fear over what may come next.
Abdulla Yahya, a 25-year-old construction worker in Sanaa, said civilian suffering becomes “unseen during the chaos of war”.
Abdulla told Al Jazeera that any Houthi-Saudi Arabian military face-off will complicate the lives of everyday people in Yemen and will make “survival a harder task”.
“The moment a full-scale war begins, the basics we have today will no longer be available or affordable. Prices will soar, fuel supply will be disrupted, and work opportunities will decline. Neither side of the conflict will be aware of our suffering,” said Abdulla.
Yemen’s warring parties have emphasised their preparedness for war, but Abdulla says he is not.
“I wanted to buy an extra cooking gas cylinder and get additional food commodities, such as flour, rice and cooking oil. But I could not afford that. Getting those would cost me about 55,000 Yemeni riyals [$230],” said the father of three.
The ongoing escalation risks dragging Yemen back into wider conflict, further compounding a hunger crisis that aid agencies have said is already spiralling.
Almost 20 million people in Yemen need humanitarian aid, according to United Nations estimates, and the lack of a political settlement to the conflict continues to add to the complexity.
‘Long overdue’
A sense of euphoria prevailed among Houthi supporters in Sanaa when the group announced the naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Mohammed Ali, a Sanaa-based 26-year-old Houthi supporter, said that Sanaa will not be subordinate to Riyadh forever, and that the embargo is a reminder to Saudi leadership: “We can hurt you if you insist on harming us. You are not unbreakable.”
Ali, a university graduate, argued that Yemen was a sovereign state, and that Saudi leaders had “no right to decide which ship is allowed to sail towards our ports and which plane is permitted to fly in our sky”.
“We feel Saudi Arabia is suffocating us. Let us give them a dose of their own medicine. This measure has been long overdue,” Mohammed told Al Jazeera.
Mohammed is not worried about a renewed war with Saudi Arabia. “We confronted America, Israel and, before them, the Saudi-led coalition. Now, the kingdom can try its luck in this new round,” he said.
A full closure of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, could hamper Saudi oil exports to Asia, particularly in light of the continued difficulty of passage through the Strait of Hormuz due to the US war on Iran.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it would respond to the Houthi threat to its commercial ships with resolve. “Such threats are a blatant violation of international law and fall under acts of maritime piracy,” the coalition said in a statement on Tuesday.
‘An act of obedience to Iran’
Despite the Houthi justification, many Yemenis opposed to the rebels see their latest attacks as evidence of their subservience to Iran.
Mohammed Karim, a 30-year-old resident of Hodeidah in western Yemen, describes the Houthi blockade on Saudi Arabia as an “act of obedience to Iran” that has nothing to do with defending Yemen’s sovereignty.
“Why have the Houthis not imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia over the past years of war? Why now,” Mohammed asked. “Iran needs such a move now, and the Houthis have carried it out.”
Last week, the Reuters news agency reported that Iran had asked the Houthis to stand ready to close Bab al-Mandeb if the US struck Iranian power infrastructure, as Washington has threatened.
The US is currently conducting nightly strikes on Iran and hitting more civilian infrastructure after a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran broke down.
Mohammed Karim is angry, saying that Houthis “seek to attract Iran’s ongoing chaos to Yemen”.
“It hurts them to see Iran bleed, but they would not feel hurt to see us bleed,” he said. “Over a decade of suffering in Yemen has not led them to rethink their approach and seek a settlement with their Yemeni opponents and Saudi Arabia. That is because of their deep-rooted attachment to Tehran.”
He believes that the Houthi-declared maritime embargo is a wake-up call for Riyadh. “It could be a powerful reason for the kingdom to seriously work on toppling the Houthis and restoring the Yemeni government,” the Hodeidah resident said.
On Monday, Yemen’s Minister of Defence Taher al-Aqili said that the UN-recognised government’s “patience has run out”, indicating the government would be ready to end the “Houthi coup”.
The Yemeni government has used the months since it defeated – with the support of Saudi Arabia – the separatist Southern Transitional Council to attempt to unite the country’s anti-Houthi armed forces.
Recent fighting has been reported between the Houthis and government forces in Hodeidah, with the Red Sea coast being a likely location for any government offensive.
‘Seed of collapse’
Saddam Al Huraibi, a Yemeni political analyst, believes that Iran does not want to launch a direct war on Saudi Arabia and, instead, has delegated the Houthis.
While the Houthis’ resolution to fight a war against the kingdom is “unwise and reckless”, it could be the seed of their collapse, Al Huraibi told Al Jazeera.
If this blockade does lead to a wider conflict, the Houthis will “suffer military losses and potentially break down”, the analyst said.
“Today, the Yemeni government sees the military option as the only viable route to deal with the Houthis. I think Saudi Arabia and other regional and international actors have also reached the same conclusion, especially after the declaration of the naval blockade,” he added.
But the talk of war is chilling for many Yemenis, who fear that stopping the fighting would be difficult if full-fledged war started again.
“It is like a fire, and no fire would be extinguished without losses and damages,” Ammar, the Sanaa schoolteacher, said. “We cannot endure any more losses or pain.”
