title: Why health officials do not have a good handle on the current Ebola outbreak
summary: To get slightly ahead of the virus, health officials need to quickly identify people at risk of infection, a practice known as contact tracing. That's a challenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
full_text:
Why health officials do not have a good handle on the current Ebola outbreak
Ebola death toll reaches nearly 1,000 as the DRC struggles to contain the virus
The key to ending any infectious disease outbreak, especially one for which there's no approved vaccine, like the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, is getting slightly ahead of the virus.
To do that, health officials need to quickly identify the possible routes a virus might spread, a practice known as contact tracing, says Armand Sprecher, an infectious diseases physician with Doctors Without Borders.
"We find a sick person and say, 'Who was in contact with that sick person? Who took care of them? Who did their laundry, who touched them? Or who went to a burial where somebody had died of this?'" he says.
Spread by bodily fluids, the virus can only travel to these contacts. Identifying them all quickly, informing them of their exposure and keeping tabs on them can help prevent them from spreading the virus to others and get care faster if they develop symptoms. "It's labor-intensive, but if you can do it well, you've got a really good handle on the outbreak," says Sprecher.
Health officials do not have a good handle on the current outbreak.
Just over two months in, over 1,000 people have died, and more than 2,400 people have been sickened by the virus. Daily case counts show no signs of slowing down. Perhaps most concerningly, more than 80% of new cases are popping up outside of known contacts.
"That is an alarm bell for me," says Nahid Bhadelia, an infectious disease physician at Boston University who has worked on previous Ebola responses. "It means that a lot more people have this disease than we think, and contact tracing is not keeping up."
That high percentage could stem from the inability to trace all contacts of cases, giving them only a partial view of known transmission chains.
The outbreak is centered in a region with a lot of transient workers and ongoing conflict, which can make it difficult to track down everyone who comes into contact with a known case. More contact tracers would help, and the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that 21,000 community workers are being trained right now.
But it's also likely that entire chains of transmission are occurring outside the view of health officials before a very sick — or dead — person gets on their radar. "There's probably a lot more cases that we're missing," says Bhadelia. "This means people are presenting much later to care, which means their survival rates could be lower."
Many people aren't coming to clinics at all. Roughly two-thirds of deaths occur outside of the health system, according to WHO.
"There are still lots of people with symptoms that could be consistent with a concern for an Ebola diagnosis that are going 'underground,'" says Boghuma Titanji, an infectious disease physician at Emory University. Instead, she says they may be seeking care with traditional healers, staying home with family or unable to access — or even purposefully avoiding — treatment centers.
"It's important to remember that there's a lot of stigma associated with Ebola," she says. And where this outbreak is unfolding, there's "lots of mistrust toward the medical science and the people who are investigating the outbreak."
The fact that so much sickness and death is happening in the dark, outside the view of health officials and clinicians, has made responding harder, says Titanji. "I view it as just seeing the tip of the iceberg, but not being able to see just how big that iceberg is because we just don't have the lens that allows us to see that."
Improving that view, in part, will require building trust with affected communities. That's hard work, says Bhadelia, but some recent good news in the response could help — the start of clinical trials for treatments and a drug that could protect exposed people from getting sick.
"I think that you can build trust by providing better care," says Bhadelia, "and that better care can, of course, be access to potentially promising treatments."
Access to these therapies is still quite limited, since they're only available through clinical trials. But Bhadelia hopes that over time, the prospect of receiving better care or a drug that could prevent disease after an exposure could attract more people to seek help through clinics or contact tracers. Ultimately, she says that's what's needed to reduce the toll of this outbreak and get it under control.

title: U.S. nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia faces criticism in Israel
summary: The nuclear power deal between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia was met with alarm in Israel as it deepened concerns that Israel, a major American ally, and Trump are increasingly diverging on foreign policy and security.
full_text:
U.S. nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia faces criticism in Israel
TEL AVIV — An agreement for U.S. companies to build and run nuclear energy plants in Saudi Arabia was met with alarm in Israel on Thursday, as the U.S. and Iran continued to trade strikes in the latest escalation engulfing the Persian Gulf.
The nuclear cooperation agreement, signed on Wednesday by the Trump administration with Saudi Arabia, gives American companies priority access to supply nuclear reactors and fuel to the Saudi nuclear energy program, according to an administration memo about the agreement seen by NPR. The agreement must be reviewed by Congress, which has 90 days to consider it.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest oil producers, but the Gulf state has been trying to pivot to other energy sources. Its nuclear energy program is expected to last decades and be worth billions of dollars, according to the Department of Energy.
Nuclear power would allow Saudi Arabia to use less petroleum energy domestically and maximize exports as well, Matthew Bunn, a nuclear proliferation expert at Harvard University told NPR's All Things Considered.
"But they also want to provide the foundation, over time, for having more options to move toward nuclear weapons, should they feel the need," Bunn said.
While Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has said the kingdom does not want a nuclear weapon, he also has said Riyadh will pursue one if Iran develops a nuclear weapon first.
Yoel Guzansky, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said what he found alarming was that the agreement appeared to let Saudi Arabia enrich its own nuclear fuel in-country.
"Saudi insistence on enrichment in Saudi Arabia ... was the thing that got [previous] negotiations stuck and U.S. administrations, one after another, did not permit enrichment," Guzansky said.
He said the agreement may lead the United Arab Emirates to reverse course on its own deal with the U.S. In the 2009 nuclear deal with the U.S., the UAE voluntarily gave up the ability to enrich nuclear fuel on Emirati soil, but the agreement allows it to ask for better terms if another regional country, such as Saudi Arabia, signs a nuclear energy agreement with the U.S. that contains more favorable conditions.
"You know, everyone can blackmail the U.S. They'll say we want enrichment. Okay, if not enrichment, give me the F-35," fighter planes, Guzansky added.
Netanyahu under fire for "failure" to prevent the nuclear deal
The deal was met with alarm in Israel, deepening concerns that Israel, a major American ally, and Trump are increasingly diverging on foreign policy and security.
Israel's former defense minister and foreign minister Avigdor Lieberman criticized the agreement on Israel's public broadcaster on Wednesday, saying it risked pulling the entire Middle East into an escalating nuclear arms race.
Ehud Barak, a former prime minister of Israel, told Israel's army-run radio station the agreement was a sign of the "loss of trust between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump."
Opposition leader Yair Lapid told an Israeli podcast: "I can't explain just how much this is a total failure of Netanyahu's. That's his job. His job is to prevent a Saudi nuclear program."
The agreement is likely to deal a blow to Netanyahu and his Likud party ahead of general elections scheduled to be held in October.
No "gold standard" anti-enrichment agreement
Under the agreement, Saudi Arabia is not permitted to reprocess American nuclear material for weapons, but the deal and a bilateral security protocol with the U.S. does not forbid the kingdom from using American-technology to enrich uranium or other nuclear fuel provided by third countries.
It also does not require from Saudi Arabia to adopt terms that would lead to greater oversight from the International Atomic Energy Agency, according to the memo seen by NPR.
The U.S. required these provisions known as "gold standard," from the United Arab Emirates in a deal inked under the Obama administration in 2009.
Saudi Arabia has been angling for nuclear cooperation with the U.S. for at least a decade, but concerns about the kingdom's human rights abuses and its possible aspirations to develop a nuclear weapon in the future stalled that cooperation.
Then-senator and now Secretary of State Marco Rubio co-sponsored a bipartisan bill in 2019 that would have banned nuclear energy cooperation with the U.S. unless Saudi Arabia was transparent about the killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in a Saudi consulate and committed to the "gold standard" provision, forgoing uranium enrichment.
"Trump's and Secretary Rubio's hypocrisy is matched only by their recklessness. They are allowing Saudi Arabia, a belligerent and authoritarian nation, to develop nuclear weapons technologies while starting a war with Iran under the guise of preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb," Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass), who co-sponsored the 2019 bill with Rubio, wrote in a statement in response to the nuclear agreement.
The U.S. energy department argues the deal expands American technology exports.
The agreement also ties the U.S. and Saudi Arabia, a key ally, closer together at a time when the Gulf states, including the Kingdom of Saud, have paid a heavy price for aligning with the U.S. The Arab Gulf states continue to be hit by Iranian drone and artillery strikes in a war with Iran that the U.S. began. 
Saudi Arabia, in particular, has had to contend with the economic shock of having to curtail its oil exports since Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz and with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels now attacking Saudi oil vessels in the Red Sea.
U.S.-Iran attacks continue as the Houthis strike tankers in the Red Sea
U.S. Central Command said it struck Iranian military and logistics sites on Wednesday in the latest round of attacks. Iran said it responded by targeting three U.S. bases in Kuwait, as well as U.S. military infrastructure in Jordan and Qatar.
The Jordanian military said Thursday it country's air force shot down four missiles and six Iranian drones.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran's army has enhanced its preparations for every enemy scenario, and new scenarios have been predicted and worked on," Iranian military spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Iranian state-run media.
In the Red Sea, Yemen's Houthi rebels said they attacked two Saudi oil tankers. The Saudi state news agency said one of its tankers had been hit and was on fire. It said the crew was unharmed.
Civil war has split control of Yemen between the Houthi group Ansar Allah and an internationally recognized government supported by Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have also launched attacks in support of Iran, and most recently warned Saudi Arabia that they will not allow its tankers through the key shipping route Bab el Mandab near the Red Sea.
NPR's Jane Arraf contributed reporting.

China and the United States’ agreement to pursue stability appeared to be holding, analysts said, even as President Donald Trump seemed determined to rock the boat ahead of the leaders’ second summit of the year in September.
The assessment came as Beijing issued a measured response to his allegations of Chinese interference in the 2020 US elections.
That restraint and recent tangible gestures – including Washington lifting sanctions on Hong Kong and the expected trip to the US this week by a senior Chinese official – signalled a shared appetite for stability, experts said.
That was in sharp contrast with the Joe Biden era, when the downing of a high-altitude balloon originating from China in early 2023 undermined efforts to mend strained relations.
In a prime-time televised address last week, Trump accused Beijing of orchestrating the “largest compromise of election data in history”, a claim that contradicts assessments made by US intelligence agencies in 2021.
Beijing opted for a controlled response. Concerns that the controversy would derail Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to the US did not last long, as both sides confirmed that preparations were still under way.

title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
summary:
The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year

Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying, after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying, after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.
Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.
From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.
Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola used “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.
Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.
Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.
Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.
Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.
In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.
In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.
Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.
Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. Sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.
Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, Lusa reported.
Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Press contributed to this report

title: More than 20,000 evacuated after intense wildfire in France
summary:
Reception centres open to thousands of evacuees after blaze begins in pine forest 45km west of Bordeaux

  • Europe live – latest updates

More than 20,000 people, including thousands of tourists from campsites and other holiday accommodation, have been evacuated as a “particularly intense” wildfire advances on the Atlantic coast of south-west France, authorities have said.

The blaze, which began in dense pine forest near the village of Saumos about 40km (25 miles) west of Bordeaux and just north of the bay of Arcachon, a popular tourist destination, had burned 2,400 hectares (5,928 acres) in less than 24 hours, firefighters said on Thursday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
More than 20,000 people, including thousands of tourists from campsites and other holiday accommodation, have been evacuated as a “particularly intense” wildfire advances on the Atlantic coast of south-west France, authorities have said.
The blaze, which began in dense pine forest near the village of Saumos about 40km (25 miles) west of Bordeaux and just north of the bay of Arcachon, a popular tourist destination, had burned 2,400 hectares (5,928 acres) in less than 24 hours, firefighters said on Thursday.
No casualties had been reported or homes destroyed so far, they said, but the Gironde prefecture said that while 700 firefighters and four waterbombing planes were battling to bring the fire under control, the situation “remains unfavourable”.
France has endured three almost back-to-back heatwaves since May as climate breakdown leads to more frequent and intense extreme weather events causing thousands of excess deaths, evaporating soils and waterways and fuelling wildfires.
Patrick Martineau, 69, who was evacuated from the village of Le Porge, told Agence- France Presse that police had “come banging on the doors … It’s scary – hard to take in. When we bought a home here, we never thought there’d be a fire risk.”
Sylvie, a holidaymaker from Paris staying in the relatively more built-up area of Lège-Cap-Ferret, said a neighbour had told her: “‘Get your bags ready, we’re going to be evacuated during the night.’ We put the bulk of our stuff in the car boot and left.”
In 2022, a wildfire burned more than 30,000 hectares in the same area, forcing about 50,000 people to be evacuated. In tinder-dry conditions and fanned by a strong wind, the latest blaze has torn through the forest, with flames reaching 10m high.
Nine local municipalities have opened reception centres for evacuees and were sheltering more than 2,500 people, the prefecture said. About 8,800 people were evacuated at midday on Thursday, after 2,000 in the morning and 10,000 overnight.
Numerous roads in the area – including those leading to the Cap Ferret peninsula a few kilometres to the south, home to the villas of celebrities and millionaires and one of France’s most exclusive holiday spots – were closed to all but essential traffic.
Police have opened an investigation into the causes of the wildfire, which the mayor of Le Porge, Martial Zaninetti, said on Wednesday appeared to have been started by a machine that was clearing undergrowth.
Elsewhere in France, a fire near Pontevès, about 70km north of the Mediterranean port city of Toulon, had been “stabilised” on Thursday after burning through 2,500 hectares of land and destroying at least 10 houses, firefighters said.
The prefect of the Var department, Simon Babre, on Thursday allowed 400 people who had been evacuated from the area to return to their homes to “assess the damage”, but said that the fire was not yet fully under control.
A fortnight ago, flames devastated a tenth of the Unesco-listed Fontainebleau forest outside Paris in a rare wildfire so far north. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has said more than 12,500 wildfires have broken out since the beginning of the year.
In Spain, most of the people evacuated on Wednesday evening owing to a fire 70km south-west of Madrid were also allowed to return home. A fire that has burned 32,000 hectares in the province of Guadalajara, north of the capital, was also described as stable.

title: Dubai offers £600 rewards to residents who convince friends to come on holiday as tourism numbers plummet
summary:
Residents eligible for dining and hotel packages if they can persuade family and friends to city spurned by visitors amid Iran war

  • Middle East crisis – live updates

Dubai is offering to pay residents who attract family and friends to visit the emirate in an effort to revive tourist numbers that have plummeted since the city was drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Dubai Invite scheme, an initiative of the department of economy and tourism, allows residents of the United Arab Emirates to nominate friends and relatives and then to receive benefits worth more than 3,000 UAE dirham (about £610) if they visit.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Dubai is offering to pay residents who attract family and friends to visit the emirate in an effort to revive tourist numbers that have plummeted since the city was drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran.
The Dubai Invite scheme, an initiative of the department of economy and tourism, allows residents of the United Arab Emirates to nominate friends and relatives and then to receive benefits worth more than 3,000 UAE dirham (about £610) if they visit.
Visit Dubai’s website says residents will receive a “benefits package” including hotel stays, dining deals and attraction tickets.
Eligibility terms state that each resident is eligible for a maximum of three benefit packages for visitors arriving before 31 October, but benefits can be redeemed until December.
The visitors must be non-UAE residents, arrive on a valid tourist visa and can only be nominated once.
The scheme comes as the UAE’s tourism sector experiences a significant downturn, with international passenger numbers falling sharply after the Gulf states became drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran.
In February, Iran retaliated by firing missiles and drones which hit the world-famous Fairmont hotel and Dubai’s international airport, shattering the image the city had sold influencers and the ultra-rich of a gilded playground, safe from the volatility of the wider region.
In 2025 Dubai welcomed nearly 20 million tourists, a record. However, since the conflict the number of airlines operating at Dubai airports has halved as many planes were turned around due to missiles and tourists eschewed routes over the Middle East.
There are reports of massive hotel vacancies and businesses suffering declines in revenue of more than 50%.
Some of Dubai’s most famous hotels have shut entirely, many bringing forward plans for renovations and refurbishments such as the sail-shaped Burj Al Arab, which will close for 18 months for a major restoration.
Other hotels and businesses are leaning into the government’s new scheme, offering discounts of 45% and free nights.
Local media on Thursday reported that within the first 48 hours, the scheme had attracted more than 10,000 applications.

title: Saudi Arabia and US strike deal for kingdom to enrich uranium
summary:
Donald Trump approves agreement to help country make fuel for civilian nuclear programme

Donald Trump signed a nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that could enable the kingdom to enrich its own uranium for nuclear reactions.

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed “a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” and “an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement,” according to a statement from the US Department of Energy.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Donald Trump signed a nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that could enable the kingdom to enrich its own uranium for nuclear reactions.
The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed “a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” and “an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement,” according to a statement from the US Department of Energy.
The timing of the announcement is controversial, as the US’s war with Iran is being fought in part to prevent Tehran enriching uranium domestically and make it near-impossible for Iran to build a nuclear weapon.
The US-Saudi deal is expected to last 30 years and involve US firms such as Westinghouse in developing the programme.
It could allow for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia after a joint US-Saudi study. The proposal has been in discussion for years. At one point the Biden administration wanted to condition Saudi Arabia’s access to the technology on normalising relations with Israel, something Saudi Arabia is still refusing to do.
The plan is expected to be submitted to Congress for review, where it could face opposition among lawmakers who fear a lack of monitoring safeguards to restrict Saudi Arabia’s uranium enrichment.
Saudi Arabia has in the past said it would need a nuclear weapon if Iran acquired one, an intention Iran has repeatedly denied. But in lengthy talks stretching over more than one administration, the US also feared that Riyadh would look elsewhere for nuclear technology if the US did not provide what it wanted.
It is likely the agreement will not include the enhanced monitoring by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) that is found in the so-called additional protocol to which Iran had been subjected under the 2015 nuclear deal.
Rosemary Kelanic, the head of the Middle East programme at Defense Priorities, warned in a social media post: “Giving Saudi Arabia uranium enrichment technology is a terrible idea on many counts. But it’s especially idiotic to do it *in the middle of a war over Iran’s nuclear programme*.”
She described the decision as reckless and not in the US national interest. “Saudi enrichment would put immense pressure on Iran to get the bomb. Is Trump TRYING to provoke Iran into weaponising?”
Others said it showed the US thought Saudi Arabia had matured into a country that wanted to diversify its energy mix away from oil.
The debate about the wisdom of Iran’s stated refusal to acquire nuclear weapons is very live inside Iran, and there will be anger that Tehran’s biggest regional rival is permitted to enrich uranium domestically while Iran is sanctioned for doing so.
In negotiations in Geneva in February, before the outbreak of the war, the US demanded Iran commit to a 10- to 20-year suspension of any right to enrich domestically. Iran was willing to consider a suspension of three years.
Separately, the US had been willing to consider a regional consortium to enrich uranium that would include Saudi Arabia, Iran, the US and the United Arab Emirates.
Saudi Arabia is a member state of the IAEA, a Vienna-based UN agency that promotes peaceful nuclear work but also does inspections to make sure countries do not have clandestine atomic weapons programmes.
Congress can review and block nuclear cooperation agreements, also known as “123 agreements”.
Enrichment to 90% purity is only one step in the process of acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Saudi Arabia and nuclear-armed Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact after Israel launched an attack on Qatar targeting Hamas officials. Pakistan’s defence minister then said his nation’s nuclear programme “will be made available” to Saudi Arabia if needed, something seen as a warning for Israel, long known as the Middle East’s only nuclear-armed state.
The United Arab Emirates, a neighbour to Saudi Arabia, signed a 123 agreement with the US to build its Barakah nuclear power plant with South Korean assistance. But the UAE did so without seeking enrichment, something non-proliferation experts have held up as the “gold standard” for countries wanting nuclear power.
During Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Washington in November, the White House announced a US-Saudi framework for nuclear cooperation that “builds the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar nuclear energy partnership” between the two countries “in a manner consistent with strong nonproliferation standards”.
In a report to Congress earlier this year, the US administration urged support for the US-Saudi nuclear deal, in part to “prevent strategic competition from seizing an opportunity to undermine United States national security interests for decades to come”.
The report also argued that the US must seize the opportunity to expand nuclear cooperation to “re-establish our leadership in the global civilian nuclear energy market and reap the benefits of expanded influence in foreign countries hosting our reactors”.

title: The Robots Cometh
summary: The humanoid revolution is coming—and the Chinese firm Unitree is leading the charge.
full_text:
Spectators typically leave a UFC fight with ringing ears and a sheepish resolve to get back to the gym.
went straight to his laboratory.
“I thought I could make a bigger robot for boxing competitions,” says Wang, the founder and CEO of Hangzhou-based humanoid-robotics firm
. “Then I thought, Why not do an even bigger one that can actually carry a human inside?”
The upshot of Wang’s creative fervor is the GD01, which Unitree bills as the world’s first mass-produced, transformable mecha robot. Standing 9 ft. tall and weighing half a ton, it can transport a pilot in its torso-mounted cockpit, walk on either two legs or four, and wield fists powerful enough to knock down walls. Heavy-duty mechanical hinges connect titanium-alloy limbs to a protective casing of carbon fiber, enabling smooth, deliberate strides on brutish red legs.
Wang showed off the GD01 exclusively to TIME as part of his first international media interview, revealing that beyond mixed martial arts, he took a dash of inspiration from
: “We actually drew some references from a similar robot featured in
Photograph by Mattia Balsamini for TIME
Wang has done more than arguably anyone else to bring this science fiction closer to reality. A native of China’s coastal city of Ningbo, he founded Unitree in 2016 when he was just 26 years old and has moved from robot dogs to humanoid robots and now, with GD01, human mobility machines. But while the GD01 might inspire awe, humbler humanoids like Unitree’s flagship G1 are the ones set to become the workhorses of a global robotics transformation already gathering pace in China, the U.S., and beyond.
This is the next great tech frontier, one that has previously been the purview of
AI that walks, sees, hears and physically interacts with the real world. Morgan Stanley
that as many as 13 million humanoids could walk among us by 2035—equivalent to the population of Bolivia. That number is forecast to rise to 1 billion by 2050, when the industry could be worth $5 trillion.
Unitree is hardly alone staking a claim in this space. In January,
announced the third generation of its Optimus humanoid robot with a goal to eventually produce 10 million units per year at factories in Fremont and Texas. In late June, California-based Figure dispatched its latest
to BMW’s Spartanburg plant in South Carolina, where its earlier 02 model helped assemble 30,000 cars last year. Oregon-based
, meanwhile, has secured deployments everywhere from Toyota to Latin American e-commerce giant Mercado Libre. But Unitree is the world leader in terms of volume, dispatching more than 5,500 units in 2025, comprising over a quarter of a global market that is only just waking. In June,
announced that its bleeding-edge Jetson Thor chip would be fitted into Unitree’s H2 humanoid for sale to research institutions around the globe.
We could be, Wang says, anything from two to 10 years away from a “ChatGPT moment” for humanoids, whereby a robot achieves sufficient “generalization” to be able to execute 80% of requested voice commands in an 80% unfamiliar environment. “Once the technology surpasses this ... inflection point, robots can gradually be rolled out for large-scale commercial use,” he says.
“We don’t see any significant competitors outside of China.”
—Elon Musk, on China’s dominance in the humanoid field
The company’s GD01 humanoid photographed on June 18 in Hangzhou.
If the timeline for that breakthrough is a matter of debate, its potential impact is not. Nonunion robots (the only kind) could operate around the clock on assembly lines, replace some nurses in hospitals, and pick fruit under the hot sun.
The positive outlook is that wide-scale humanoid adoption will herald an unprecedented era of global abundance, automating mundane and dangerous labor while ushering in post-scarcity societies. There is a less rosy divination, however. Amid a mass labor displacement, robots concentrate even more wealth into fewer human hands. With production severed from wages, people could face an identity crisis as robots begin to dominate manual labor and service industries, while governments contend with strained social safety nets and rising competition between the U.S. and China—leaders in humanoids as they are in AI—over raw material and technology. On June 3, three U.S. lawmakers
introduced the bipartisan Guard Act
, which seeks to ban Chinese robots deemed to be a national-security threat. Unitree was singled out by John Moolenaar, a bill co-sponsor and chairman of the House Select Committee on China, who accused Wang’s firm of benefiting from “generous state subsidies” and threatening to bankrupt American competitors.
With AI, we’ve already seen how the ability of large language models (LLM) to parse huge reams of data also makes them susceptible to
and unintended consequences, like designing biological weapons. But while an LLM can suggest harm, a robot can enact it, auguring a terrifying new cybersecurity peril in the age of embodied AI. Online scams already siphon off staggering sums, but a hacked humanoid could move the threat from screens into homes, streets, nurseries, and factory floors.
The tension between these visions can be reduced to a choice of myth: Are Wang and his GD01, and indeed their competitors, akin to Luke Skywalker and the faithful, guileless C-3PO—or more like Frankenstein and his monster?
Wang, unsurprisingly, veers toward the positive, predicting that in 10 years every household may have a small robot that can do your laundry, grill your steak, and even provide basic care if you fall ill. They can also take on tasks most humans would rather avoid, from steep mountain farming to sewer maintenance.
But if that sounds like a future arriving faster than society can absorb it, Wang insists the transition will be gradual. “It will evolve step-by-step,” he says. “If society finds that robots don’t perform well in a certain sector, or if people simply don’t like them there, we can easily pivot and re-direct their application to other fields. So, everything remains well within controllable boundaries.”
unlikely prophet of the AI age. Slight and bespectacled, he possesses none of the performative bravado associated with many technology founders. Instead, he speaks about robotics with quiet, unwavering conviction.
The possibilities and promises of a humanoid revolution have occupied him since he was 10 years old and first watched early televised robotics experiments performed at MIT by
, founder of Boston Dynamics. He spent his free time building model aircraft, conducting experiments, and, before long, assembling miniature turbojet engines.
In 2009, Wang enrolled at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University in Hangzhou, majoring in mechatronics engineering. As a first-year student, he says, he built his first small bipedal robot, capable of walking a few steps, on less than $30. That same price-conscious approach would underpin Unitree’s flourishing. While pursuing a master’s degree at Shanghai University, he developed a prototype quadruped robot, XDog, which still occupies pride of place in the Unitree headquarters. Departing from the hydraulic-powered designs popularized by his idols at Boston Dynamics, Wang opted for a cost-saving electric-motor model, which helped XDog win second prize in a national entrepreneurship competition.
After graduation and a stint at Shenzhen-based drone trailblazer
, Wang launched Unitree with 2 million RMB ($300,000) in capital from an angel investor. It has since become a cultural phenomenon;
an estimated 600 million people
watched videos of Unitree’s H2 and G1 humanoid robots
swinging nunchucks and executing flips
as part of February’s Spring Festival Gala—China’s equivalent to the Super Bowl halftime show. It was the second year that Unitree humanoids provided the headline act, and all eyes are on what Wang has planned next time. “I have no idea,” he confesses with a laugh.
In March, Unitree filed for an IPO that would value the firm at $6 billion, spar

title: 10 Foods That Food Safety Experts Never Eat
summary: Some of their no-go foods are obvious. Others are probably in your fridge right now.
full_text:
Ask someone who investigates
for a living what they
put on their plate, and the list is shorter—and stranger—than you'd expect.
It's not that these experts live in fear. Most will tell you that all
, and the real skill is deciding which risks are worth taking. Frank Yiannas, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s former deputy commissioner for food policy and response, says he doesn't think of foods as simply "good" or "bad." Instead, "I approach everything with what I would say is a quantitative risk assessment," he says. "I'm calculated."
Still, after decades of investigating
—and, in some cases, having their own lives forever changed by foodborne illness—these experts have each decided a handful of foods simply aren't worth the gamble. Some of their no-go items are predictable; others might be sitting in your fridge right now. Here’s what came up again and again.
Raw milk and raw-milk cheese
There's almost no debate about this one. "It's ridiculous," says Bill Marler, a food-safety lawyer who has spent decades suing companies over outbreaks. He says he has represented families of children who have
died or suffered kidney damage and neurological complications
after foodborne illness linked to raw milk, and to him, the risk simply isn't worth it. It’s especially hard to justify when there's a safe alternative. “You have such a great thing called pasteurization,” he says.
"It’s very risky," says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute of Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, who avoids raw milk and cheeses made from it. "We've known that for decades."
Kowalcyk knows the stakes of food safety in a deeply personal way. In 2001, she lost her young son to complications from a foodborne
infection—a tragedy that led her to leave a career in pharmaceutical research and devote her life to food safety. (She believes her son’s illness was caused by tainted ground beef in a hamburger he’d eaten.)
Ask Darin Detwiler to name some of the riskiest produce in the grocery store, and he doesn't hesitate:
. "You cannot adequately clean the outside of the cantaloupe," says Detwiler, an associate teaching professor of food policy at Northeastern University and author of
Food Safety: Past, Present, and Predictions
. Once you run a knife through the rough rind, he says, you drag whatever's on the surface straight into the flesh.
If you love it anyway, his rule is to cut it and eat it right away—never let cut melon sit out for more than two hours. And he has one warning sign to watch for: cut melon that's been sitting too long can develop what looks like a dusting of powdered sugar on the surface. It isn't sugar. "That’s when the pathogens have grown so much you can actually see them," he says. He skips the fruit entirely. For Detwiler, some food risks simply aren't worth taking. After losing his young son in the
, he devoted his career to food safety.
Raw oysters and shellfish
Raw oysters show up on a lot of experts' no-go lists. Shellfish are filter feeders, Marler explains—they pull water through their bodies, and "anything in the water that's contaminated, they suck it into their bodies." If the water is contaminated, there's a good chance your oyster is, too.
Detwiler ranks oysters among his personal top three foods to avoid. (Marler does, too.) Beyond the contaminated water, Detwiler says, they're linked to frequent illness outbreaks and can be notoriously difficult to trace back to their source.
Dr. Daniel Griffin, an infectious disease physician and president of
Parasites Without Borders
, doesn't swear off sushi entirely. He does eat it—but only after inspecting it. Some fish parasites are large enough to spot with the naked eye: thin, reddish, thread-like worms visible in a pale piece of fish. "If you Google 'fish with parasite,' you'll probably lose your appetite," he says. He examines each piece before eating it and skips rolls altogether. "I'm not gonna [eat] the roll with something hidden in there," he says.
Jill Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health, says pork is one meat she approaches with extra caution. She avoids thick cuts like pork tenderloin because they're harder to cook all the way through. "All I can see is
," she says. The parasite, which can also be spread through cat feces, has increasingly been
to undercooked pork. "I'm just out on that one."
are another easy pass for Kowalcyk. They've been linked to a long string of foodborne illness outbreaks, she says, "and there's really no good way to clean them." That's because contamination often starts before the sprouts are even grown: Bacteria can be present on the seeds themselves, and the warm, humid conditions needed for sprouting are also ideal for helping those bacteria multiply. Simply rinsing them under water isn't enough to reliably remove them. Cooking would make them safer—but then, she points out, you've lost the crunch that made them appealing in the first place.
Pre-cut fruits and vegetables
Pre-cut fruits and vegetables are another easy pass. The convenience of a tub of pre-sliced melon or a bag of shredded carrots isn't worth giving up control over how your food is handled, Marler says. "You don't know how long it's been sitting around, or whether the knife, the cutting surface, or the hands that touched it were clean," he says.
Kowalcyk feels the same way. She'd rather buy produce whole and cut it herself than trust someone else to do it.
Eggs are far safer today than they were 20 years ago, Marler notes—but he still won't eat them raw. That means no tasting cookie dough made with raw eggs, no licking brownie batter off the beaters, and no homemade Caesar dressing made with uncooked yolks. Most eggs sold in grocery stores
, he notes, so if a recipe calls for raw eggs, he'd rather use pasteurized ones—or skip it altogether.
Undercooked hamburgers
A medium-rare steak and a medium-rare burger may look similar, but Griffin says they're completely different from a food-safety perspective. With a steak, bacteria generally stay on the surface, where cooking kills them. Grind that same meat into a hamburger, though, and any bacteria get mixed throughout the patty.
"You're gonna take whatever bacterial contamination,
, or fecal contamination, and now you're gonna mix it all deep in there," he says.
That's why Griffin always orders burgers well done. Yiannas does too. At home, he uses a food thermometer instead of relying on color alone.
Potlucks and picnic foods
Roberts is wary of foods prepared outside regulated kitchens. "If it's a potluck, I'm out," she says. "If it's a bake sale, no." When coworkers organize a potluck, she jokes that she suddenly has another commitment. "I'm always ill," she says.
Family cookouts are a different story, because she can watch the food being grilled. Even then, she's vigilant about anything that sits out in the summer heat. Rather than leaving a big bowl of potato salad on the picnic table, she has her family keep most of it in the refrigerator and bring out only a small portion at a time, refilling the bowl as needed. Her sister now teases her by asking, "Do you want me to get an aliquot?"—a laboratory term Roberts has turned into family shorthand for serving a small batch.

title: U.S. Reaches Landmark Nuclear Deal With Saudi Arabia
summary: The deal has elicited criticism over its potential to fuel an arms race in the Middle East.
full_text:
Washington has reached a watershed civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, the U.S. Energy Department announced Wednesday, which could pave the way for uranium enrichment in the kingdom.
Details of the deal are sparse, though what the Trump Administration has described as a “decades-long, multi-billion-dollar” partnership is subject to review by Congress, which could oppose it over its potential to start a nuclear arms race in the Middle East.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia have been working on the deal for years, both during Donald Trump’s first presidency and that of his successor, Joe Biden. The
first reported that Trump formally approved the deal last week.
The deal also comes as the Trump Administration continues to pressure Saudi Arabia’s longstanding regional rival Iran
to give up its enriched uranium stockpiles
and curb the development of its nuclear program. Iran has repeatedly insisted that its nuclear program is peaceful.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who signed the deal with Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, sought to allay those worries. “Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world's best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States,” Wright said in
Secretary of State Marco Rubio
similarly added earlier
that the U.S. “is not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation.”
Saudi Arabia is an oil-rich nation, but
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
has stated ambitions for the country to expand its energy generation portfolio beyond fossil fuels. Developing a nuclear power program, Saudi officials have argued, could free up more oil supply and boost exports.

that Saudi Arabia plans to use its resources for producing low-enriched uranium.
Talks between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia have been going on for some time: under the
, a civil nuclear cooperation deal was envisioned as part of a broader one that would include formalizing diplomatic relations between Riyadh and Israel. The Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas and the ensuing conflict, however, made the deal elusive.

On Wednesday, the Energy Department announced that Wright and Abdulaziz signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, known as a “
”, and a bilateral safeguards agreement. The 123 agreement, the department claims, “provides great access for American companies in the Saudi nuclear energy program, benefiting American industry, workers, and supply chains while helping to meet Saudi energy needs.”
Congress is expected to know the finer details soon, but some of the core provisions have been reported. The deal, which is expected to last 30 years, would put U.S. companies front and center to develop Saudi Arabia’s nuclear infrastructure. This could include a uranium enrichment facility that could be built if a two-year joint U.S.-Saudi study determines that enrichment in Saudi Arabia is warranted and commercially viable. If, after the study, the U.S. rejects pushing through with indigenous enrichment, Saudi Arabia would, according to the
, not be allowed to enrich independently or with another foreign partner for 10 years.
A deal with Riyadh could limit the U.S.’s competitors China and Russia from having deep stakes in Saudi Arabia, which has actively
engaged with those countries
in nuclear development.  According to the
, Trump Administration officials say that the U.S.’s role would prevent diverting enriched uranium for military purposes and spent reactor fuel from being reprocessed for creating a bomb.
While no awards have been publicly announced, reports from the
say one of the biggest beneficiaries would be Westinghouse, which designs nuclear reactors sold overseas. During a House Foreign Affairs Committee Hearing Wednesday, Rep. Brad Sherman (D, Calif.)
that “Westinghouse stands to make an awful lot of money on this deal.”
Why is the deal controversial?
Some, however, have sounded the alarm on allowing a Middle Eastern country to potentially enrich uranium, as it could destabilize an already volatile region.
The U.S. has a 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia’s regional neighbor, the United Arab Emirates, though in the 2009 deal it agreed to forgo enriching uranium domestically or reprocessing the spent atomic fuel. This has since become known as the “gold standard” for civilian nuclear cooperation.

the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty
During the first-term Trump Administration,
introduced by Sen. Ed Markey (D, Mass.) and then-Senator Rubio (R, Fla.), wanted to block civilian nuclear cooperation with Saudi Arabia unless Congress voted to approve it. Markey
a similar bill earlier this year.
Such 123 agreements usually take effect unless Congress jointly disapproves the deal and a two-thirds majority vote to override a ‌presidential veto.
Some lawmakers have already sounded the alarm on the U.S.-Saudi Arabia deal. House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory Meeks (D, N.Y.)

that, as reported, the deal elicits “deep concerns.” Meeks said the accord must include “appropriate limits on enrichment and reprocessing,” as well as the
International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol

required the protocol
The deal, as reported,

for nonproliferation, according to Kelsey Davenport, director for Nonproliferation Policy at the Arms Control Association. Davenport posted on social media that a bespoke accord “risks other supplier states, say Russia, negotiating similar bilateral arrangements, rather than letting the IAEA do the job it’s designed to do.”
Bonnie Jenkins, former U.S. undersecretary of state for arms control and international security during the Biden Administration, pointed out what she sees as the U.S.’s hypocrisy.
“In all the regional chaos and the failed efforts to come to another Iran nonproliferation nuclear deal, we are agreeing to a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia,” Jenkins

title: The Debate Moment That Captures Democrats’ Worries About Troy Jackson
summary: Jackson shares Graham Platner’s ideology but none of his charisma
full_text:
Making sense of what matters most in Washington.
By signing up you are agreeing to our
It should have been a layup. Instead, the question illustrated why some Democrats fear they are about to swap out
with a candidate who's got a completely different set of problems.
During last week’s debate among potential Platner replacements, the moderators
the field to discuss the kind of oversight of the Trump Administration they would pursue if Democrats gained control of the Senate.
Former state Senate leader Troy Jackson didn’t seem to understand the assignment. “I actually come from the same area Susan Collins comes from,” Jackson began, referencing the GOP incumbent Senator he now seems poised to challenge in November. “I’ve been on the ballot with Donald Trump the last three elections. I’ve been on the ballot with Susan Collins. People in my area vote for me because they know that I stand up for working-class people. And I think, in this case, Collins has completely forgotten who she’s representing.”
He kept wandering before finding his way back to something closer to the topic at hand: oversight. “As far as something like this, prescription drugs. I mean, I live around the border. I see people in New Brunswick that are going with healthcare, they’re going with prescription drugs, the same drugs that we have, and nobody in D.C. is actually doing anything because the healthcare industry, big pharma, is buying them out and we can’t afford to buy them back.”
Other contenders on the stage gave far better answers, but Jackson is the one who is on the cusp of becoming the Democratic nominee in Maine, where the party has its most realistic shot at knocking off an incumbent Republican Senator. Collins is the only Republican incumbent on the ballot this fall hailing from a state Trump lost and after five terms in the Senate, she’s lost the support of many of Maine’s Democrats and independents. Senate Democrats had hoped to run Gov. Janet Mills, who suspended her bid before Platner was
when an ex-girlfriend
him of rape—an allegation he denies. A free-for-all to replace him quickly settled on Jackson, a former Republican and logger who ran for Governor earlier this year and came in third.
Jackson shares Platner’s progressive ideology but none of his charisma. When Jackson and Platner appeared together during their primaries, it was clear who was the headliner. Like the oyster farmer he is set to replace at a state party convention on Saturday, Jackson is closer to the Bernie Sanders wing of the Democratic Party than the Chuck Schumer one. (And, for the record, Jackson
he will not support Schumer’s continued leadership of the party in the Senate.)
Democrats, though, are plenty skittish about Jackson. It’s one thing to run a state Senate. It’s another to live under the klieg lights of a marquee U.S. Senate campaign. Collins is a canny politician who won her last campaign by nine points. And she has a much further head start than Jackson, who will have almost no time to build a competent ground game.
As a former Republican, Jackson also has a confusing policy
—past opposition to same-sex marriage and abortion, both positions he has since reversed—and little polish. His answer at last week’s debate on oversight was the most obvious example, but he concedes he is no smooth talker.
"I know I'm not a polished speaker, and I don't pretend to be,” he
a local radio host in April. “I’m just an everyday person and I don’t put on airs like I’m some highfalutin person. I’m OK with that.”
Then there’s Jackson’s personality, which can be abrasive, according to former colleagues who report
involving thrown water bottles. When a campaign’s best
is that he wasn’t throwing things
any one person, it’s a sign that the stories being spread are more than just axe-grinding.
For its part, Jackson’s team is trying to put its best spin on his sudden return to the arena. His advisers seem to resort to a single word to describe his leadership style: “passionate.”
As a practical matter, since jumping back into politics about two weeks ago, Jackson has
more than $1 million—almost as much as he raised in his entire race for Governor. Of that, more than half has come since he swept a slate of delegates to the state party event this weekend.
Collins’ fundraising? She has collected $18 million and ended last month with $11 million in the bank—plus plenty of favors to dangle as the chair of the powerful Appropriations Committee.
None of this is setting Jackson up for success. Platner’s plain-spoken pitch convinced many in Maine his multiple scandals and inexperience in politics were worth the risk to bring in a new generation of Democrats. Jackson, on the other hand, was first elected to office in 2002. At 58 years old, no one is mistaking him as the fresh-faced agent of change. Add to that his rough edges and hot temper, and Republicans are optimistic about defending Collins in a state that is, at its core, pretty even-keeled.
It’s why Democrats in Washington are currently so queasy about their prospects in Maine, where they fear they’ve just swapped Platner’s baggage with Jackson’s, which may still be tough for voters to accept.

title: In Japan, Prime Minister's Sleep Schedule Prompts Work-Life Balance Debate
summary: Sanae Takaichi posted about how little sleep she gets on the job, but it has drawn criticism from some who say she’s valorizing overwork.
full_text:
For Japanese Prime Minister
, a day off means more work.
As the country enjoyed a three-day weekend to celebrate the Marine Day national holiday, Takaichi said that she spent the weekend poring over policy documents and catching up on domestic work.
“I was able to get five hours of sleep for the first time in a while,” Takaichi
on X on Monday night, noting that she was able to do ironing and sewing she’d put off. “Since taking office, getting zero to three hours of sleep has become the norm.”
“I can work hard again from tomorrow!” she added.
It’s not the first time that Takaichi has projected an image as a tireless worker. When Takaichi was elected president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party in October, she proudly announced, “I will abandon the phrase ‘work-life balance.’ I will work, work, work, work and keep on working.” She also called on LDP members to “work like workhorses.”
In November, she told an Upper House Budget Committee session that she typically gets around two hours of sleep a night. She also faced backlash after summoning aides to the Prime Minister’s official residence at 3 a.m. that month to prepare for a Budget Committee session.
Japan’s first female Prime Minister
largely positive approval ratings
, although her popularity dipped this month. The country is contending with a rising cost-of-living and a weak yen that hit a 40-year low this week.
Takaichi’s post may be an attempt to “persuade” the public that she is working very hard, says Li Hao, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo and a research fellow at the Japan Institute of International Affairs. It’s also “a kind of appeal” to the conservative voting bloc, he adds, showing that she is maintaining both her political work and traditional gender roles of women in the home.
But some say it’s a message that increasingly falls flat with young Japanese voters.
from the Japanese public, some of whom argue that Takaichi is upholding an unhealthy and outdated standard in a country that has traditionally had a
. Opposition lawmakers have also criticized Takaichi’s post, suggesting that she is overemphasizing quantity over quality of work.
“Resting is part of her job,” Yuichiro Tamaki, leader of the Democratic Party for the People, said at a press conference on Tuesday. “I wonder, would it be better to focus her valuable time on decisions and tasks that only the prime minister can handle?”
Takaichi’s allies have been quick to defend her. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Takaichi understands the importance of work-life balance, and that she is making decisions that are “for the good of the nation and the people.”
Still, observers say the episode highlights a widening gap between traditional and evolving attitudes towards work in Japan.
Takaichi’s view is “increasingly an outlier,” says James Brown, professor of international affairs and political science at Temple University, Japan. “She represents this traditional view that many, including in her own party, have moved away from.”
Gradual shift away from overwork
The backlash suggests that the public’s “value system is changing,” Li says. “More and more people understand that the burden of housekeeping should not only be on women’s shoulders.” Some opposition lawmakers
it’s important as Prime Minister to delegate her work, and Li notes that housework could even be delegated to a housekeeping service.
Many online have also expressed skepticism towards Takaichi’s claims of sleeping less than three hours a night, Li tells TIME. But even taken at face value, many appear upset at the disregard of rest. Some critics have said that her lack of sleep could impact her health or
affect the quality of her policymaking
Still, Brown cautions that the social media backlash isn’t representative of the entire Japanese population, as older and more conservative people are more likely to hold onto traditional expectations around work and gender. In May, Yawata Mayor Shoko Kawata
faced public criticism
after announcing that she would become the first sitting Japanese mayor to take maternity leave.
Instead, the Takaichi criticism reflects a gradual shift in attitudes towards work and gender roles, especially among younger Japanese, Brown says. Brown tells TIME, anecdotally, that he has seen more young fathers take on tasks traditionally done by mothers, like pushing strollers or carrying their children around.
Traditionally, Japan’s work culture has rewarded self-sacrifice and long hours at work, at times at the expense of employee health and family life.
“The traditional expectation was that a big part of your identity is as an employee,” Brown says. Employees often felt a “duty to the organization that goes beyond your contract,” he adds.
“If there’s work that needs to be done, it doesn’t matter if your contract says you’re supposed to be out the door at 5 p.m., you continue on until it gets done,” Brown says. “Your boss is not just someone whom you report to; it’s someone you have significant obligations to.”
Typical expectations would include staying in the office until the boss leaves first. Traditional attitudes towards work also discouraged employees from taking holidays, as holidays were seen as a kind of privilege rather than a contractual right, Brown adds.
Public officials are traditionally equally expected to dedicate long hours and put their public duty over their personal lives.
However, several high-profile
“karoshi” or “overwork death” cases
have prompted labor reforms aimed at bettering work-life balance. In 2015, 24-year-old Matsuri Takahashi died by suicide after working more than 100 hours of overtime per month at the advertising company Dentsu.
Several Japanese bureaucrats also died by suicide in recent years in cases linked to overwork.
Attitudes are gradually shifting alongside policy changes around work regulations, Brown says. After Takahashi’s death, the government stepped up its Work Style Reform agenda, including capping overtime at 45 hours per month. More employers also understand that holidays
help employee productivity
, Brown says. Parts of the LDP have also shown more concern toward the issue given Japan’s ageing population and low birth rate, as young women may be less inclined to have children if they are expected to work long hours and to manage housework alone.

from the National Defense Counsel for Victims of Karoshi, which is led by Hiroshi Kawahito, an attorney who represented Takahashi’s family.
“Most people are regarding [Takaichi’s post] not as a role model,” Brown says, “but rather as an outdated and very negative way of addressing work-life balance.”

title: The right-wing boomers protesting data centers have a lot in common with the left
summary: On a gray, humid Saturday morning in central Florida, a little under a dozen people gathered outside the Spring Hill Branch Library to protest the construction of a hyperscale data center in their community. There was no immediate threat - the Hernando County commission had unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on such developments in June […]
full_text:
On a gray, humid Saturday morning in central Florida, a little under a dozen people gathered outside the Spring Hill Branch Library to protest the construction of a hyperscale data center in their community. There was no immediate threat — the Hernando County commission had unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on such developments in June — but the organizers weren’t satisfied. A temporary pause wouldn’t be enough. They wanted a ban.
The right-wing boomers protesting data centers have a lot in common with the left
The conservative backlash is about jobs, the environment, quality of life — and China.
The right-wing boomers protesting data centers have a lot in common with the left
The conservative backlash is about jobs, the environment, quality of life — and China.
“We are going to fight, fight, fight,” said a 71-year-old woman named Carol, who was manning a table with flyers and a petition the group, No Data Centers Hernando County, planned on presenting to the local government. Carol, a retired country music radio host, is a staunch conservative and a proud Floridian. The American flag on her red T-shirt was made up of little sea turtles. A white visor, bedazzled with red and blue rhinestones, shielded her face from the late-morning sun. “How would you like to have one by you? If you live within 15 minutes of a data center, night and day you’re going to hear: EEEEENNNNNNHHHHHHHHHHHH.”
Beyond the noise pollution and environmental destruction — the frequencies emitted by data centers, she told me, hurt bees and other pollinators — Carol was concerned about the social cost of mass AI adoption. She told me about a woman she knows who cut off all her friends because “ChatGPT told her to.”
“She consults with ChatGPT what time she should wake up in the morning, what time she should go to bed, who should be her friends,” she said.
The small rally in this Tampa exurb was one of nearly 150 protests affiliated with Humans First, which describes itself as a “conservative social movement that is dedicated to ensuring that the future of AI is in the hands of everyday people.”
Carol recited a litany of harms caused by data centers, some of them more dubious than others. Cows raised on ranches near data centers, she claimed, were giving birth to stillborn calves. Hyperscale facilities source their parts from China, an American adversary, threatening national security. “We’re setting ourselves up,” Carol told me. “Do you know what’s in those chips?” I told her I do not. “We’re blindly trusting the Chinese?” she continued, incredulous. “To give us chips?” (Conservative proponents of data centers, meanwhile, claim China is funding anti-AI campaigns in the United States.)
Communities across the country are pushing back on data center construction. A recent Gallup poll found that seven in 10 Americans oppose construction of data centers in their area. Nearly two-thirds of Republicans and 75 percent of Democrats surveyed said they objected to local data center construction. Americans may be more polarized than ever, but the backlash to data centers is bipartisan — and it may cement new, surprising political alliances. The concerns animating the conservative backlash are similar to those motivating liberals: the environmental costs of data center construction and maintenance; the ethical problems of AI, ranging from its use for mass government surveillance to its effects on users’ mental health; and fears that having a data center nearby will hurt their quality of life. But there are also some partisan anxieties behind the right-wing data center backlash, namely the threat of Chinese infiltration of US technology.
Humans First, a once-bipartisan offshoot of the Center for AI Safety, is helmed by Amy Kremer, a longtime conservative organizer who is arguably one of the people most responsible for the Republican Party’s populist turn. Kremer was an early leader of the Tea Party and a cofounder of both Women for Trump and Women for America First, the latter of which hosted the Stop the Steal rally in Washington, DC, that devolved into the January 6th riots. (Kremer was not among those who stormed the Capitol.)
Despite Humans First’s partisan bent and Kremer’s political bona fides, the concerns at the Humans First-affiliated rally in Hernando County were decidedly local. A firefighter running for agricultural commissioner dropped off signs; a Republican candidate for county commissioner stopped by. The gathering ended with a lecture from a land use expert who explained how to change zoning codes to prevent the construction of hyperscale data centers — those that occupy at least 10,000 square feet and have a minimum energy draw of 100 megawatts. Before the lecture, No Data Center Hernando County member Kim Belanger, who works in IT, pulled up an article on data centers from the progressive website More Perfect Union. Even though the room skewed conservative, the article, she said, was “very informative.”
Patti Zirhut, the organizer, told me that she found out about Humans First on Facebook. Participating in the national day of action was a no-brainer, since Zirhut and her friends had already started No Data Center Hernando County to thwart data center construction in their community.
“I am very conservative and I don’t believe in all the stuff that Democrats believe in at all,” Zirhut told me. But she also feels betrayed by Florida’s Republican leadership. She was a big fan of Gov. Ron DeSantis — at first. But in his second term, she said, “he’s been nothing but pro-development, just inviting everybody here, tearing up our state.”
DeSantis has positioned himself as an AI skeptic and signed a law in May requiring hyperscale data centers to cover their own utility costs and letting local governments set water use regulations for data center projects. But his administration has given data center developers millions in tax breaks, according to the Tampa Bay Times. The governor reportedly pushed to alter the state’s tax exemption for data centers so it would only apply to hyperscale facilities.
As they tabled outside the library, Zirhut and her friends discussed DeSantis’ prospective successors. “This is probably the most important governor’s race of your lifetime,” Belanger told me. She’s also concerned about a DeSantis-backed ballot amendment that would eliminate property taxes for most homeowners, since it would deprive county governments of much-needed revenue — potentially making developments like data centers more enticing.
“If Byron Donalds wins the primary, I’m voting Democrat. I will not vote for him.”
Zirhut and the others were disappointed by Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican front-runner in the gubernatorial primary and a vocal supporter of data center construction in Florida. “I just don’t understand why Trump would back him,” one of them said.
“I’m not anti-data center. I’m pro having a plan,” Donalds said in February. “Data centers are going to be a function of American life going forward.” Donalds has said he wants to bring more outside investment to Florida — a comment that has since come back to haunt him. “My vision is to make Florida the financial capital of the world,” he said at an event hosted by The Hill.
“That is not what we want here in Florida at all,” Zirhut told me.
Donalds’ support for data centers is now costing him supporters from his own party. Recent attack ads have focused on the support he’s received from the tech industry, including more than $5 million in donations from Leading the Future, a $100 million pro-AI super PAC whose funders include Andreessen Horowitz and Joe Lonsdale of Palantir, according to the Tallahassee Democrat, as well as $500,000 from American Mission, which is itself funded by Leading the Future. Donalds appears to be staking out a middle ground between the industry that supports him and the voters whose support he needs to win the primary. title: Google hit with $1 billion fine for breaking EU antitrust rules
summary: The European Union has fined Google's parent company Alphabet €890 million (about $1 billion) for two separate violations of the bloc's Digital Markets Act (DMA). One penalty is for giving its own products preferential treatment in search results, while the other is for blocking Android developers from sending users to alternate payment options. A €460 […]
full_text:
The European Union has fined Google’s parent company Alphabet €890 million (about $1 billion) for two separate violations of the bloc’s Digital Markets Act (DMA). One penalty is for giving its own products preferential treatment in search results, while the other is for blocking Android developers from sending users to alternate payment options.
Google hit with $1 billion fine for breaking EU antitrust rules
Google is required to change its policies for both Search and the Play Store.
Google is required to change its policies for both Search and the Play Store.
A €460 million fine has been issued to Google for giving preferential treatment to its own Shopping, Hotels, and Flights services in Google Search results. The second €430 million penalty is for Play Store rules preventing developers from freely steering consumers to alternative payment systems that may be cheaper.
As part of the ruling, Google has been given 60 days to make changes to its policies, or face further periodic penalty payments. In Search, it will be required to treat third-party services “in a fair and non-discriminatory manner,” while it will also have to allow Android developers to freely promote offers to users both inside and outside the Play Store.
The fines were announced by the European Commission today, more than two years after it first opened a non-compliance investigation, and follow a preliminary ruling in March 2025. Google was given time to address the EU’s concerns, with an extension granted in May 2026 after the Commission said a previous proposal from the company “is simply not strong enough.”
Google made and tested several changes to its Search services in an effort to comply with DMA rules, such as removing the Google Flights widget for Search users in the EU, and boosting links to third-party comparison websites via an updated search result layout. The company has previously fired back at the EU’s criticisms of its Search product, telling Reuters in May that changes it made in an attempt to achieve DMA compliance “represent the biggest downgrade in the product’s history, creating a second-rate experience for Europeans to the benefit of a few self-interested complainants.” These changes were made prior to Google introducing a reimagined AI-focused search box at its I/O conference in May, however, which has also rolled out to EU users.
Google was previously hit with a €2.42 billion fine in 2017 for a similar breach of the EU’s antitrust rules, after it was charged with giving its comparison shopping service an illegal advantage over competitors.
As for the Play Store, Google has repeatedly objected to rules requiring it to open up app distribution on Android systems, claiming doing so poses a security risk to users. The company repeated these objections following the Commission’s preliminary finding and in a blog posted last year, said “the DMA is making it difficult to protect users from scams and malicious links on Android by forcing us to remove our legitimate safeguards that protect users’ security and safety.” Nevertheless, it updated certain terms following consultations with the European Commission and other experts, revising fees and restrictions on Android developers. The Commission says these changes “constitute good progress towards compliance.”
Google is also facing a reckoning over its Play Store policies in the US after Fortnite publisher Epic Games successfully sued the company over in-app purchase fees, and it will be forced to carry rival Android app stores inside its own.
The DMA targets the largest “gatekeeper” companies that provide core digital services in Europe, and requires them to act in a fair manner — not stifle competition by abusing their market dominance. The maximum fine for breaching DMA rules is 10 percent of the company’s global annual revenue — $40 billion in Google’s case, based on the $400 billion it reported for 2025.
“The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine,” says Teresa Ribera, the Commission’s executive vice-president for clean, just and competitive transition. “And European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut. This is the promise of the DMA, protecting fairness, choice and innovation in digital markets for the benefit of all European citizens.”
