title: Chris Mason: What Burnham's first week in power tells us about his agenda
summary: The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, the BBC's political editor Chris Mason explains.
full_text:
Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
- Published
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.
It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.
The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.
There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.
On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.
Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No10 North in Manchester.
Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".
His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.
It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.
So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?
The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.
With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.
He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.
Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.
She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.
"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."
Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.
But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.
Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.
Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again.
Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.
He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?
It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.
And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".
What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.
Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.
Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?
And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?
Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?
Given the intended long term home of No10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032, this is a live question.
- Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM - Published2 days ago
 
- Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North - Published23 hours ago
 
- Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? - Published3 days ago
 
And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.
Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".
It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?
The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.
It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.
His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.
Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.
Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."
Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

title: Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over nightclub attack in London
summary: Assault and grievous bodily harm (GBH) charges against the US singer and a co-defendant are dropped.
full_text:
Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over nightclub attack
- Published
US singer Chris Brown has pleaded guilty to affray over an attack in a London nightclub in 2023.
The 37-year-old star had been due to face a trial in October on more serious charges, which he denied - attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, causing actual bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, namely a tequila bottle.
However, those charges have now been dropped. He will be sentenced for affray in October.
His co-defendant, 40-year-old Omololu Akinlolu, a rapper who performs under the name Hoody Baby, also pleaded guilty to affray - which is defined as using or threatening violence towards someone and making them fear for their safety.
The attack happened at the Tape venue, a private members' club in Mayfair, on 19 February 2023.
Brown entered his plea at Southwark Crown Court on Friday in a hearing that took less than five minutes.
Judge Tony Baumgartner scheduled the sentencing hearing for the affray charges for both men for 26 October, 2026.
Brown is known for tracks including Loyal, Look At Me Now and With You.
He waved at fans as he arrived at court, flanked by security guards while wearing a beige suit and baseball cap.
Fans played Brown's music, held up signs and shouted his name, with the PA news agency reporting that one said: "I love you Chris".
At earlier hearings, he was ordered to pay a £5m security fee as part of his bail conditions, which also allowed him to go on a world tour as long as he surrendered his passport on arrival in each country.
Last summer, the performer joked on-stage about his "nice" time in jail in Manchester as he kicked off his tour at the city's Co-Op Live arena.
"Thank you for coming and supporting me," he said to fans in Manchester. "And thank you to the jail," he joked, referring to a spell in custody after his arrest. "It was really nice."

title: Four men dead after car crashes into lamp-post
summary: The car left the road and crashed on Liverpool Road in Huyton just before 02:00 BST.
full_text:
Four men dead after car crashes into lamp-post
- Published
Four men have died after a car hit a lamp-post on Merseyside, police have said.
The car left the road and crashed on Liverpool Road, Huyton, just before 02:00 BST.
The men, two aged 23, and two others, aged 24 and 26 died at the scene, Merseyside Police said.
A 27-year-old man who was a passenger inside the vehicle has been taken to hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.
The black Seat Cupra had been travelling from Liverpool towards Knowsley before it came off the road and hit the lamp-post.
Eleven roads in the area have been closed, including Liverpool Road and East Prescot Road, from the junction of Princess Drive and Finch Lane while police carry out their investigations.
The closures are likely to remain in place over the weekend, the force said.
Supt Paul Holden of Merseyside Police said the force's priority was to get answers for the families of those affected over how the crash occurred.
He said: "We know this happened very early this morning, but if anyone saw what happened or were driving through the area just before the incident occurred then please get in touch."
'Exploded'
Corina Thomas who lives nearby told BBC Radio Merseyside said she heard helicopters in the area "at about two in the morning".
"It woke me up and it was hovering here, and just coming round and checking the area."
Tyler Montague who lives on Dinas Lane with Ayla Kirchner, said it sounded like a "petrol tank had exploded" and they could smell fuel in their house.
Kirchner said she heard what she described as "rubble falling" after a big explosion at about 02:00 BST.
"We came out to see what happened, and a lot had happened."
They said they saw half a car, and another half of a car scattered down the road, but did not see where the accident had happened.

title: Jurgen Klopp starts his new job as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit
summary: Jurgen Klopp starts his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.
full_text:
Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit
- Published
Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.
The former Liverpool manager was appointed on a four-year deal on Friday to replace Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned this month after Germany's shock World Cup defeat by Paraguay in the last 32.
But the 59-year-old issued a warning to the media as he held his first news conference as Germany's head coach.
"If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace then I'll be gone, I'll just turn away," Klopp said.
"I know there are other countries where national team coaches are treated even worse.
"I'm not doing this job for myself, I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel.
"I love this job but I am always ready to call it quits if need be."
Both Nagelsmann and England boss Tuchel came under media scrutiny after their exits from the World Cup, with Tuchel criticised for his defensive tactics and substitutions as the Three Lions let slip a 1-0 lead in their semi-final defeat by Argentina.
Klopp's appointment was widely expected for weeks and his contract will see him through to the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco.
"Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team," he added.
"This is the pinnacle, the absolutely high point of my footballing career as coach. I will give everything I have got."
- Messiah or papering over cracks? Klopp must sway doubters in Germany rebuild - Published4 hours ago
 
It is Klopp's first coaching job since ending his nine-year tenure at Liverpool in the summer of 2024 after "running out of energy".
He said he feels "the time is right" for his return to coaching and to take up his first role in international football.
"Over the last few days it was almost like a movie happening to myself," he said.
"I have always surmised the job of Germany head coach is really big but now it is really dawning on me what being the national team head coach is all about.
"For many, many years it was unimaginable for me to assume this position. As the years went by, it became more or less evident that sooner or later I would be asked to do this job.
"Now I think the time is right."
His first game in charge will be against the Netherlands in a Nations League group-stage match on 24 September.
- Published30 June

title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges – how much do they add up to?
summary: BBC Verify has looked at how much Burnham's new spending commitments cost and how they will be paid for
full_text:
Andy Burnham's first week pledges – how much do they add up to?
- Published
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.
He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.
BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about £1.5bn.
Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.
End rough sleeping in England
Cost: £340m over five years, funded
In his speech outside Downing Street , externalon Monday, Burnham said his "first instruction" would be "to end rough sleeping in our country".
The most recent official data , externalsuggests that there were around 4,800 people sleeping rough on a single night in England in 2025, up from 1,800 in 2010.
The government announced that Burnham's "instruction" would be delivered by £340m of spending, which it said would support at least 3,000 people over a five year period.
It said this money would come from existing "uncommitted" budgets in the housing department.
This means that the funding has been made available by the Treasury to the department but had not yet been assigned to a specific project.
VAT cut from electricity bills
Cost: £850m, unfunded
On Tuesday morning the Treasury announced that it would cut, external VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, knocking an estimated £45 from the typical household's annual bill from the autumn.
It said this would cost £850m in 2026-27 - to be funded by scrapping the previous government's digital ID scheme, which had been estimated to cost £1.8bn over the next three years.
However, the Office for Budget Responsibility, the official spending watchdog, made clear in the last budget that the digital ID scheme was itself "unfunded" , externalat that stage.
That implies that while scrapping the digital ID scheme will reduce a spending pressure on the government it will not, in itself, pay for the VAT cut.
That tax cut will have to be funded in the next budget, either by tax rises or specific spending cuts elsewhere.
- Five headaches Andy Burnham will have to deal with as PM - Published7 days ago
 
- Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high - Published2 days ago
 
- Can Andy Burnham solve the housing crisis? - Published16 July
 
£2 cap on bus fares
Cost: £500m, funded
On Wednesday, the government announced it would reduce the cap on bus fares, external in England from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027, though this does not include London.
It estimated this cap would cost the Department for Transport more than £500m.
It said most of this would be found by replacing grants for international climate projects with loans. This would save the government money because the loans would be expected to be paid back in full, plus interest, freeing up funds to pay for the bus cap policy.
But there are still uncertainties with this approach, said Max Warner from the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
"It's not clear how much we would expect to be paid back nor what the interest rates will be," he said.
Cut in business rates for pubs
Cost: £100m, funded
On Thursday the government announced it would cut business rates for pubs, external, clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April 2027, saving a typical pub £1,100.
It estimated that this tax cut would cost the Treasury around £100m a year.
The government claimed it would be "fully funded" but did not provide details, beyond stating that part of the cost would be met by "reviewing reliefs for businesses that do not make a positive contribution to local communities, such as vape shops". It did not state what other kinds of businesses would fall into this category.
The Starmer government had already announced a business rates support package, external for pubs in England in January, with a 15% cut applying in the current financial year of 2026-27 and a real-terms freeze in their rates for the subsequent two years.
At that time officials estimated that package would cost £80m in its first year, and the cost in the subsequent two years would be calculated in due course by the Office for Budget Responsibility.
The latest business support for pubs from the Burnham government will come on top of that earlier support - so the Treasury will have to provide an official costing for the overall package announced since January in the Autumn budget.
No 10 North
Cost: Downing Street says no additional cost to taxpayers, funded
Burnham ended his first week as PM by working out of the new No 10 North, external, based at Heron House in Manchester's city centre, which he claimed will be the "situation room for making Britain better".
He's expected to work from there each week, with other ministers including Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster Louise Haigh, who is overseeing the department as part of her role, also working there on a regular basis.
Up to 300 civil servants are expected to join the operation by the end of the next year, but Downing Streets insists it will cost taxpayers no extra money.
"The running of No 10 North will be covered by existing Cabinet Office budgets. There is no additional cost to taxpayers", Burnham's spokesman told reporters earlier this week.
How does it all add up?
These pledges add up to about £1.5bn. That might sound like a lot, but they are small commitments relative to overall government spending, which is projected to be around £1.4 trillion (£1,400bn) this year - making it about 0.1% of total public spending.
The bigger question is whether Burnham is likely to follow through with some of the more expensive policies he's previously signalled, including reforming social care or expanding council house building.
Burnham earlier this week indicated he could raise the income tax personal allowance, which the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated could end up costing £8.5-9bn but the idea of this happening imminently was downplayed within days.
Chancellor John Healey is likely to want to take defence spending from 2.7% to 3% of GDP by 2030, given he resigned as Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the Treasury's failure to commit the money to do that. But that would cost an additional £9bn a year in today's money.
Burnham has also promised the "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period". While the details are unclear, estimates from the Centre for Cities think tanks , externalsuggest that to match the English council house building rates of the 1950s to the 1970s would require another £13bn a year in public subsidy.
Policies on this scale, which could run into several billions, would likely need to be set out in future budgets and spending reviews, alongside detailed plans about how they would be paid for.
However, Burnham has said he will stick to the government's existing fiscal rules - not borrowing for day-to-day spending and having debt fall as a share of the economy by the end of the Parliament.
That means any major new spending commitments would likely require difficult choices: such as raising taxes or cutting spending elsewhere.

title: Sarah Ferguson's charity formally closes down
summary: Sarah’s Trust had previously said it was closing “for the foreseeable future”.
full_text:
Sarah Ferguson's charity formally closes down
- Published
Sarah Ferguson's charity, Sarah's Trust, has formally wound up and is marked as "removed" on the public register of charities.
The charity said in February it would close "for the foreseeable future" days after new details emerged about the former Duchess of York's friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Among more than three million documents released by the US Department of Justice (DoJ) earlier this year were emails appearing to show Ferguson was in contact with Epstein while he was in prison for soliciting sex from a minor. Being named in the documents does not indicate wrongdoing.
The BBC has contacted Ferguson's representatives for comment on the closure of her charity.
Established in 2020, Sarah's Trust was "dedicated to supporting frontline, grassroots work to address the humanitarian and environmental crisis, the hunger crisis and issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty", according to its website.
In February, a spokesperson for the foundation said the decision to close had come after "some months" of discussion.
The foundation did not provide further details behind its decision to close at the time.
The massive drop of files by the DoJ earlier this year suggested Ferguson had been closer to Epstein than previously thought.
In the files, Ferguson was seen praising the late sex offender in 2009 as "the brother I have always wished for".
The emails also suggest she took her daughters along for lunch with him in Miami, days after his release from prison.
Ferguson's representatives have not responded to previous requests for comment on the documents.
The former duchess has already been dropped by multiple charities over her Epstein links.
In October, she lost her duchess title when her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, relinquished his Duke of York title over his links with Epstein, and she was also forced to move out of his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge, where the couple lived together, despite having divorced in 1996.

title: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting
summary: Palestinians say villagers came under attack by settlers, while the Israeli military says a Palestinian stole a weapon and opened fire on hikers.
full_text:
Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting
- Published
At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incident there in months.
There are conflicting accounts of the sequence of events in the northern village of Tal. Palestinian sources told the BBC that residents confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them when Israeli soldiers arrived and started shooting. The Palestinian foreign ministry said several other Palestinians were wounded.
Israel's military said "terrorists stole the weapon" of a security guard who was then killed before shooting at Israeli hikers who had reported coming under attack.
It later announced that an Israeli soldier had also been killed, but did not give details.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it was preparing for a major operation in the area and had cancelled soldiers' leave.
Violence has surged in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war in 2023 following the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Ahmed Zeidan, an eyewitness, told the BBC the latest incident began early in the morning, when locals in Tal rushed to confront about 30 settlers who were attacking Palestinian homes.
He said hand-to-hand clashes broke out in the presence of Israeli soldiers, before escalating into gunfire between the settlers and the young men.
A local leader of the ruling Fatah party, Essam Saifi, told Reuters news agency that settlers opened fire before Israeli forces arrived and also started shooting.
He said two brothers and two of their cousins were among those killed.
The IDF said Palestinians began the attack.
It said soldiers had gone to Tal following a report of an attack on Israeli civilians who were hiking in the area. A security guard from a nearby settler outpost went to the scene but had his weapon stolen by a Palestinian who shot and killed him, it said.
Soldiers then "eliminated the terrorist who executed the terror attack", the IDF added.
It later said a 27-year-old soldier "fell during operational activity in the area of the village".
The Israeli ambulance service said two Israelis were also wounded.
The Palestinian foreign ministry said it "condemns in the strongest terms the massacre" in Tal.
It said "the escalation of settler terrorism is a direct consequence of the protection, political backing, and complete impunity granted by the Israeli government and occupation forces".
"Official Israeli incitement continues to fuel and encourage these crimes, creating an environment in which settler violence flourishes without accountability," it added.
An AFP reporter at the site, south-west of Nablus, said roadblocks had been set up and troops were searching for additional suspects.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to act "with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them".
He called an emergency meeting with security officials, and reinforcements have been sent to the area, close to the settlement of Havat Gilad.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
In that period, 1,114 Palestinians have been killed there, the vast majority by the IDF, the UN says. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers.
The UN says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.

title: Ten killed in Russian attack near Kyiv
summary: A rescue operation is under way following a deadly Russian missile strike just outside of the Ukrainian capital
full_text:
Ten killed in Russian attack near Kyiv
- Published
At least 16 people have been killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight, with 10 dead in ballistic missile strikes just outside Kyiv, according to a national official.
Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed about 100 people had been injured in Kyiv, where emergency services are still at the scene, with five other people killed in the eastern city of Sloviansk.
Meanwhile, an overnight Ukrainian strike killed six people and wounded 26 near the Russian city of Kirov, more than 1,000 km (600 miles) behind the front line.
Ukraine also attacked the warehouses of Wildberries - Russia's biggest online retailer - in St Petersburg and the surrounding area, setting off huge fires.
In the attacks near Kyiv, Russia also appeared to have targeted Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, aka Flash, and Lyuba Shypovych, who has been involved in developing technology for the Ukrainian army.
Following the incident, both took to social media to confirm they were OK.
Ukrainian air force spokesman Yuri Ihnat told Ukrainian TV the attack involved three ballistic missiles, only one of which was intercepted.
The attack took place in the middle of the day at a training ground not far from Kyiv where a military exhibition was being held and representatives of Ukraine's defence industry were present.
This is at least the third time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 when an exhibition of this kind has been hit.
There's widespread outrage that public event of this kind was being held at all and had, apparently, been widely advertised.
President Zelensky said the incident was being investigated, while Ukraine's prosecutor general said efforts were under way to establish who decided to hold the event and what safety measures were in place.
In Ukraine's attacks on Russia, drones have now hit Wildberries warehouses across Russia three times in six days, with Friday's attacks targeting a facility near Saint Petersburg.
In Ukraine's first attack on Wildberries at the weekend, two warehouses were hit, at Elektrostal east of Moscow and in Kotovsk in the Tambov region, some 400km (250 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Seven workers on a nightshift were killed in Kotovsk and one was fatally wounded at Elektrostal. Dozens more were injured and goods worth an estimated at £750m ($1bn) were destroyed.
The attacks on the retailer have dealt a blow to a large number of small and medium-sized businesses within Russia.
In separate strikes, President Zelensky said the attack on Kirov also targeted "one of the most important military facilities" in Kirov, which "supplies components for aircraft and missile equipment" used in strikes against Ukraine.
After months of drone attacks on oil depots and refineries, Kyiv says it is now targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.
Meanwhile, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said a Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a Russian drone breaching the country's airspace on Friday.
The Romanian authorities had earlier issued alerts across several eastern and south-eastern counties.

title: Meta glasses banned by Comic-Con promoter after 'secret filming'
summary: A number of guests said they would be reluctant to appear at conventions again after cases of recordings taking place without their knowledge.
full_text:
Meta glasses banned by Comic-Con promoter after 'secret filming'
- Published
The promoter behind some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK has banned Meta glasses from its events to stop "secret filming" of guests and attendees.
Monopoly Events said a number of guests had told the company they would be reluctant to appear at Comic-Con shows again after cases of recordings taking place without their knowledge.
The ban is applicable to Meta glasses and any other "wearable recording devices".
Attendees caught using the devices will be asked to leave the convention, but some fans on social media warned the move could negatively affect disabled attendees.
Devices like Meta glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, with small speakers in the arms.
Wearers can record video or take a photo by touching the frame - usually activating a light on the glasses in the process.
In a social media statement, Monopoly Events said: "After a consultation period we can no longer permit the wearing of any recording device at our events.
"The vast majority of the talent and agents at our events felt that these were a violation of their privacy and were damaging and spoiling the interactions at the tables. Several expressed concerns that they might not continue to attend in-person events if they were being recorded in secret.
"We had similar feedback from event attendees, many of whom are not comfortable with the knowledge that other convention goers might be filming them without consent.
"Anyone seen using one of these devices might be asked to leave the event and forfeit any unfulfilled autographs or photographs they had purchased. Please let's make these events a safe space for everyone."
Monopoly Events run scores of conventions, including Comic-Cons in Edinburgh, Aberdeen, Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham and the north east of England.
They also organise specialised events dedicated to the likes of professional wrestling, horror and anime, featuring celebrity guests from across the world.
The announcement has been met with mixed views by fans.
Some praised the decision, saying they had no desire to be "plastered all over some drab blogging YouTube page", with others saying they did not like the possibility of children being filmed by people they did not know.
One fan wrote: "It's one thing walking around with your phone, which someone could see and ask you not to film them, but your glasses aren't as obvious."
Could this affect disabled people?
However others raised concerns about the impact on disabled people. One wrote: "Have you considered how this will affect disabled people and how that affects you under the Equality Act? Many people in the blind and partially-sighted community use them to safely navigate surroundings and be able to attend the event."
There was also scepticism from some fans regarding how enforceable a ban would actually be.
Female attendees at comic conventions have previously spoken out about suffering harassment and unwanted attention from other people while there.
Earlier this week the ferry operator CalMac paused bridge visits on its vessels after a passenger used "smart glasses" to film without permission.
The man was caught filming passengers and crew using Meta glasses.

title: Indian student protests: What’s next after Modi’s promise on exam leaks?
summary: Leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) insist on the removal of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
full_text:
Indian student protests: What’s next after Modi’s promise on exam leaks?
Leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) insist on the removal of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Late on Thursday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised stern action against perpetrators of examination paper leaks that have snowballed into the biggest protest movement against his government in its third term.
Modi pledged to set up fast-track courts to punish those involved in the leaks, addressing students in an Instagram-style phone recording. This was his first spoken response to the youth-led protests that have exploded across the country, with their epicentre in the heart of the capital, New Delhi.
The same night, Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk, a supporter of the students, called off a 26-day hunger strike aimed at pressuring the government to respond to their demands.
However, the student activists have said that they would continue with the agitation until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan steps down.
We break down the latest protests that have not only roiled New Delhi, but also spread to other cities including Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna, and look at what’s next.
What is the protest about?
The protests have been organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical online movement formed in May that has evolved into a national platform demanding structural education reforms and Pradhan’s resignation over a series of leaks of examination papers.
The protests came after recent scandals pertaining to examination paper leaks, technical faults and cancelled tests triggered outrage.
The main protest site is Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, a historic 18th‑century astronomical observatory, close to Parliament Street.
Demonstrators have also occupied parts of Parliament Street since Monday, with many demonstrators camping on the key thoroughfare that connects Parliament House to Connaught Place, the Indian capital’s central commercial square.
The Jantar Mantar site has seen bouts of unrest and violence this week. On Monday, the protests escalated after police fired tear gas and baton-charged demonstrators as they tried to march to parliament.
Rights groups Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have condemned the Indian government over “excessive use of force” by the police and suspension of mobile internet services at Jantar Mantar.
The CJP’s demands include Pradhan’s immediate resignation, the dropping of cases against peaceful demonstrators and 10 million rupees ($104,000) in financial assistance for each of the families of more than 20 students who have died by suicide since recent exam cancellations.
Sonam Wangchuk calls off his hunger strike
Indian activist Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike, also demanding the resignation of Pradhan.
In a post on X late on Thursday night, Wangchuk, 59, said he ended his fast after “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country”.
Wangchuk’s fast was broken in the presence of Indian Health Minister JP Nadda and the junior Atomic Energy Minister Jitendra Singh, who offered Wangchuk his first sip to end the protest.
“The government is positive on not registering cases against those protesting peacefully at Jantar Mantar in Delhi, and those participating in the march to the Parliament on July 20, 2026,” Nadda said, according to the social media platforms of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Nadda added: “The government has already assured threadbare discussions to find solutions to paper leaks and educational reforms for exams in the Parliament. Besides, the government is also positively considering suitable compensation for the suicide victims of recent NEET paper leaks.”
The National Eligibility cum Entrance Test or NEET is a national examination for entry into medical schools. It is taken by more than two million students each year, but examination papers have leaked thrice in the past five years — including this year.
What have Modi and other leaders said?
Hours after Wangchuk ended his hunger strike, two senior government ministers and two leaders of the CJP met for talks.
The meeting raised hopes that the sides could be moving towards a breakthrough in the crisis in which tens of thousands of angry youth are demanding Pradhan’s resignation as a measure of accountability from the government over paper leaks.
“Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!” Modi wrote on X on Thursday.
“We have decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks. … Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared.”
What have the students said?
On Thursday, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation announced that 16 Metro stations in New Delhi would be closed until further notice.
In response to this, the CJP’s founding president, Abhijeet Dipke, wrote in an X post: “Modi is ready to shut down all of Delhi, but not sack Dharmendra Pradhan.”
Dipke made a series of posts on X on Friday emphasising the demand for Pradan’s removal.
CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka dismissed Modi’s judicial proposal as insufficient to address underlying systemic failures.
“The announcement of fast-track courts is not a real solution. It is merely a distraction,” Ranka said in a statement at Jantar Mantar. “Paper leaks are not happening because India lacked fast-track courts. They are happening because Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has been completely incompetent.”
What’s next?
After the meeting on Friday, CJP’s leaders said the government asked to be given until Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for Pradhan to resign.
A senior Indian government minister said on Thursday that the government was always open to talks, for however long it would take, and that it would not “stand on prestige”.

title: US summons Malaysia envoy over Israel policy
summary: Malaysia does not have any diplomatic ties with Israel and has long maintained its support for the Palestinian cause.
full_text:
US summons Malaysia envoy over Israel policy
Malaysia does not have any diplomatic ties with Israel and has rooted its stance within the Palestinian cause.
The US Department of State has summoned Malaysia’s ambassador to the United States over his country’s longstanding policy on Israel, state news agency Bernama reported.
Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Thursday night that Ambassador Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob told the US State Department that Malaysia’s policy on not recognising the state of Israel was not new.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Four Palestinians killed as Israeli settlers raid occupied West Bank town
- list 2 of 4China’s Xi Jinping launches new AI alliance: What is it?
- list 3 of 4How have countries around the world responded to the US-Israel war on Iran?
- list 4 of 4Southeast Asia’s homegrown artists are knocking K-pop off its pedestal
“It has always been Malaysia’s policy. Our immigration policy does not recognise the State of Israel or the Zionist regime. This has long been our position,” Bernama cited Hasan as saying.
“There was an individual with dual citizenship, the US and Israel, who entered Malaysia using his US passport. However, subsequent checks revealed that he also held Israeli citizenship, and we asked him to leave.”
Malaysia does not have any diplomatic ties with Israel and has emphasised its support for the Palestinian cause and against Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
But the incident was triggered after the Network School, a “digital nomad” community founded in the country by US investor Balaji Srinivasan, came under fire when social media users claimed it included participants from Israel.
A probe into Network School followed, and while Malay authorities found that all participants had valid travel documents, the school was still shut down on Tuesday.
Later, eight US congressmen sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressing outrage over Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s plan to track any Israeli citizens in the country and immediately deport them.
However, on Wednesday, Ibrahim reiterated that Malaysia would continue to bar Israeli citizens from entering the country despite objections raised by the members of the US Congress.
Anwar added that Malaysia was guided by its commitment to defending the rights of the Palestinian people and opposing the “oppression, aggression and continued killing” of Palestinians in Gaza, Bernama reported.
“That will not deter us. They may issue threats, but I will firmly defend the rights of the Malaysian people and uphold the government’s decision to continue prohibiting the entry of any Israeli national into Malaysia,” he added.
The US congressmen urged the State Department to review economic and security ties with Kuala Lumpur.
They called for funding to the International Military Education and Training programme, which provides professional US training for Malaysian military personnel, to be cut off unless the decision is reversed within 15 days.

title: Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigns
summary: Shahabuddin, 76, cited health reasons for leaving two years before his five-year term was meant to expire.
full_text:
Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigns
Shahabuddin, 76, cited health reasons for leaving two years before his five year term was meant to expire.
Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin has resigned two years ahead the end of his full five-year term.
Shahabuddin, 76, cited health reasons for his decision on Friday. The move comes amid rising demand from opposition parties for him to step down.
“Recent medical examinations have diagnosed me with a condition known as Autonomic Neuropathy. Due to this condition, I occasionally experience momentary loss of consciousness,” Shahabuddin said in a statement released by his press secretary.
The speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad, the national parliament, will perform the duties of the president until a new one is elected, the statement added.
A new president must be elected within the next 90 days, according to the constitution.
“I am seriously ill … therefore, I am unable to perform my duty of the constitutional post,” Shahabuddin said in a letter to Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed on Friday.
Ahmed said he accepted his resignation, the Associated Press reported.
“According to the Constitution, the president’s resignation becomes effective upon submission of a signed letter to the speaker,” the president’s spokesperson, Sarwar Alam, said.
The resignation comes amid media reports that Shahabuddin spoke on the phone with ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who is living in India, during a visit by the former to the UK for medical treatment in May this year, according to Dhaka-based The Daily Star.
Shahabuddin has refuted the media report.
“I am suffering from various health complications,” he told The Daily Star when asked about the reason for his resignation. “I have nothing more to add at this moment.”
He had travelled to London on May 9 and returned on May 18.
Shahabuddin has been the president of the South Asian nation since April 2023. His term was meant to end in 2028.
He oversaw the country during a volatile period after Hasina was ousted in August 2024 by youth protesters and until a caretaker government was formed days later.
Hasina is currently living in exile in India’s capital, New Delhi, but is expected to return to Bangladesh in December, according to the Reuters news agency, which reported news of Shahabuddin’s expected resignation on Thursday.
His resignation leaves Hasina with no allies in high office five months before her planned return.
But as Bangladesh’s president, his role is largely ceremonial. While he is the head of state, the executive power rests with the prime minister and cabinet.

title: Spain’s De la Fuente slams Argentina’s World Cup conduct as ‘unacceptable’
summary: While Argentina faced criticism through World Cup 2026, post-final altercations are now being investigated.
full_text:
Spain’s De la Fuente slams Argentina’s World Cup conduct as ‘unacceptable’
While Argentina faced criticism throughout World Cup 2026, post-final altercations are now being investigated by FIFA disciplinary prosecutor.
As FIFA investigates Argentina’s conduct after the World Cup final, Spain coach Luis de la Fuente has described the incidents as “intolerable and unacceptable.”
FIFA asked one of its disciplinary prosecutors on Monday to report back on testy on-field confrontations after Spain’s 1-0 win in extra time on Sunday to dethrone the defending champion.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Germany appoint Klopp as ex-Liverpool coach sought to lift World Cup blues
- list 2 of 4Australia World Cup star Volpato faces speeding, cocaine charges
- list 3 of 4FIFA ‘destroying football’ for the World Cup, says Spanish football chief
- list 4 of 4What next after World Cup? Club football transfer window takes centre stage
Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes physically tangled with Spain players Eric Garcia and Gavi, and Spain captain Rodri was hit in the stomach as he ran past Argentina defender Nahuel Molina.
“It cannot be allowed,” De la Fuente told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Thursday, adding he did not see the incidents at the time while “celebrating with other people”.
“In any case, I find it intolerable and unacceptable from players of that calibre, whom I had been praising in the days before and who have a magnificent coach,” the Spain coach said.
FIFA has given no details of the remit for its investigator, or if witness statements could be sought from Spain players and staff.
Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala apologised on Wednesday for his confrontation with Dani Olmo, which he described as a shove and not a punch.
De la Fuente praised his players in the TVE interview for how they handled the situation at MetLife Stadium.
“I want to highlight our behaviour in the face of that kind of aggression and provocation,” the coach said. “Our players always kept their composure and behaved like true professionals.”
The Spain squad stood in a guard of honour for Argentina players walking to the podium to get their medals from US President Donald Trump. Minutes later, when Rodri lifted the trophy, most of the Argentina squad turned their backs on the ceremonial moment.
FIFA disciplinary rules allow a special prosecutor to “request the opening of disciplinary proceedings and propose that disciplinary measures be imposed on member associations, clubs and individuals”.
FIFA gave no timetable for any cases, and it is unclear when any potential bans for Argentina players would apply as the team does not have competitive games scheduled in the coming months.

title: At least 11 killed in Ukraine as Moscow and Kyiv continue to trade attacks
summary: Six people also killed in Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Kirov, and Wildberries warehouses hit again.
full_text:
At least 11 killed in Ukraine as Moscow and Kyiv continue to trade attacks
Six people also killed in Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Kirov, and Wildberries warehouses hit again.
At least 11 people have been killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, while Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s Kirov region killed six others, officials on both sides of the conflict said.
A Russian missile attack killed six people and wounded “dozens” in the Kyiv region on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3What are the security implications of the US-Saudi nuclear deal?
- list 3 of 3Has Russia helped Iran target CIA sites in the Gulf?
“A rescue operation is currently underway in the Kyiv region following a Russian missile strike … tragically, six people were killed,” Zelenskyy said.
Earlier, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the city and called on residents to stay in shelters as air defence systems were operating.
Separately, Vadym Filashkin, the governor of the city of Sloviansk, said five people were killed and nine others injured after Moscow dropped two aviation bombs on the city.
“Russians attack our cities daily – and for the second day in a row, their attacks have led to numerous casualties in Sloviansk,” Filashkin said. “I call on everyone who is still near the front line: evacuate.”
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said: “It’s quite irregular for Russian attacks, especially ballistic ones, to take place during the daytime hours so this marks something new.”
Meanwhile in southern Mykolaiv region, a Russian drone attack on port infrastructure damaged two civilian vessels, acting regional governor Heorhii Reshetilov said on Telegram. No one was injured in that attack.
Russia also claimed to have taken control of the villages of Zakharivka and Ivashchyne in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, and also said Russia had struck 27 vessels used by the Ukrainian military in the past week.
“We’re getting reports from certain Telegram channels and officials that another massive attack could be imminent in the coming several days,” MacAlpine said. “These ballistic threats on cities around Ukraine have been escalating over the summer and show no signs of slowing down.”
Ukrainian attacks on Russia
At the same time, in Russia’s Kirov region on Friday, six people were killed and 26 injured in a Ukrainian missile attack on a factory, the regional governor, Alexander Sokolov, said.
A warehouse for the Russian e-commerce giant, Wildberries, was also hit as Kyiv continues its attacks on the retail giant’s warehouses.
Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim said the latest attacks had targeted warehouses in Saint Petersburg, in the surrounding Leningrad region and in Simferopol, the main city in Crimea.
“We managed to save some of the premises and goods. I would like to thank our staff, our heroes – a swift evacuation was carried out at all warehouses,” Kim said in a statement.
“According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties.
“All of our efforts are now focused on redistributing goods across our warehouses to ensure more efficient stock turnover and the economic stability of our partners,” she said.
Still, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed the strikes and said in a post on social media that the operation against Russian logistics “remains under way”, calling the attacks “successful”.
As of Friday’s attack, Wildberries warehouses have been targeted four times since last weekend.
According to the Russian Ministry of Defence, it shot down 571 Ukrainian drones overnight, in one of the largest barrages sent by Kyiv as it increases long-range strikes.
The ministry said that the attacks had targeted more than a dozen Russian regions and the annexed Crimea region.

title: Is the US-Saudi nuclear deal on, or in limbo?
summary: Trump's last-minute demand for Saudi normalisation with Israel has complicated the already sensitive deal.
full_text:
Is the US-Saudi nuclear deal on, or in limbo?
Trump’s last-minute demand for Saudi normalisation with Israel has complicated the already sensitive deal.
The United States and Saudi Arabia have agreed a nuclear cooperation deal to establish a civilian nuclear programme in the kingdom.
This would allow Riyadh to harness nuclear power to generate electricity, allowing it to export more of its natural resources and deal with an expansion of energy-hungry data centres.
But a day later, US President Donald Trump announced a new condition on social media, saying that Saudi Arabia must first normalise relations with Israel.
So, what is the status of the US-Saudi nuclear deal and what does this mean for Riyadh?
What is Saudi Arabia’s position on normalisation with Israel?
Saudi Arabia has long insisted it will not establish formal relations with Israel until there is a clear path for Palestinian statehood, which Israel’s current government staunchly opposes.
Riyadh has yet to respond to Trump’s latest statement tying the nuclear deal to normalisation.
What do we know about the deal?
The new nuclear deal is expected to last 30 years, transferring US technology and expertise to the kingdom to help meet the kingdom’s growing energy needs.
While its full text has not been released, some details have emerged through media reports. The Wall Street Journal reported that one provision would potentially see US companies build a uranium enrichment facility in the kingdom, though Trump in his social media post suggested Saudi-based enrichment may be off the table.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the agreement bolsters “efforts to diversify energy sources, advance cutting-edge technologies, and expand opportunities for cooperation and investment in ways that serve the mutual interests of the two friendly countries”.
Trump said the deal “pertains only to nonmilitary use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have”.
What’s next for the deal?
The deal must first be submitted to the US Congress for review.
However, Trump’s new condition of Saudi-Israeli normalisation has complicated the path forward, leaving it unclear when, or whether, the deal will be put before Congress.
Saudi Arabia has long insisted that it will not recognise Israel without a pathway for the creation of an independent Palestinian state, something that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ruled out.
Steven Cook, a senior fellow for Middle East and Africa studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote that Trump’s demand has left the deal “in a state of diplomatic suspension”.
“This situation is likely to cause tension between Washington, which treats the president’s social media posts as official policy, and Riyadh, which has committed to a diplomatic agreement,” wrote Cook in a post published by the Council on Foreign Relations.
If the deal fails, Saudi Arabia could change course and look to cooperate with other countries with nuclear industries, such as China, Russia, South Korea, the UAE or France.
What are other challenges for Saudi Arabia’s nuclear plans?
Even if the deal with the US goes through, Saudi Arabia faces several major hurdles to building a full civilian nuclear industry, including securing nuclear fuel.
While the deal reportedly opens the door to a Saudi-based uranium enrichment facility that would be run by US companies, with sensitive technology tightly controlled, it would only be allowed based on the determination of a joint two-year study by Saudi Arabia and the US.
Otherwise, Saudi Arabia would have to import commercial-grade low-enriched uranium from abroad, as other countries with nuclear energy programmes do.
The deal also raises questions about international oversight. Saudi Arabia has reportedly not agreed to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) “additional protocol” document, which allows for expanded monitoring, inspections and verification. But it has agreed to a bilateral safeguards agreement with the US, according to reports.
The IAEA has said it is awaiting a request from Washington and Riyadh to implement verification measures under the agreement before seeking authorisation from its board of governors. The deal will next go to Congress for review, as it will need approval from the legislative branch of the US government.

title: Gangs taking villages on Brazil-Peru border ‘hostage’, say Indigenous leaders
summary:
Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon

Indigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.

Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Indigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.
Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.
The Asháninka people, who have faced threats from intruders for decades because of their efforts to protect the forest and eject narco smugglers, say this is the worst danger they have faced, prompting an emergency delegation to Brasília this week to appeal for support from the government of the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
“Either the state steps in to provide protection, or communities will start organising to defend themselves – and that would be disastrous,” said Francisco Piyãko, the general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, who is part of the delegation. “We are not facing a local conflict. We are facing the expansion of transnational criminal networks into Indigenous territories that currently represent one of the last barriers against the illegal occupation of this region of the Amazon.”
The petition of the Asháninka people comes amid growing concerns about the nexus of drug trafficking and environmental crime, which Brazilian climate scientist Carlos Nobre has described as the greatest new threat to the Amazon Forest.
The Brazilian side of the border is in Acre state, where the forest is still relatively healthy compared with the Peruvian side, which has experienced heavy logging and violence. Acre has sometimes been a perilous area for environmental and land defenders. One of the country’s most celebrated forest campaigners, Chico Mendes, was shot dead there in 1988. After that, there was a period of relative peace in Acre, compared with other countries in the Amazon or other Brazilian states such as Pará. More recently, however, there has been a rise in tension, much of it from the outside. Isolated Indigenous communities from Peru have been increasingly crossing the border to escape confrontation with loggers and drug cartels.
Apiwtxa was the last Indigenous village visited by the British journalist Dom Phillips before he was murdered in the neighbouring Brazilian border state of Amazonas in 2022 while researching illegal extractivist activities in another area menaced by arms and drug smugglers.
According to the Asháninka petition to the Brazilian government, the most recent intrusion into Apiwtxa involved five heavily armed, Spanish-speaking men arriving on the evening of 6 July at the home of one of the Asháninka leaders, who was out of the village at the time. “They were clearly poised to attack with lethal intent,” said one member of the community. It was the second time in several days that masked gunmen had entered the village looking for leaders.
Frightened villagers took their children into one building for protection and notified the authorities. The army arrived at midnight, by which time the would-be assassins had disappeared back into the forest, leaving only tracks.
“For us, this was a threat unlike any other, because they came right into our home – they entered our house,” said Piyãko. “We realise that the context we’re living in now isn’t just about drug trafficking; you can see it’s a movement involving everything from wildcat mining and illegal mining to illegal logging, drug trafficking and other issues.”
The Asháninka delegation in Brasília is calling for a permanent security presence along the border to prevent the free movement of drug traffickers, illegal loggers and the illicit construction of “virus roads” that push into the forest without environmental oversight. They also want greater protection for their leaders and operations to combat organised crime in the area.
The neighbouring Peruvian department of Ucayali has the widest network of illegal roads in the Peruvian Amazon, providing transport for gangs involved in environmental crime, gold, money laundering and drugs. In the past five years, coca cultivation in Ucayali has tripled.
The Igarapé Institute, a public security thinktank, has said that organised crime – which often intersects with narcotics and illegal extraction of natural resources – needs a more robust response by governments across the region: “It is increasingly clear that the fight against organised environmental crime in the Amazon ultimately demands better intelligence and strategic prioritisation. The goal must be to strengthen Brazilian state authority to deter and repress crimes and those who commit them.”
Piyãko said this was now a matter of urgency. He added: “If the Peruvian and Brazilian governments joined forces and wanted to resolve the situation, they could. Because they have the means to combat this.”
“If the state doesn’t protect these territories, they will be dominated by this criminal system, or the people will be forced to defend themselves on their own. This could lead to very serious situations, because as the net tightens around these territories, tensions rise.”

title: Woman and man arrested in Ireland after police intercept ‘highly sophisticated’ bomb
summary:
Detectives targeting dissident republicans stopped a vehicle containing explosives near Carrickmacross

Two people have been arrested after police in Ireland targeting dissident republicans intercepted an “extremely significant” bomb that was being transported in a vehicle near the border.

Members of the Garda Síochána’s special detective unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, County Monaghan on Wednesday afternoon.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Two people have been arrested after police in Ireland targeting dissident republicans intercepted an “extremely significant” bomb that was being transported in a vehicle near the border.
Members of the Garda Síochána’s special detective unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, County Monaghan on Wednesday afternoon.
Revealing details of the interception on Friday, Garda sources said the bomb was “highly sophisticated” had been completed and was ready for use. It contained a power unit, a detonator and military grade explosives.
Security sources said the probable intended use was as an under-car explosive for an attack in Northern Ireland.
Gardaí then requested the assistance of the Irish Defence Forces EOD (explosive ordnance disposal) team, which completed an examination of the vehicle south of Carrickmacross. It is understood the device found contained suspected military grade explosives.
The vehicle’s driver, a woman in her 20s, was arrested at the scene and remained in Garda custody on Friday. Another suspect, a man in his 40s, has since been arrested and is being held at a Garda station in the Dublin area.
The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, confirmed details of the operation as he spoke to media at a Garda graduation event in County Tipperary on Friday.
“To be clear, what we found was an extremely significant seizure,” he said. “So this was an explosive device.”
Kelly added: “Any seizure of this nature is really concerning. However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday agreement, they did not put weapons and explosives [out of use], they didn’t, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning. So that is something that we continue to deal with.”
He went on to say: “There’s a small minority of these individuals, I would describe them as radicalised republicans, and this is a threat that we’re going to continue to face for some time in An Garda Síochána.
“But what I will say, certainly, it was a significant explosive device. So certainly not just the seizure of components or pieces. This was an explosive device and it would have or could have potentially caused significant damage.”
The commissioner confirmed the operation relied on intelligence. “Obviously, this was not a random stop,” Kelly said. “This is an intelligence-led operation, so we certainly do have information in relation to the individuals involved.”
A security source said that the fact a bomb of that nature had been built and transported to the border was “worrying” because of the “level of skill” involved, which required mechanical and electrical knowledge and the sourcing of explosives.
They said that “radicalisation of individuals captured by the internet” meant individuals, rather than organised networks, could be at the centre of the incident.
Pipe bombs that have been used in the recent past to target members of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) can be “relatively crude” but this bomb appeared to be different and would have needed an initiative device and a timer.
The fact that the Garda intercepted the bomb shows its intelligence gathering is working. However, the incident will fuel concerns over the level of counter-terror resourcing since the 1998 peace deal.
Kelly said: “We work very closely with our colleagues in PSNI and the intelligence services in the UK to deal with this threat. But I want to commend the members of An Garda Síochána who are involved in this operation.
“A female (aged in her 20s), the driver of the vehicle, arrested and detained pursuant to Section 30 of the Offences Against the State Act, 1939 (as amended), continues to be detained.
“A male (aged in his 40s) has since been arrested in connection with the investigation, and is detained pursuant to Section 30 of the Offences Against the State Act, 1939 (as amended), at a Garda station in the Dublin region.”

title: Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visit
summary:
Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble.

In an interview with Loomer, the Ukraine president said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble.
In an interview with Loomer, the Ukraine president said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress.
Loomer interviewed Zelenskyy in the garden of the presidential palace in Kyiv – a remarkable move for the online provocateur who has previously minimised Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and amplified Kremlin propaganda to her nearly 2 million followers on social media.
This week, however, she performed a stunning about-turn. “Just experienced my first air raid in Ukraine. Sirens blaring. This is every day for every Ukrainian,” Loomer wrote on X. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. We need to have moral clarity.”
Loomer posted a photo of her one-on-one meeting with Zelenskyy as well as a clip from her interview with him in which she asks about his infamous confrontation last year with Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, in the Oval Office. No questions were off limits, she said.
In the clip, Zelenskyy said his relationship with Trump had significantly improved and describes their brief conversation in the Vatican in April 2025 as a “historic moment”.
“We changed the relations during 15, 20 minutes,” Zelenskyy added.
Writing on Truth Social, Trump praised Loomer’s interview, calling it “Very good!!!!”. Commentators in Kyiv said Trump’s message confirmed his administration’s once negative view of Kyiv was changing at a time when Ukrainian long-range drones are pummelling Russia.
Russia has continued to strike Ukraine, with a daytime ballistic missile attack on Friday killing six people in the Kyiv region and injuring dozens more. Another five people died when an air bomb hit the eastern city of Sloviansk.
Expressing support for US sanctions on Russia, Loomer said the Kremlin was a close ally of the Iranian regime. “Russia is funding Iran and providing them with explosives to murder US soldiers as Iran has called for President Trump’s assassination,” she wrote, arguing: “The United States needs to break Russia’s economy until they submit to peace.”
Loomer’s comments are a reversal for a woman who has spent years criticising US support for Ukraine’s defence, declaring it “a country full of
 Nazi apologists” – a claim used by Russia to justify its full-scale 2022 invasion – and “led by a Jihadi apologist”.
Her scepticism towards Kyiv has been shared by other major conservative
 influencers, including Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host. The issue became a big point of contention between more traditional Republicans, such as Mike Pence, a former vice-president, and Trump’s Maga base.
Anton Gerashchenko, a popular blogger and former Ukrainian government adviser, described Loomer’s interview with Zelenskyy as “important and necessary”. “It records a public break with Russian narratives and propaganda by part of the Maga movement. We are seeing a shift in rhetoric regarding Russian aggression,” he said.
“It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are,” Zelenskyy’s office added this week. “It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens. Thank you, Laura.”
Loomer also visited the Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of the country’s most significant religious landmarks, which came under Russian drone attack in June.
In a video recorded from inside the church, she accused Vladimir Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as a pro-Christian nation – a perspective many US evangelicals appear to share. “I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ,” Loomer remarked.
Loomer also met Ukraine’s chief rabbi, Moshe Reuven Azman, and toured a branch of McDonald’s hit repeatedly by Russian missiles. Loomer ordered a cheeseburger and sat demonstratively on an outside table in front of a wrecked building, in Kyiv’s much-bombed Lukianivka district.
On Friday, the chief rabbi wrote: “I had the honour of welcoming @LauraLoomer – whose views have a significant influence on the U.S. audience and who is well known for her close ties to President Donald Trump – to the Central Synagogue of Ukraine.
“The conversation was candid. I told her the truth about this terrible war – about the daily Russian shelling, the children and civilians killed, the destroyed cities and villages, and the pain that Ukrainian families endure every day.”
